timestamp, resource, lifecycle, and case-id aliases, and optionally keeps one
occurrence per case. The standalone CLI, `POST /api/attribute-statistics`,
strict request parser, and typed frontend API share the
`ATTRIBUTE_STATISTICS` envelope; focused tests cover both scopes, deduplication,
missing values, custom attributes, and count validation.

Attribute-distribution evidence: `discover_event_distribution` implements the
calendar buckets `DAYS_MONTH`, `MONTHS`, `YEARS`, `HOURS`, `DAYS_WEEK`, and
`WEEKS`, fills the complete fixed ranges where applicable, and validates every
configured timestamp. The standalone CLI, `POST /api/attribute-distribution`,
strict request parser, and typed frontend API share the
`ATTRIBUTE_DISTRIBUTION` envelope; focused tests cover custom timestamp keys,
zero-filled bins, ISO week boundaries, and malformed values.

Attribute-KDE evidence: `discover_attribute_kde` follows the reference
DataFrame statistics (`get_kde_numeric_attribute`, `get_kde_date_attribute`:
reference grids, single-value spikes and the sorted points-to-sample pick;
fuzzed against pm4py on 2026-11-05, see "Fresh sweep: attribute KDE,
performance spectrum and XES float text"). The standalone CLI, `POST /api/attribute-kde`,
strict request parser, and typed frontend API share the `ATTRIBUTE_KDE`
envelope; focused tests cover numeric/date parsing, finite non-negative
density validation, deterministic grids, sampling bounds, and malformed
requests.

Boundary-activity evidence: `discover_boundary_activities` exposes START, END,
and BOTH counts for configurable activity-like event attributes, skipping empty
traces and missing boundary values. The standalone CLI,
`POST /api/boundary-activities`, strict request parser, and typed frontend API
share the `BOUNDARY_ACTIVITIES` envelope; focused tests cover all variants,
custom keys, empty traces, and malformed counts.

Variant-statistics evidence: `discover_variant_statistics` groups complete trace
activity sequences, sorts them by descending frequency and deterministic
sequence order (descending activity tuple: the order of the reference's
`get_variants_sorted_by_count`, not the first-appearance order of
`get_variants_as_tuples`), and emits normalized stochastic-language probabilities with an
optional result bound. The standalone CLI, `POST /api/variant-statistics`,
strict request parser, and typed frontend API share the `VARIANT_STATISTICS`
envelope; focused tests cover empty traces, custom keys, limits, and probability
validation.

Case-statistics evidence: `discover_case_statistics` emits one deterministic
timing row per non-empty trace, supports case-id and timestamp attributes,
ascending/descending case-id/start/end/duration sorting, result limits, and
optional business-hour elapsed durations. The standalone CLI,
`POST /api/case-statistics`, strict request parser, and typed frontend API share
the `CASE_STATISTICS` envelope; focused Release tests cover sorting, limits,
business-hour slots, invalid timestamps, and malformed response values.

Rework evidence: `discover_rework` exposes the activity variant (number of
cases containing repeated activity occurrences) and the cases variant (total
events and total repeated-activity count per case), with custom activity and
case-id attributes. The standalone CLI, `POST /api/rework`, strict request
parser, and typed frontend API share the `REWORK` envelope; focused tests
cover duplicate activities, empty cases, custom keys, and count validation.

Chaotic-activity evidence: `discover_chaotic_activities` implements the single
entropy-based ranking variant with configurable activity attribute, smoothing,
and bounded input size. It returns deterministic frequency, entropy,
entropy-gain, and combined-score metrics. The standalone CLI,
`POST /api/chaotic-activities`, strict request parser, and typed frontend API
share the `CHAOTIC_ACTIVITIES` envelope; focused tests cover repeated runs,
custom attributes, empty input, invalid bounds, and malformed response data.

OCEL statistics evidence: `object_type_activities` returns deterministic
lexical object-type keys with deduplicated related activities, while
`objects_ot_count` returns deterministic event/object-type maps and counts
duplicate relation rows independently. Activity associations support none,
start, and end relation prefilters; object-type-dependent associations and
event-edge metrics include event couples, unique objects, event-object triples,
and sorted elapsed-time or configured business-hour samples. The native APIs, `minera_ocel --statistics`,
multipart local `POST /api/ocel/statistics`, and typed frontend
request/response guard share the `OCEL_STATISTICS` JSON envelope. Empty logs,
unreferenced objects, duplicate relations, invalid identifiers, prefilters,
repeated activity labels, and malformed timestamps are covered by focused
Release tests.

Process-cube evidence: `process_cube` validates rectangular typed feature tables,
supports exact numeric and categorical columns, composite categorical dimensions,
prefix indicator columns, mixed numeric/prefix Cartesian cells, explicit or
equal-width numeric edges, and mean, sum, min, max, count, median, first, and last
aggregation. The deterministic
`PROCESS_CUBE` JSON envelope is shared by the native tests, the headless
`minera_process_cube` CLI, local `POST /api/process-cube`, and typed frontend
request/response guards. Explicit bins are sorted and deduplicated, configured
cells retain their case-id sets, composite names accept escaped comma-delimited
CLI/query lists, and malformed JSON, ragged rows, mixed scalar types, non-finite
values, and unsafe division limits are rejected at the boundary.

Activity-split evidence: the native log filter splits every non-empty trace at
one or more anchor activities, preserves event/trace/log attributes, rewrites
case ids with a deterministic separator and zero-based suffix, and supports
both anchor-in-new-case (`this`) and following-event-in-new-case (`next`)
modes. Strict request parsing, CLI flags, local mine-server fields, and the
frontend form/serializer expose the same operation; focused tests cover
multiple anchors, no-match traces, attributes, case-id synchronization, and
invalid options.

Attribute-value repetition domain banks (2026-10-24): the pandas and Polars
companions are complete over disjoint seeded banks covering NumPy
weak-scalar/array comparisons, categoricals, zoned datetimes, the Polars
literal model, optimizer bound folding and diagnostics. The log module is
complete too (2026-10-25): the XES importer records the public shape of
`<list>`/`<container>` elements (wrapper around None, None, or not stored),
and a fifth disjoint bank of 18,557 calls with such elements passes. See
[attribute-repetition-domain-parity.md](attribute-repetition-domain-parity.md).

Attribute-value repetition evidence: a whole-trace filter counts matching
activity, resource, lifecycle, timestamp, or generic event-attribute values
and keeps traces inside an inclusive repetition range. The native operation
preserves log and trace attributes, validates min/max ordering, and is wired
through strict mine-request fields, CLI flags, local-server form handling, and
frontend serialization/controls. Focused tests cover default and zero ranges,
generic attributes, missing values, aliases, and invalid bounds.

Case-grouping evidence: consecutive activity runs support first/last event
retention, while same-timestamp groups support first, last, and deterministic
lexical activity concatenation. First-class and generic event keys, custom
timestamp keys, and a configurable non-empty concatenation separator are
validated. Native, request, CLI, local-server, and frontend surfaces share
the same grouping options and focused edge-case coverage.

DFG interchange evidence: the strict classic text parser and deterministic
writer now have public input and output adapters. `minera_dfg INPUT.dfg` reads,
validates, and normalizes a document (or writes it to an explicit output path),
and its `--clean-noise` mode applies the native noise-threshold edge filter
with optional most-common-path overrides. The cached `GET /api/dfg` route
accepts the same cleaning query, while local `POST /api/dfg` accepts raw DFG
text and returns the canonical document. The typed frontend `importDfg` and
`fetchDfg` helpers expose the corresponding validation and export paths.

DFG conversion evidence: both classic DFG-to-workflow-net constructions are
available as deterministic native APIs: activity-defines-place emits one
visible transition per start or edge occurrence, while invisibles-no-duplicates
emits one visible transition per activity and silent edge routing. Boundary
activities are inferred when omitted, artificial names are collision-checked,
and the standalone DFG CLI, local conversion endpoint, and typed frontend
adapter share a validated `DFG_CONVERSION` envelope.

Genetic-matrix conversion evidence: the public causal-matrix model retains the
stable activity table plus every alternative/concurrent input and output group.
The `TO_PETRI_NET` construction normalizes set-like groups, builds complete
shared places where both matrix projections agree, and replaces incomplete or
transitively conflicting regions with silent routing. Disconnected and cyclic
boundaries receive deterministic workflow entry/exit routing, and the returned
initial/final markings target the unique source and sink. Classic genetic
discovery exposes its winning normalized matrix and reconstructs its final net
through this public converter. Native JSON, `--genetic-matrix-convert`, cached
`/api/genetic-matrix-convert`, and typed frontend adapters expose the explicit
variant. Focused fixtures cover sequence, parallel split/join, fallback routing,
normalization, malformed references, deterministic transport, replay, and
mined-matrix reconstruction.

Traditional log-conversion evidence: the native conversion API exposes the six
selectors for EventLog identity, flattened event streams, typed rectangular
tables, attributed directed graphs, one trace per control-flow variant, and all
frequency-preserving variant copies. Stream conversion preserves event order,
typed scalar fields, first-event trace attributes, configurable case-field
prefixing, and stable trace-index glue when case attributes are disabled. Graph
conversion supports optional directly-follows edges, selected case/event
attribute nodes, simple directed-edge overwrite semantics, and explicit node
and edge limits. Variant projections use deterministic descending frequency
and sequence ordering, support an optional variant limit, and can return
output-trace indexes. Strict request
parsing, the standalone export CLI, cached local-server route, deterministic
JSON, and typed frontend request/response guards share the same option family;
focused tests cover round trips, sparse table cells, graph bounds and edge
orientation, selector validation, variant multiplicity, and malformed payloads.

Trie conversion evidence: prefix tries now convert to deterministic workflow
nets with shared prefix places, silent terminal-prefix exits, and explicit
source/sink places. Every root branch is converted; the reference converter
keeps only the root's first child (a declared difference, see "Trie, OCEL
readers, passed time and eventually-follows (2026-11-03)"). The export CLI's
`--trie-to-petri` mode, cached local `/api/trie-to-petri` route, and typed

## Delivery order

1. Stabilize the native semantic contracts and differential fixture format.
2. Finish remaining traditional discovery and conformance variants.
3. Add OCEL 2 data, I/O, discovery, conformance, filtering, and visualization.
4. Add declarative/POWL/transition-system and advanced simulation families.
5. Add streaming, privacy, clustering/drift, transformations, and ML.
6. Add optional renderers, connectors, querying, and LLM integrations.

Every completed row must include focused unit tests. Algorithms with
non-unique models compare canonical behavior (language, footprints, fitness,
or replay) rather than generated node identifiers. Floating metrics use an
explicit tolerance. Performance claims require representative logs and may
not replace semantic tests.

## Petri-analysis parity evidence

The native analysis surface now exposes the classic integer marking equation,
the split-aware extended marking equation, structural workflow-net validation,
and bounded soundness diagnostics, including an explicit `woflan` family
selector over the same reachability, coverability, invariant, and pair
diagnostic contract. Woflan additionally constructs the silent sink-to-source
short circuit, reports its transition id and strong-connectivity result, and
serializes a separate short-circuit reachability projection while retaining
the original graph for completion witnesses. Woflan marking inputs follow its
single-place boundary contract. The soundness family also exposes a strict
`return_asap_when_unsound` control: a structural S-component coverage failure
returns immediately with invariant evidence, while a reachable non-final
deadlock or improper completion marking returns with the partial reachability
graph and its shortest witness. Structural pair diagnostics use a deterministic
node-split unit-capacity flow graph and report both directions whose maximum flow
exceeds one, preserving the duplicated-node coordinates in the JSON contract.
Bounded exploration also returns every shortest path to a marking that cannot
reach the final marking as `locking_scenarios`, alongside the compact first
witness and the `dead_tasks` alias for never-enabled transitions. Woflan's task
projection is derived from the short-circuited coverability graph and reports
the dead visible tasks plus the short-circuit transition itself when it is
dead (its id is `short_circuit_transition`, after the input transitions),
while the generic `dead_transitions` field retains the exact original-net
firing result. The native `not_well_handled_pairs` name is
serialized alongside the historical `handled_pairs` compatibility field.
Every pair coordinate also has a stable place/transition input-output label for
renderers.
Woflan now also exposes its `left` decision and a deterministic restricted
coverability-tree projection. The tree preserves one first-seen edge per
transition at each node, accelerates only against ancestors using the omega
marker `-1`, reports explicit state-cap exhaustion, and is kept separate from
the minimal coverability graph. These artifacts are available in the native
result, JSON envelope, and frontend response guard for both bounded and
unbounded workflow diagnostics.
The extended equation keeps trace events in
ordered segments, assigns each event to a synchronous or log move, constrains
segment-boundary markings, and solves the resulting integer state equation with
caller-controlled costs and deterministic node limits. Recovery separately
attempts a concrete firing sequence, so an incidence-feasible result that is
not realizable is reported rather than silently presented as a replay.

Strict request parsing covers family, miner, trace index, markings, transition
cost vectors, split indices, split limits, solver limits, bootstrap, and
diagnostic settings. The CLI emits a focused JSON document for any discovered
or imported Petri model, the local server exposes `POST /api/petri-analysis`,
and the frontend conformance tab provides the same controls with generation-safe
on-demand caching. Native, request, frontend, CLI, and hidden-server smoke
tests cover the current vertical. Karp–Miller-style coverability witnesses now
include a compact omega-marking graph, while bounded exploration exposes its
deterministic reachability markings and transition edges. Positive invariant
diagnostics expose the original, uniform-support, and relative-weight families
separately, including coverage gaps for each family and for S-components. These
projections are serialized by the CLI, local server, and frontend contracts.
Uniform-support vectors are retained only after rechecking the incidence
equation; when a single weighted certificate is not uniform, a bounded binary
invariant search recovers valid combinations of weighted rays. Weighted vectors
remain valid after normalization, and S-components retain the complete support
of each valid state-machine invariant (including a disconnected support when
the invariant itself spans it). The search has a shared caller-configurable
budget and reports exhaustion explicitly; an exhausted search never drives the
Woflan structural branch decision. A focused registered contract suite now
separately exercises the classic and extended equations, workflow validation,
the full Woflan pipeline, all three marking graphs, graph edges, structural
pairs, invariant bases, S-components, and uniform and weighted invariants. Exact
selector and module proofs tie those cases to distinct public declarations.

## Conformance parity bank evidence

Petri-net alignments, DFG alignment and forward/backwards token replay are
bound to black-box captures of the pinned reference in
`src/backend/tests/test_conformance_parity_contracts.cpp`
(`minera_conformance_parity_contracts_tests`). Three banks feed the generated
fixture `conformance_parity_reference_cases.inc`:

- `docs/reference-2.7.22-conformance-parity-bank.json.gz`: 60 seeded random
  process trees converted to workflow nets, 9 traces each.
- `docs/reference-2.7.22-conformance-parity-nets-bank.json.gz`: 40 nets
  discovered by the alpha, heuristics and ILP miners plus nets with duplicate
  labels (frozen in `docs/reference-2.7.22-conformance-parity-nets.json.gz`),
  with random model, sync and trace cost functions.
- `docs/reference-2.7.22-conformance-parity-external-bank.json.gz`: the
  weighted silent-pump and noisy heuristics nets from the quality-metrics
  fixtures (`docs/reference-2.7.22-conformance-parity-external-nets.json.gz`).

Each bank merges independent captures under different `PYTHONHASHSEED` values
and PNML element orders (`scripts/capture-conformance-parity-reference.py`,
`scripts/merge-conformance-parity-reference.py`,
`scripts/generate-conformance-parity-fixture.py`). The contract:

- Where every run agreed, native must equal the reference; where runs differ,
  native must equal one of the observed values. Calls the reference could not
  finish within the capture time limit bind nothing.
- Petri enum variants bind cost, best-worst cost and fitness exactly, plus no
  alignment (unreachable final marking) and the discounted variant's error.
  The returned alignment must be a valid run of the net whose cost under the
  variant's cost function is the reported cost. Which of several equally
  cheap alignments is returned is a reference tie choice that changes with
  hash seed and PNML order, so it is not bound.
- The reference discounted A* is not always optimal. Where native differs
  from it, native must be no more expensive than every observed run.
- Generators bind the cost and require every reference alignment to be among
  the native ones, unless either side stopped at its 64-alignment limit.
- DFG classic binds the alignment, cost and visited-state count.
- Replay binds every per-trace row (fitness, activated transitions, problems,
  enabled transitions, reached marking, token counters) for the default
  options and each public option toggled.
- Decomposed `RECOMPOS_MAXIMAL` (each trace aligned in a log of its own, as
  captured) binds the best-worst cost of every row exactly and pins the cost
  and fitness agreement as a tally: 770 of 809 rows equal, 39 differ. The
  reference composition is not reproducible from its outputs: it reports some
  moves twice or drops them, and a few costs have no optimal explanation (on
  `->('h', X('f','c'), tau)` the trace [f,h] costs one log move while
  [f,h,f], [c,h,f] and [f,h,c] cost nothing).

Reference semantics established black-box and implemented natively:

- fitness = 1 - floor(cost / 10000) / floor(bwc / 10000), 0 when the
  denominator is 0. bwc is the variant's cost for the empty trace plus 10000
  per event, or plus the supplied trace costs. Less-memory adds only supplied
  trace costs; discounted reports the sum of supplied trace costs (0 by
  default) and always searches with unit costs discounted by 2^-index,
  ignoring cost functions.
- Less-memory charges a silent move 1 only when a visible transition whose
  label occurs in the trace has all of its input places among the silent
  transition's input places (an empty preset included), else 0. Its generator
  charges 1. Both run a pruned Dijkstra over (marking, trace position) that
  skips a marking already closed at the same or a later position; this is not
  always optimal and the reference reports the pruned cost.
- Every variant except less-memory and its generator reads each ordinary arc
  as weight 1. Less-memory honors arc weights, which lets silent cycles pump
  tokens; the reference then usually does not terminate.
- Unreachable final marking: enum variants return no alignment, generators an
  empty list, discounted raises.
- Backwards replay ignores `walk_through_hidden_trans`.
- Forward replay with `consider_activities_not_in_model_in_fitness=True`
  keeps one flag for the whole log: variants replay by descending frequency,
  ties by descending activity tuple, and once a variant holding an activity
  outside the model was replayed, it and every later variant are unfit. Trace
  fitness values are unchanged. This matched all 390 bound rows.
- Decomposed `RECOMPOS_MAXIMAL` uses the maximal decomposition (places joined
  through silent and duplicate-label transitions). A component that sees no
  event of the trace is not aligned, events of activities outside the net are
  dropped, and components that disagree on a border activity are merged and
  realigned. bwc is 10000 per event plus the visible moves of the cheapest
  model run (silent moves excluded; log moves only when the final marking is
  unreachable). The cost includes silent moves (1 each) but fitness does not:
  fitness = 1 - (cost - silent moves) / bwc, unclamped. The empty trace has
  cost 0 and no bwc or fitness. A component without any alignment empties
  the result (cost 0).
- Replay orders routing candidates and the enabled-transition worklist by
  transition and place name, so callers must pass the PNML ids as
  `TokenReplayOptions::transition_names` and `place_names`.

Reference nondeterminism: equal-cost alignment choice, generator enumeration
order, search counters, discounted costs on some nets and forward-replay
silent routing on nets with competing silent paths (25 of 30 rows of the
noisy heuristics net vary with the hash seed) all change between runs.

Open divergences:

- Decomposed `RECOMPOS_MAXIMAL` differs on 39 of 809 rows in cost and
  fitness (above).

### Process-tree alignments

`src/backend/tests/test_process_tree_alignment_parity_contracts.cpp`
(`minera_process_tree_alignment_parity_contracts_tests`) binds all four
variants to the 60 trees of the first bank plus
`docs/reference-2.7.22-process-tree-alignment-bank.json.gz` (400 seeded random
trees, seed 99, 9 traces each, three hash seeds; captured with
`--families tree:` and generated into `process_tree_alignment_parity_cases.inc`
by `scripts/generate-process-tree-alignment-parity-fixture.py`). Each of the
4140 rows per variant is classified as equal (cost and fitness), native
cheaper, native costlier, or equal cost with another fitness, and the tallies
are pinned:

| Variant | Equal | Native cheaper | Native costlier | Fitness only |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `SEARCH_GRAPH_PT` | 4112 | 28 | 0 | 0 |
| `DYNAMIC_PROGRAMMING` | 4126 | 11 | 3 | 0 |
| `MILP` | 4116 | 10 | 0 | 14 |
| `APPROXIMATED_ORIGINAL` | 3976 | 164 | 0 | 0 |

Reference behaviour found by probing and now implemented:

- Fitness is `1 - cost / (len + floor)` without clamping (it can be negative).
  The floor is the variant's own empty-trace cost, except for
  `APPROXIMATED_ORIGINAL`, whose floor reads n-ary operators as right-nested
  binary ones: 10000 per visible leaf, 1 per tau leaf, 2 per binary operator,
  a loop running its body once, an XOR taking its cheapest child at that
  child's depth (this matches all 4140 rows).
- `SEARCH_GRAPH_PT` alignments list each executed tau leaf as a silent model
  move. Native alignments are checked to replay the trace and to be a word of
  the tree with its tau leaves at the reported cost.
- `DYNAMIC_PROGRAMMING` loops: an empty segment skips the loop at no cost; any
  other segment is an optional leading redo, the body, (redo, body) rounds
  whose redo consumes at least one event, and an optional extra body.

Remaining divergences, all where the reference is not cost-optimal or
inconsistent: the search-graph search prunes some optimal paths (sync moves
taken first, nested loops behind a silent redo); the DP reuses a cached loop
iteration for a reordered segment; MILP gives the empty trace a positive cost
on root loops with a tau body and uses it as the fitness floor; the
approximated variant splits traces over subtrees by its activity-set
heuristic, while native splits optimally. Reference alignments of the DP,
MILP and approximated variants omit silent and some model moves and are not
bound by these tallies (all four variants are matched by the reference ports
below).

### Search-graph variant, replay semantics and frequency annotation

`include/minera/process_tree_search_graph_reference.hpp`
(`reference_search_graph_align_variant`, `reference_search_graph_alignments`,
`ProcessTreeReplaySemantics`, `reference_search_graph_frequency_annotation`)
ports `algo.conformance.alignments.process_tree.variants.search_graph_pt` and
its helpers `util.search_graph_pt_replay_semantics` and
`util.search_graph_pt_frequency_annotation`. The bank
`docs/process-tree-search-graph-bank.txt.gz`
(`scripts/capture-process-tree-search-graph-bank.py`, 1,200 seeded trees,
four hash seeds that must agree) records 60,000 calls from random walks over
the replay states (every predicate, vertex move, `transform_tree` and
shortest path), 7,200 `align_variant` runs (six traces per tree, with the
leaves handed over as a preorder list), 3,072 public `apply` traces on trees
without repeated labels, and 400 public searches with their search-state
chains and the annotation the reference wrote.
`minera_process_tree_search_graph_parity_tests` matches every replay path and
state, every cost, alignment and fitness, and every annotation.

Reference behaviour found by probing (the header lists the full rules):

- Process trees compare structurally, so a sequence child's position is its
  first equal sibling's: in `->('a', 'a')` the second `a` can be enabled as
  soon as the sequence opens, while `shortest_path_to_enable` closes the
  earlier siblings by real position first.
- Closing a choice with no child started runs the first child whose own
  closing opens the fewest visible leaves (tau children win).
- Enabling a closed node resets the nearest enclosing loop whose redo is not
  that closed node; when that loop is not open, opening it is the whole reset.
- `apply` hands `align_variant` a frozenset of `(id(leaf), leaf)`, so with
  repeated labels the order in which candidate leaves are tried, and with it
  tie choices and sometimes the cost, follows object addresses. Given a fixed
  order the search is deterministic, and the native search takes the leaves
  in preorder; with one leaf per label the order cannot matter.
- The search is a heapq best-first search over (cost, trace index, vertex
  states), ties going to the higher index, that tries synchronous moves first:
  a log move is only added when the event has no candidate leaf, a candidate
  cannot be enabled, or an enabling path does more than enable the leaf
  through sequence, parallel and choice bookkeeping. A cheaper duplicate
  takes over an existing state's cost, parent and leaves but keeps its path,
  and descendants' costs drop with it. This pruning is why the search is not
  always cost-optimal (the 28 rows above).
- Alignments are rebuilt from the states' opened leaves: each state's last
  leaf is the synchronous one, while the final state syncs the last leaf
  labelled like the trace's last event and only adds that event as a log move
  when its cost grew by more than its leaf count, so a log move ahead of a
  final tau-only closing is dropped. The empty trace gives an empty
  alignment, its cost is the fitness floor, and fitness is
  `1 - cost / (floor + len)` (0 when that is 0).
- The annotation walks `get_bottomup_nodes`, which keeps one node per
  structural class (leaves breadth first, then parents whose children are
  all kept), so equal subtrees pool their counts onto one node and the others
  get no properties. Per alignment a node counts the ENABLED assignments of
  its class in the chain's paths, or the OPEN ones when there are none (which
  is how the root counts its openings); the root state's path is not read.
  `num_cases` counts alignments with a positive count. In 5 of the 400
  searches the reference hands a search state a path that does not replay
  from its parent state; the annotation still matches there.

The replay covers the four operators SEARCH_GRAPH_PT aligns (binary loops).
The older native `align_process_tree` keeps its optimal search for the CLI
and server; the contract tallies above still bind it.

### MILP variant

`include/minera/process_tree_milp_reference.hpp` ports
`ProcessTreeAligner` of `variants/milp` as observed from its inputs and
outputs: the flow graph built from the tree, the mixed-integer program handed
to `pm4py.util.lp.solver`, the alignment read back from a solution, and
`apply`. `scripts/capture-process-tree-milp-bank.py` captures 300 random trees
(the empty trace plus 4 random traces each, 1500 traces, hash seeds 0 to 3)
into `docs/process-tree-milp-bank.txt.gz`, and
`minera_process_tree_milp_parity_tests` checks:

- the graph (nodes with source/sink/split/join flags, inverse capacities and
  shuffle groups; edges in networkx order with labels, capacities and costs)
  exactly for all 300 trees;
- every one of the 1180 distinct programs exactly (objective, bounds,
  integrality, equality and inequality rows and right-hand sides);
- the alignment and cost extracted from the reference's own solution exactly
  (1166 solutions);
- the native solver's optimum against the reported cost within 1e-6 on 1460
  traces, with a well-formed alignment of the same length; 1392 give the same
  alignment and 68 sync other events at the same optimal cost;
- `align`'s cache (298 repeated traces need no solve), the 33 programs without
  variables (a tau root, cost None) and the 7 infeasible programs;
- `apply` on 1430 traces: costs and fitness within 1e-6, the 11 trees where
  the reference raises (a tau root, where the empty trace's None cost meets
  arithmetic), and the 3 trees whose fitness floor comes from an infeasible
  empty-trace program.

The rules are in the header comment. The native solver is a dependency-free
best-first branch and bound over a bounded primal simplex; tying every flow
of a shuffle-group row to its share of the group's binary keeps the
relaxations tight (the gap drops from about 10% to about 1%) and the bank runs
in about 14 s. Divergences: CBC reports values to about 1e-8, so costs and
fitness are bound within 1e-6; optimal ties may pick another alignment; and an
infeasible program (the empty trace on a root loop with a tau do) makes the
reference report whatever CBC left behind, where native throws. The older
native `MILP` selector keeps its exact residual search for the CLI and server.

### Approximated original variant

`include/minera/process_tree_approximated_reference.hpp` ports
`variants/approximated` (`original`, `utilities` and
`calculate_a_sa_ea_sets`) as observed from the inputs and outputs of its
helpers. `scripts/capture-process-tree-approximated-bank.py` captures 400
seeded n-ary trees (22 with a single-child operator, which the reference
rejects), each with an event log of 5 to 7 traces under one of five
(max_trace_length, max_process_tree_height) settings, into
`docs/process-tree-approximated-bank.txt.gz`: the binary tree, the sets and
heights of its nodes, and for every aligned variant each program handed to
PuLP with CBC's solution, each choice, each base alignment and each
operator's returned alignment, in call order. The base alignments break
ties by object addresses, so each case runs once, under hash seed
`index % 4`. `minera_process_tree_approximated_parity_tests` checks:

- the binary tree and all 4746 node sets and heights exactly;
- all 3133 programs exactly (objective, constant and every row in order),
  and the native optimum (an exact dynamic program over the same
  structure) against the objective of CBC's solution; CBC treats the
  objective as integral and stops short of the -1e-05 rewards for empty tau
  executions in 2 programs, where native is better by those rewards only;
- the 755 choices, and the 3888 operator returns composed from the
  reference's own child alignments, exactly;
- that each of the 5122 base alignments is optimal: the native Dijkstra
  alignment on the same bordered net has the same deviation and tau-leaf
  counts (4769 are identical);
- replaying CBC's solutions and the base alignments, apply's alignment, cost
  and fitness for all 2098 traces (158 None) exactly;
- the fully native apply: a well-formed alignment of every trace with cost
  and fitness following from it. 1733 of 1932 traces get the reference cost;
  the others take another optimal split where CBC's choice among ties is
  not reproduced, and 12 traces are None on one side only for the same
  reason (with max_process_tree_height 0 a leaf longer than
  max_trace_length gives None).

The rules are in the header comment. Divergences: ties among optimal splits
and among optimal base alignments, and CBC's integral cutoff above. The
time limits (`max_align_time`, `max_align_time_trace`) are not ported. The
older native `APPROXIMATED_ORIGINAL` selector keeps its exact residual
alignments for the CLI and server.

### Decomposed RECOMPOS_MAXIMAL

`include/minera/decomposed_reference.hpp` ports
`algo.conformance.alignments.decomposed.variants.recompos_maximal` and the
maximal decomposition it uses (`objects.petri_net.utils.decomposition`) as
observed from the inputs and outputs of their helpers.
`scripts/capture-decomposed-bank.py` converts 400 seeded process trees to
accepting Petri nets with the reference converter and captures, for an event
log of 4 to 6 traces each, into `docs/decomposed-bank.txt.gz`: the net in the
reference's place and transition iteration order, the components `decompose`

aligned variant every `align` call with its result, every
`merge_sublist_nets` call with its result and the component list handed to
`recompose_alignment`. Component alignments break ties by object addresses,
so each case runs once, under hash seed `index % 4`, with a 3 second limit.
`minera_decomposed_parity_tests` checks:

- all 765 components of the 400 nets exactly, in order, and all 190 merges;
- the best-worst cost (visible model moves of the empty trace's alignment of
  the whole net, at the same optimal cost);
- that each of the 2144 component alignments is optimal: the native Dijkstra
  alignment has the same cost (1047 are identical);
- replaying the reference's component alignments, apply makes the same
  align, merge and recompose calls in the same order (variants in order of
  first occurrence, alignments cached by component object and projected
  trace, merges by the merged transition sets) and gives the cost,
  alignment, fitness and bwc of all 1402 traces exactly;
- that apply raises for the 82 logs where the reference never returns: its
  first recomposition queue has no visited check, so it runs forever once a
  link cycle between component alignments is reachable from a component with
  an initial marking, and the native port detects exactly those cycles;
- the fully native apply: costs follow from the alignments, and 1310 of 1393
  traces get the reference cost (another optimal component alignment changes
  which border activities disagree and so the merges and the recomposition).

The rules are in the header comment, including two reference quirks: of the
visible transitions sharing a label, only the last in iteration order joins
its places, and a disagreement on an activity merges every component holding
that activity, aligned or not. The time limits and the border-agreement
threshold are left at their defaults. The older native `RECOMPOS_MAXIMAL`
selector (`align_decomposed`) keeps its own composition for the CLI and
server.

## Connector parity bank

`include/minera/connector_reference.hpp` ports `algo.connectors` as observed
from the outside with stubbed sources, returning the reference's dataframe
(columns, pandas dtypes, row labels and every value as the reference prints
it). `scripts/capture-connector-bank.py` captures
`docs/connector-bank.txt.gz`, replayed by `minera_connector_parity_tests`.

Browser history: 600 seeded Chrome History and 600 Firefox places.sqlite
databases (iterdump statements in the bank) cover urls with and without
schemes, several `//`, queries, commas, ports, user info, empty and NULL urls
and titles, NULL and out-of-range visit times (both bounds of years 1..9999),
transitions with qualifier bits, durations, dangling from_visit and url ids, a
visits table without `visit_duration`, and databases without the expected
tables. All 655 frames match exactly and the 545 raising cases raise the same
Python exception type. Rules found (header comment): Chrome resolves
`from_visit` through the urls table's ids rather than the visits'; the
activity, domain and url_wo_parameters come from the text after the last
non-overlapping `//` (so `file:///x` gives `/x` and an empty domain), with
commas removed from the activity only; per row the visit time is converted
before the url is split (and, for Chrome, before the transition is decoded),
and rows with an empty activity are dropped only after those conversions;
Firefox divides the microsecond integer by 10^6 (correctly rounded) and lets
`datetime.fromtimestamp` round half-even to microseconds.

Database connectors: 300 seeded cases each for Camunda (real
`act_hi_procinst`/`act_hi_actinst` tables in SQLite, ISO-like start times in
four shapes with NULL and invalid values), SAP accounting (BKPF/BSAD/BSAK,
with and without a schema prefix, compact `YYYYMMDD HHMMSS` stamps) and SAP
order-to-cash (whose Oracle SQL SQLite cannot run, so the cursor answers with
staged rows). The bank records the SQL text the reference issued, the rows
its cursor returned and that it closed the connection. Native issues the same
SQL text (the SAP queries with every `OWNED.` replaced by the prefix), reads
the rows as `pandas.read_sql` types them, closes the connection and formats
with the native `format_dataframe`: all 900 frames match exactly. The bank
exposed three formatter gaps, now fixed: the public parser also accepts the
compact `YYYY`, `YYYYMMDD` and `YYYYMMDD HHMMSS` shapes; date columns are
converted on the whole table before rows missing a case, activity or
timestamp are dropped (a dropped row still keeps its column text or sets its
unit); and a canonical case or activity column whose values all parse as
dates (SAP document numbers such as `0001`) is converted and then printed as
pandas prints a timestamp (`0001-01-01 00:00:00+00:00`).

GitHub: 600 seeded repositories served by a stub `requests` (zero to three
issue pages, timelines of up to five events, ISO dates in eight shapes plus a
few non-dates, null users, actors and logins, dropped keys, pull requests
with null or empty values, `committed` events without `created_at`, issues
sharing a timeline url, with and without a token, the empty token included).
Every GET is recorded with its headers; all 600 frames (3010 rows) and GET
sequences match exactly. Rules found by recording the reference's key reads
(header comment): an issue without `timeline_url` is skipped, but every other
key is read directly and any failure (a missing key, a null user, a date
dateutil rejects) ends the whole extraction, keeping the rows read so far;
an event is used only when it holds `created_at`, `event` and `actor`; the
timeline is walked from its last event (the reference reverses the list it
receives in place, so the stub serves fresh copies); the date offset is
dropped and the wall clock labelled UTC. Native accepts the ISO 8601 forms
the API writes instead of all of dateutil's grammar, a documented narrowing.

Outlook and Windows events: win32com and pythoncom are stubbed with objects
that raise AttributeError for a missing attribute (KeyError for a missing WMI
property), and 600 seeded cases per connector cover missing, None and
wrongly typed attributes, naive and aware datetimes, int, float, bool and
text minutes, meeting states, reminders on and off, senders and recipients
without Name, mail classes 43, 46 and others, and WMI times with and without
fraction and offset, overlong fractions and impossible dates. All 1214 frames
match exactly and the 586 raising cases raise the same exception type; 60
util.mail.connect cases match their COM call sequence. Rules found (header
comment): the calendar keeps an item only when its four main times and
Duration convert, and drops a cancelled or reminder row alone when its
attribute is missing (a float reminder minutes value drops it too); the
mail extractor walks sent items before the inbox and compares str(Class);
the WMI times are cut at the first '+' or '-' and parsed by time.strptime,
whose regular expression native reproduces (so "2024012030405.123" is
2024-01-20 03:04:05.123), and the first failure raises.

## LLM connector parity bank

`include/minera/llm_connector_reference.hpp` ports
`algo.querying.llm.connectors` (anthropic, openai, google) as observed with
`requests.post` stubbed: each connector builds one POST from the prompt and
parameters and reads its answer out of the response.
`scripts/capture-llm-bank.py` captures `docs/llm-connector-bank.txt.gz` (800
seeded cases per connector: urls with and without a trailing '/', urls naming
api.openai.com elsewhere, keys including None and '', thinking budgets,
use_responses_api as bools, ints and None, overriding extra payloads, images
with odd or missing extensions and missing files; responses mostly well
formed, the rest other providers' shapes, API errors, empty lists and missing
keys), replayed by `minera_llm_connector_parity_tests`. All 918 answers and
every POST (url, headers in order, payload with keys in order, timeout)
match, and the 1482 raising cases raise the same exception type (API errors
with the same message). Rules found (header comment): the media type is
"image/" plus the lowercased extension (so `.jpg` is `image/jpg`); a thinking
budget raises max_tokens by itself; OpenAI picks the Responses API by
default only when the url contains `api.openai.com`, defaults the model to
gpt-5 with an image and gpt-4.1 without, and sends max_tokens to chat
completions always with an image (16384 by default) but otherwise only when
given; answers are content[-1], output[-1].content[0],
choices[0].message.content and candidates[0].content.parts[0] by direct
indexing.

## Embedding parity bank

`include/minera/embedding_reference.hpp` ports
`algo.transformation.to_embeddings` with the sentence-transformers model as a
hook. `scripts/capture-embedding-bank.py` stubs the model with dyadic float32
vectors (md5 bytes, so every float32 sum is exact and BLAS's summation order
cannot show) and captures `docs/embedding-bank.txt.gz`: 3000 seeded calls of
embed_sentence, similarity (sentence and list targets, float32 arrays and
lists), the case and event transformers and both keep_top_k_per_similarity
functions (k of 0, 1, 2, 3, 10 and -1, own or given identifiers and
embeddings, keep_cases on and off) over small logs with repeated sentences,
duplicate event identifiers, empty logs and missing columns, every encode
call recorded. `minera_embedding_parity_tests` replays the encoder: all 2879
results and every encode call (model and sentences) match exactly, and the
121 raising cases raise the same exception type. Rules found (header
comment): single sentences are encoded as a one-element batch; the cosine
is float32 only when both vectors are float32 arrays; keep_top_k embeds the
target with the default model whatever the parameters say and ranks by
(similarity, identifier) descending, so ties go to the larger identifier;
keep_cases keeps the whole cases of the top events.

## XES importer-variant evidence

The native importer explicitly accepts `ITERPARSE`, `LINE_BY_LINE`,
`ITERPARSE_MEM_COMPRESSED`, `ITERPARSE_20`, `CHUNK_REGEX`, and `RUSTXES` (plus
their documented string aliases). These selectors share the native pull parser
with variation-specific date conversion. XML
trace and event order is retained by default. Optional timestamp sorting first
orders every trace and then orders traces by their first event, with a reverse
mode and stable ties. Empty traces are omitted only by the requested timestamp
sort, matching that transformation's result shape. `CHUNK_REGEX` ignores the
timestamp-sort request and retains input order. Sorting compares whole seconds
and fractional digits separately, preserving adjacent microseconds at distant
dates even when their double timestamps coincide. Trace caps apply in XML
order, while a scalar-attribute projection keeps selected generic keys without
discarding the case, activity, timestamp, resource, or lifecycle selectors
needed to form the native log. All selectors, the timestamp requirement,
ordering controls, trace cap, and projection are validated through the native
API, shared request parser, main CLI, cached local-server upload, and typed
frontend request builder. Positive fixtures cover all selectors, both sort
directions, document-order default, aliases, projection, and trace limiting.

Both XES exporter selectors share the same deterministic typed EventLog
contract and are available from the native API, export CLI, cached local-server
route, and frontend download controls. Binary-safe gzip output can be selected
explicitly or inferred from a `.gz` path. Import transparently recognizes gzip
headers and enforces a caller-configurable expansion limit. The native decoder
handles stored, fixed-Huffman, dynamic-Huffman, and concatenated members while
validating member checksums and sizes. Focused fixtures cover both exporter
selectors, typed metadata round trips, independently compressed dynamic-Huffman
input, corrupt trailers, expansion bounds, filename detection, and compressed
file adapters.

### XES reader rules matched to `read_xes` (review F3)

`pm4py.read_xes` uses `ITERPARSE` by default (checked with a spy across hash
seeds), so the iterparse family (`ITERPARSE`, `ITERPARSE_20`,
`ITERPARSE_MEM_COMPRESSED`) follows lxml and the iterparse converters:

- **Well-formed XML only.** A strict pull-parser mode rejects, with
  "XML is not well-formed: ... (line L, column C)": a document that ends
  inside an element (truncation on an element boundary included), a missing
  root, text or a second element after the root, mismatched end tags, bare
  `&` or `<` in an attribute value, duplicate XML attributes, undefined or
  external entities, character references and raw characters outside the XML
  Char production, malformed UTF-8 (the reader decodes UTF-8 whatever the
  declaration says, as `read_xes` passes `encoding=utf-8`), more than 256
  nested elements and attribute values over 10,000,000 bytes. Internal DTD
  entities are expanded, with an amplification cap. An XML declaration that
  does not open the document (after whitespace, a comment or another
  processing instruction) fails with "XML declaration allowed only at the
  start of the document", and a case variant such as `<?XML` with "Invalid PI
  name"; `<?xml-stylesheet` and other targets are skipped. The XES layer also
  rejects a root other than `<log>` and, with the reference's messages, a
  `<trace>` inside an open `<trace>` (also one inside an `<event>`: "file
  contains <trace> in another <trace> tag") and an `<event>` inside an open
  `<event>` ("file contains <event> in another <event> tag"); an `<event>`
  directly under `<log>` is never closed in the reference, so any later
  `<event>` fails the same way, while a trailing one is read and ignored.
  Declared residual: the reference also counts `<trace>` and `<event>` tags
  nested inside attribute elements (an `<event>` inside a trace's `<string>`
  becomes an event of that trace, a `<trace>` inside a log attribute a
  trace); Minera's attribute reader treats them as attribute children.
  The line and regex readers scan text and keep their lenient parsing.
- **Attribute-value normalization.** Literal TAB, CR, LF and CR LF in an
  attribute value become one space each; character references keep their
  character. The writer escapes TAB, CR and LF as `&#9;`, `&#13;`, `&#10;`.
- **Text XML cannot carry.** Both XES writers refuse invalid UTF-8 (WTF-8
  lone surrogates included) and code points outside the XML Char production
  (NUL, other C0 controls, U+FFFE, U+FFFF), in values, keys and metadata, with
  "XES cannot represent this text: ...". The reference ETREE writer refuses
  them too; its LINE_BY_LINE writer emits NUL and controls raw into a file
  that its own `read_xes` then rejects (declared divergence: Minera refuses
  instead, so whatever it writes reads back). Workbench routes report the
  message in `xes_error` (or the export's `*_error` field) with a null XES.
- **JSON responses are valid UTF-8.** A log can hold bytes that are not UTF-8
  (a Latin-1 CSV, which the reference's `read_csv` refuses with a decode
  error, so it shows no text for them). Every `/api` JSON body, results and
  errors alike, follows one policy (`src/backend/json_utf8.hpp`): a WTF-8
  surrogate code unit keeps its identity as a `\udXXX` escape, as Python's
  `json.dumps` writes a lone surrogate, and every other ill-formed sequence
  becomes one U+FFFD per maximal subpart, as `bytes.decode("utf-8",
  "replace")` and the browser's `TextDecoder` read it (`Pr\xfcfung` is
  `Pr\ufffdfung`, a truncated `\xe2\x82` is one U+FFFD). U+FFFD was chosen
  over a surrogateescape `\udcXX` because it is what the frontend would decode
  anyway and what the error bodies already used. The server applies it as
  the last step of every JSON response; XES, CSV and other exports keep their
  own rules (the XES writers refuse such text, see above).
- **Typed values.** `int` reads like Python `int()` (surrounding whitespace,
  single underscores between digits, Unicode decimal digits of Unicode 14),
  `float` like `float()` (`inf`/`infinity`/`nan` in any case, overflow to
  infinity), and `date` like `datetime.fromisoformat` (the OCEL K5 reader,
  shared through `src/backend/python_isoformat.hpp`), keeping the clock fields
  and attaching UTC. A value that does not convert drops that attribute, with
  its children, and keeps the event; `CHUNK_REGEX` and `LINE_BY_LINE` raise as
  the reference does. Declared divergence: an integer outside the 64-bit range,
  which Python keeps exactly, is treated like an unconvertible value (dropped
  by the iterparse family, an error for `CHUNK_REGEX` and `LINE_BY_LINE`).
- **Valueless and keyless attributes.** A keyless attribute is skipped (the
  reference stores it under the key `None`). A valueless `string` or `id` is a
  null and a valueless `boolean` is false, as in the reference; a valueless
  `int`, `float` or `date`, on which the reference fails, is skipped.
- **Containers** are dropped at every level by `ITERPARSE` and
  `ITERPARSE_MEM_COMPRESSED`.
- **Metadata.** Extensions and classifiers are keyed by name: a repeated name
  replaces the earlier declaration in its place. An extension without a name,
  prefix or URI and a classifier without `keys` are skipped. A repeated
  `<global>` scope keeps the last declaration. Declared divergence: a nameless
  classifier is stored under `""` (the reference uses `None`), and a
  `scope="log"` global stays in the document-order `globals` list.
- **Column order.** The importer records where the selected first-class cells
  stood among the attributes, and `to_data_frame`-style tables list event
  columns in document order followed by the `case:` columns in trace order,
  matching the reference dict order. The event filters that regroup events
  into traces (timestamp and attribute `apply_events`) drop an event's own
  `case:` cells as the reference does and move the recorded positions with
  them, so the selected cells keep their place among the attributes left.

Declared variant quirks that Minera does not reproduce:

- `CHUNK_REGEX` in the reference drops `<id>` attributes, does not decode
  entities or character references, flattens container children into the
  event, and after a `<container>` swallows the following trace. Minera's
  `CHUNK_REGEX` keeps ids, decodes references and reads every trace.
- `LINE_BY_LINE` and `ITERPARSE_MEM_COMPRESSED` in the reference intern values
  across the whole log by hash, so `True`, `1` and `1.0` (or `False`, `0` and
  `-0.0`) collapse to whichever was seen first. Minera keeps each value's own
  type.

DFG text reading follows `read_dfg`: labels and rows are stripped as
`str.strip()` strips them (Unicode whitespace included), section sizes, counts
and ids are read like `int()` (surrounding Unicode whitespace, a sign, Unicode
decimal digits, single underscores between digits, `-0` as zero), ids index the
label list as Python does (`-1` is the last label, so `-n` to `n-1` are valid),
a negative section size reads no rows, zero counts are accepted (and written),
a repeated label names the same activity, and a repeated start, end or edge row
replaces the earlier one. Writing follows `write_dfg`: every label goes on its own
line as given, empty and padded labels included (review X2-5); only a label
with a line break or a NUL is refused. A blank row, a BOM and an out-of-range id are errors,
as in the reference. Declared difference: Minera stores counts as unsigned
64-bit integers, so a negative count (which the reference keeps, e.g. `{'A': -3}`)
is refused with `DFG: negative counts are not supported`, and a count beyond
2^64-1 (which Python's unbounded int keeps) with `DFG: count is too large`.

PNML choices: Minera reads the first `<net>` and merges every page, nested
pages included (PNML pages only partition a net), while the reference reads
the last net and only its last top-level page. Minera rejects dangling and
place-to-place arcs, duplicate transition ids and negative markings, which the
reference drops, keeps or ignores.

## Native event-data interoperability evidence

The traditional event-data layer now has four explicit native forms: trace
logs, ordered flat streams, rectangular eager tables, and restartable lazy
tables. A tagged non-owning view normalizes any form to the other three while
preserving row order, typed scalar kinds, log attributes, and shared metadata.
Lazy scans validate every row, restart from the beginning, and enforce an
optional hard materialization cap without truncation. Compatibility aliases
keep the original stream and table API source-compatible.

Table cells distinguish a missing column value, a present null, and a present
empty string. Optional stream post-processing removes only present nulls.
Conversions validate unique column names (including a single literal empty
name), rectangular rows, non-null case
glue, custom case selectors and prefixes, and stable type-aware case identity.
Extension, classifier, trace-global, event-global, log-property, and
trace-property metadata is carried by the native log model and retained by
log-preserving transformations. Synthetic variant projections deliberately
remain metadata-free.

The XML log reader and writer preserve extension declarations, quoted
classifier keys, typed trace/event globals, and selector properties in
deterministic order. Empty scalar strings remain values; explicit nulls are
omitted because the interchange format has no null scalar. Stored declarations
are retained, while canonical prefixes are generated only when undeclared. The
new stream post-processing, copy/compression compatibility controls, lazy
output selector, and row cap are exposed through strict request parsing, the
headless export CLI, bounded local-server queries, and typed frontend guards.
Focused native fixtures cover metadata cycles, interleaved grouping, typed case
identities, missing/null/empty distinctions, malformed tables, restartable
scans, and cap failures.

## Extended Petri-arc evidence

Petri transitions now retain ordinary, reset, and inhibitor input arcs as
separate deterministic lists. Reset firing clears every token in its place;
inhibitor firing requires an empty place. Token replay is the exception: like
the reference it reads every place-to-transition arc as an ordinary input of its
weight (row R1 of the broad audit). Alignment
search, reachability/soundness exploration, model footprints, and basic,
stochastic, and extensive playout all use these enablement and firing rules.
PNML round-trips annotate extended input arcs with `reset` or `inhibitor`, and
the analysis JSON and frontend model type preserve both lists. Linear marking
equations deliberately return a structured unsupported result for these
nonlinear arcs instead of claiming an unsound solution; focused native tests
cover both arc kinds, transport, replay, playout, and that guard.

## Petri usage comparison evidence

Element-usage comparison replays two logs on a selected or supplied Petri net
and emits deterministic place, transition, and arc records with both log
counts, totals, and signed direction. The CLI supports CSV/XES references and
inductive, Alpha, heuristic, and POWL model selection. The CLI also accepts
`--compare-petri-model model.pnml`, preserving the file's complete initial and
final markings, including zero markings and empty or disconnected general
nets. Explicit CLI markings override the corresponding PNML marking. The
general-net import mode is opt-in; workflow import defaults retain their
existing structural requirements. The local server accepts
the same reference as multipart `reference_log` against its cached session;
both adapters accept comma-separated initial and final place markings, while
the frontend exposes those controls beside the reference upload. Pre-event
hidden routing, post-trace final-marking routing, immediate-stop replay, and
token-flood cleaning
controls retain their established defaults and are selectable through native,
CLI, local-server, and frontend surfaces. An optional
trimmed activity selector applies to both replay logs; resource, timestamp,
and lifecycle aliases resolve to their first-class event fields, while the
CSV/XES import paths accept either short or qualified standard keys even when
the default activity column/key is absent. Custom CSV/XES keys are retained
through import. Replay uses normal, reset, and inhibitor arc semantics and
preserves weighted arcs in the usage records. Ordinary input/output, reset,
and inhibitor arcs are emitted separately with an explicit kind; the legacy
input projection remains true for every place-to-transition arc. Every element carries a
deterministic `(log1/log2/total)` label and a signed-direction color generated
from the public 256-bin blue-to-red palette; arc decorations mirror their owning
transition.
Place counts include consumed tokens and, for each place, the greater of
residual tokens and required final tokens, plus cleaning removals when enabled.
Final demand contributes even to an incomplete trace. Hidden final routing
stops once every required final place has a marking entry, including an explicit
zero-valued entry, even when its requested token count is larger. Immediate-stop mode stops before firing a disabled transition;
unknown activity labels are skipped, while missing selected activity fields
are rejected before replay, including fields after an immediate-stop event.
Present null values are skipped, and first-class projection
precedence applies to nulls and values alike. A forced weighted activation
adds the full input weight to each deficient place before consumption,
preserving a partially available token count. JSON directions retain double
precision. The static color helper exposes the separate five-color public
palette, including its asymmetric neutral interval `(-0.1, 0]`.

The public comparison capture and native PNML differential scripts are
`scripts/capture-petri-element-usage-reference.py` and
`scripts/check-petri-element-usage-native.py`. Element identities are
canonicalized by PNML IDs. A public weighted arc corresponds to native
unit-arc records with repeated endpoints; the checker verifies the exact
multiplicity and identical activation statistics before collapsing them,
without summing their firing counts. Native regression coverage additionally
checks reset/inhibitor arcs, selector aliases, malformed nets, and the
explicit silent-search budget. `comparison_module_contract` directly
exercises both native comparison entry points and JSON serialization.

The expanded public corpus contains 570 observations. All 566 cases mapped to
the native replay controls match, covering weighted deficits, silent routing,
incomplete traces, empty nets, zero/multiple markings, duplicate labels,
parallel joins, custom keys, and missing-key rejection. Four observations of
`disable_variants` and `consider_remaining_in_fitness` are explicitly skipped
by the CLI checker because these parameters have no native option. Registered
tests also check 2,766 dynamic-color and 2,013 static-color observations, plus
typed-null and alias-collision cases. The transport checker
`scripts/check-petri-element-usage-transports.py` verifies 128 server/CLI
combinations (four miners, CSV/XES, and every combination of four replay flags),
32 observable cleaning effects, two custom activity-selector cases, and ten
rejection paths. Comparison
CSV references opt into fallback between `case_id` and `case:concept:name`;
exact matches win and custom selectors remain strict.
The reviewed Release build, all 150 registered native tests, and the normal
catalogue verifier pass for this comparison increment.

The combined cleaning, component, final-routing, pre-event, and marking-key corpus contains
1,374 completed public observations, all of which match native output: 1,371
by element identity and three under an explicitly declared net automorphism.
The latter exchange equivalent silent branches in the six- and eight-stage
parallel fixtures. Fifteen additional bounded public calls, varying insertion
order and branch names, observed both choices; their complete usage records
agree after the branch exchange. The checker first attempts identity matching
and permits a declared exchange only after validating a bijection that preserves
node kinds, visible labels, the weighted arc multiset, and both markings.
Only element keys are renamed; every usage field remains checked. Nine focused
checker tests cover valid exchanges, invalid declarations, and count mismatches.
The checker reports these matches separately, and capture metadata distinguishes
declared equivalences from captured public results. Independent review found no
actionable issues in this normalization.

Token-flood cleaning is selectable through the native option,
`--compare-petri-cleaning-token-flood`, the server's `cleaning_token_flood`
query, and the frontend checkbox. It defaults to false. After a forced visible
activation introduces a new marked place in a structural component, cleaning
removes old places that remain marked in that component and records one
remaining occurrence per removed place, irrespective of its token count.
Increasing an already marked output does not introduce a new place. Enabled
firings, silent firings, and immediate-stop events do not trigger cleaning.
For a `p0-A-p1-B-p2` net and trace `B,A`, cleaning raises both endpoint usage
counts from one to two.

The independent component model matched 196 public observations across 28
nets and depth limits zero through six. The traversal saturates one-output
routes, retains prefixes, and explores each split output independently; its
default depth limit is six. It differs from Woflan invariant supports.
Multiple boundary marking keys disable components; an empty initial marking
otherwise rejects cleaning. Native component generation explicitly reports
its 4,096-expansion or one-million-stored-place resource limits.

Hidden final routing retains enabled prefixes of shortest structural paths,
including progress toward a join that remains disabled. It makes at most six
passes, with at most 51 silent transitions in each candidate path. Competing paths
prefer shorter routes, then source place names, then target place names. The
supplied-PNML comparison route preserves original place and transition IDs for
these choices. Pre-event
routing separately targets deficient transition inputs, retains enabled
prefixes, and recursively supplies blocked joins. Candidate paths have at most
51 silent transitions, and a hidden transition is not repeatedly fired to
fill a weighted deficit during one event. The selected visible transition
remains fixed while that routing runs. Disabled duplicate-label candidates
use the greatest transition name; when several candidates are already enabled,
the reference can choose either according to its set iteration. Native replay
uses the least enabled transition name as a deterministic choice.
Native structural searches report their 4,096-place and one-million-stored-step
limits explicitly. Pre-event dependency routing reports its 4,096-call guard
separately from the observed public path and final-pass limits.

Default pre-event routing fires enabled path prefixes until the target becomes
enabled or a candidate yields no new firing, then recomputes candidates and
explores blocked dependencies. Each recursive invocation freezes its initially
deficient target input places; recomputation uses those same target places with
the updated marking keys. A prefix that supplies an input does not remove that
input from the invocation's later path search. Pre-event paths prefer shorter
routes, then source place names, then target place names. Routing stops before
dependency exploration if the prefix already enables the target. Visited targets
remain visited even if they never fire, and a blocked step does not discard later
steps of its path.
With `exhaustive_invisible_exploration=true`, candidate paths supply a transition
pool in first-occurrence order. Breadth-first exploration tries enabled pool
transitions on temporary markings, using each transition at most once per trial
and excluding transitions already visited by the surrounding search. Only a
sequence that enables the selected target is retained. Successful trial firings
do not themselves mark those transitions visited in the surrounding search.
This prevents a fallback dependency from refiring a visited producer merely to
fill a weighted deficit. The native trial search reports its 4,096-state bound
and 64 MiB retained-node payload budget explicitly; temporary firing scratch
is outside that accounting. If no trial succeeds, dependency
exploration runs without the preliminary
prefix pass. Both modes allow two invocation levels. The dependency phase never
stops early: in both modes it walks every step of every recomputed candidate
path, firing each unvisited enabled step and recursing into each unvisited
blocked one, even after the selected target has become enabled (see *Token
replay hidden-routing second pass and precision path*).
This option defaults to false and is available in the native API,
`--compare-petri-exhaustive-invisible-exploration`, strict server parsing, and
the frontend comparison controls.
