## Object-centric Petri net and SAW net bank (2026-10-25)

`docs/ocel-nets-bank.json.gz` (`scripts/capture-ocel-nets-bank.py`, about
50 s) holds 120 seeded OCELs (two to four object types, objects without
events, shared and repeated objects, timestamp ties, event tables not in time
order, events without objects in a quarter of the logs), captured under four
hash seeds. Each OCEL goes through the public OCPN dispatcher (defaults, the
`imd` inductive variant, double-arc threshold 0.5, token-based-replay
diagnostics, custom activity/object-type selector columns, the WO_ANNOTATION
selector), the internal `ocpn.variants.wo_annotation` module and the public
SAW-net dispatcher (defaults and custom selectors). OCPN results are recorded
by their OCDFG fields, double-arc map, per-type nets with markings and replay
counters; SAW results by the per-type and merged nets with every arc's weight
distribution.

`minera_ocel_nets_parity_tests` compares all 1,080 calls, 72 of them raising,
and every call passes. The OCDFG fields and double-arc map compare exactly.
Nets compare up to isomorphism (transition names are random UUIDs, and the
merged SAW net repeats place names), with markings, replay counters and arc
weights bound in the node and arc colours. A native result must match one of
the outcomes the reference showed under the four seeds.

Reference behavior found and now implemented natively:

- **Tree to net:** `process_tree_reference_net` builds the reference's
  workflow net from each per-type tree. Sequences chain children through fresh
  places, choices share entry and exit places, parallel blocks add a silent
  split and join with a place pair per child, and loops add a silent entry, the
  redo children into a fresh place with a silent step back, and a silent exit.
  A silent step from the source or into the sink is added for a choice,
  parallel or loop root, and for a sequence root whose first child starts with
  a loop (or begins with a choice or parallel block and ends with a loop) or
  whose last child ends with a loop. A silent transition is then folded into
  its neighbour through any place with one input and one output arc. The
  construction matches the public converter on 6,000 random trees.
- **Miner policy:** the OCPN dispatcher and SAW discovery mine without
  fall-throughs and without the strict sequence cut.
- **Event order:** the classic miner reads each object's events by time. The
  `imd` variant, SAW discovery and both replays (OCPN diagnostics, SAW weights)
  read them in relation order (an event's first relation to the object places
  it).
- **Selectors:** a custom object-type selector names the types, but each
  type's log is still flattened from the objects whose canonical type equals
  the label. With labels that never match, every net is a single silent step
  and SAW weights are empty.
- **Errors:** OCPN raises (`KeyError`; natively `std::invalid_argument`) when
  an object type has no object related to an event; SAW keeps such types. IMd
  raises (`IndexError`; natively `std::out_of_range`) when a single-activity
  sub-graph without a self-loop has no start activity.
- **Merged SAW net:** per-type places and silent transitions stay separate,
  visible transitions merge by label, and every arc keeps the weight
  distribution of the type it came from (`SawNet::arc_weights`).

Contract decision: the internal wo_annotation module and the WO_ANNOTATION
selector both return the full classic payload, annotations included, so both
bind to the classic native discovery.

## Link analysis and timestamp interleavings bank (2026-10-25)

`docs/ocel-links-bank.json.gz` (`scripts/capture-ocel-links-bank.py`, about
10 s) holds two groups, captured under four hash seeds.

- **Link analysis:** 100 seeded event tables (case, activity, minute
  timestamps, half of them not in time order, `doc`/`ref` link columns from a
  small pool) go through the public `link_analysis.algorithm.apply`. Each table
  runs with the default columns and with `doc`→`ref` under all eight
  LOOK_FORWARD/KEEP_FIRST_OCCURRENCE/PROPAGATE combinations. Results are
  recorded by their `@@index_out`/`@@index_in` pairs.
- **Interleavings:** 100 seeded related left/right logs with case relations,
  some naming unknown cases, go through the public `interleavings.algorithm.apply`.
  Results are recorded by every row's `@@` columns; ten logs use naive
  timestamps.

`minera_ocel_links_parity_tests` compares all 1,000 calls, 54 of them raising,
and every call passes.

Reference behavior found and now implemented natively in
`discover_timestamp_interleavings`:

- **Indices:** each log is numbered as the start boundaries of its cases in
  case-id order, then every case's events ordered by (timestamp, input
  position), then the end boundaries. Native previously used input positions.
- **Boundaries:** the start and end boundaries sit at the extreme nanosecond
  timestamps `1677-09-21T00:12:43.145224193Z` and
  `2262-04-11T23:47:16.854775807Z` (INT64_MIN + 1 and INT64_MAX
  nanoseconds). Elapsed seconds are whole seconds plus whole microseconds
  times 1e-6 plus the remaining nanoseconds times 1e-9, each step rounded to
  double; this can differ from the nanosecond count divided by 1e9 by one ulp.
  An elapsed time that does not fit in nanoseconds makes the whole call raise
  (`OverflowError`; natively `std::overflow_error`). That happens for a row
  from the start boundary to an event after the epoch, or from an event
  before the epoch to the end boundary.
- **Naive timestamps:** timezone-naive timestamps raise (`TypeError` in the
  reference; natively `std::invalid_argument`).
- **Row order:** rows are ordered by the indices of the two pairs' first
  events. Native previously ordered them by the reported indices.

Contract decisions:

- Link rows are grouped by ascending source index. Within a source, the
  reference lists targets in the iteration order of a hash set, which depends
  on the set's insertion and resize history, so targets are compared as a
  set.
- Beyond sixteen rows, the reference's sort of the sorting column is not
  stable: its tie order comes from the sort implementation and the machine.
  Larger bank tables therefore have distinct timestamps; up to sixteen rows,
  ties are bound and follow input order.
- The error class name is not bound, only that the call raised. Reference
  timestamps (`YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS+00:00`) are compared as the same UTC
  instant in native ISO form.

`algo.discovery.ocel.link_analysis` and `algo.discovery.ocel.interleavings`
are promoted to complete.

## Native full forward result API

The production `replay_token_result` API now returns source-order trace rows and,
when `enable_pltr_fitness` is true, complete place fitness, visible-transition
fitness and unknown-activity context maps. The new API is forward-only. Its
`disable_variants` optional policy defaults to source traces for PLTR and activity
variants otherwise. Explicit false generates activity-only Trace keys without
case attributes or event payloads. Value-equal source Trace keys retain the first
representative and combine their ordered context occurrences.

Grouped PLTR counts event repair missing tokens once per variant. Final-marking
missing tokens and remaining/consumed/produced place counters retain variant
frequency. Place underfed membership comes from event repair; final deficits alone
do not create it. Reached-marking membership retains explicit zero and signed keys
in overfed cohorts, with underfed membership taking precedence for that trace and
place. Visible transitions are precreated even when never examined; silent
transitions are omitted from the transition fitness map. Known examined events
merge the final context used by earlier observations. Unknown events do not update
it. A stopped blocked known event updates that context but adds no transition
underfed observation. Repeated unknown events retain one final context per Trace
key. These rules are implemented in C++, using the same replay path and shared
owned trace equality/context helpers.

`token_replay_result_json` is an explicit tagged object codec. It retains the
list/tuple/set/Marking carrier kinds, Place/Transition keys and source/generated
Trace values, exact signed integer tokens and declared float hexadecimal values.

parallel activation/enabled label lists. PLTR dictionary keys remain objects.
The generic `replay_token_traces`, `replay_token_diagnostics` and their existing
JSON route continue to account for each source trace independently.

The standalone CLI selects this transport with `--token-replay-result` alongside
`--token-replay-model`. The boolean `--token-replay-enable-pltr-fitness`,
`--token-replay-disable-variants` and `--token-replay-return-names` options also
select the full result route. Request parameter parsing accepts the corresponding

### Alpha+ expands original causal seeds and contained branch pairs

Alpha+ now expands each original causal singleton seed against the later candidates accumulated before that seed's turn. A containment on either side permits merging both sides when their activity sets remain admissible; the merged pair does not require every cross edge to be causal. Newly grown pairs do not become outer seeds, and dominated pairs are removed after expansion. For example, traces `[A,x]`, `[A,y]`, `[B,x]` now produce the combined `{A,B} -> {x,y}` place. Classic retains its complete cross-causality closure. Typed null, blank and literal string identities and nullable structural-name members are retained. ### Alpha+ canonical string relation-set ordering

Alpha+ now uses an independently written canonical seed-zero SipHash13 string hash and open-addressed set ordering for its target relations. Unicode labels use their narrowest code-point width with explicit little-endian bytes. Follows sources retain their first-seen order. Each follows target set is constructed and iterated, filtered for causal membership, then reconstructed as a separate causal target set before original-seed pair expansion. Both directions of a length-two loop are causal only when both alternating patterns occur. Classic closure remains unchanged. For traces `[A,z]`, `[B,x]`, `[B,z]`, `[C,x]`, `[C,y]`, the Alpha+ interior pairs now match `{A,B,C} -> {x,z}` and `{B,C} -> {x,y,z}`. Native regression tests check this overlapping case and a separate case that collapses to one combined pair.

### Alpha+ sparse discovery markings and removed-place identities

Alpha+ convenience discovery now returns nets whose initial marking refers to a place removed from the net's root set. `PetriNet::discovery_markings()` carries explicit sparse initial/final entries, each identifying either a live root place or a separate detached place. Detached identities are stored with opaque structured names; equal names or numeric IDs across the two namespaces do not merge places. Alpha+ embeds its actual result markings in the returned net and retains the existing rich DTO fields. A detached initial entry leaves `has_source()` false and does not create a phantom live source or mark a live same-name loop place. An empty trace now returns the single live end place plus a detached initial marking; all-loop traces retain their separate unmarked loop places. An event log containing no traces still raises the measured boundary-cleanup error. The default Classic path and the rich CLI/HTTP schemas retain their previous behavior.

The generic carrier accepts exact `TokenInteger` counts, including signed arbitrary-width values and explicit sparse zero keys. Both roles can refer to one detached identity. These component cases establish native carrier behavior; reference Alpha discovery behavior for unobserved token domains is not inferred.

### Feature delivery first: independent full token replay

An independent original-log/PNML replay workbench is available from landing and
both ordinary/object-centric toolbars. Forward replay exposes its complete typed
public carrier and PLTR maps, grouping, names/labels, native policies and hidden
path caches. Backwards exposes complete native trace diagnostics. All four native
input shapes, source/evaluated counts and original PNML markings are retained.

Flat CSV inputs retain original parser rows. The shared CSV reader now accepts
quoted LF/CRLF fields and escaped quotes while preserving source positions and
existing grouped-log timestamp sorting. Quote placement follows the default
`pandas.read_csv` tokenizer (2026-11-04): a quote opens a quoted field only as
the field's first character, a quote elsewhere in an unquoted field is literal
(`5" pipe`), and text after a closing quote joins the field (`"ab"cd` is
`abcd`); an unterminated quoted field is still refused, as read_csv's "EOF
inside string". The /api/mine size estimate tokenizes quotes the same way.
Black-box fuzz of 3,000 generated files with random quote placements: every
file both sides parse gives identical cells (2,591), and every "EOF inside
string" is refused natively. Rows with more fields than the header (pandas:
"Expected N fields" or an implicit index) and short rows follow read_csv
too since 2026-11-04 (see "CSV row shapes follow `pandas.read_csv`"). Declared empty CSV inputs resolve their
actual activity field in every shape, including custom/aliased columns and zero caps.

## Decision-mining bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-decision-mining-bank.py` (seed 20261030, 150 seeded logs,
four hash seeds, no seed variation) mines each log with the public inductive
miner and records, per decision point of
`algo.decision_mining.algorithm.get_decision_points`, the public `apply`
table (columns, dtypes, cells, targets, classes) or its error, the
`get_decision_tree` outcome, and the guards of
`create_data_petri_nets_with_decisions`. The fixture
`src/backend/tests/fixtures/decision_mining_bank.txt` drives
`minera_decision_mining_parity_tests`: all 632 points, 134 tables and 498
ValueErrors, match `reference_decision_table` (include/minera/decision_table.hpp)
exactly, and the decision-point sets and labels match.

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- Rows come from token replay. Each fired transition whose label (None when
  silent) occurs among the labels of the place's outgoing transitions gives a
  row, even when that transition does not consume from the place, carrying the
  attributes of the last visible event replayed before it. Firings before the
  first event give none. Traces are visited by activity variant in
  first-appearance order, then in log order.
- Only event attributes present in every trace are encoded: string attributes
  one-hot per value seen in the rows (values sorted), then numeric ones
  (int64 when every row has an integer, else float64). Booleans, concept:name,
  time:timestamp and lifecycle:transition are skipped; org:resource is a
  string attribute. No rows or no string column raises ValueError.
- Classes are the fired labels in first-appearance order; silent labels read
  "None" when all labels are silent and "nan" beside visible ones (pandas str
  inference). Targets index the classes.
- Column order across different attributes follows Python set order and
  moves with the hash seed; the bank only uses one string and one numeric
  attribute, so it never sees that. Minera uses lexical key order per group.

Contract decisions:
- `get_decision_tree` raises ValueError for every point in the pinned
  environment (sklearn rejects the object target) and
  `create_data_petri_nets_with_decisions` returns no guards; the bank pins
  both. Minera's native trees, guards and `mine_decision_tables` stay as
  documented extensions rather than reproducing a broken path.
- The package is complete on the reference table and decision points.

TRACE_BASED under default parameters, explicit event/case attribute lists,

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- TRACE_BASED column order follows Python set order and moves with the hash
  seed (240 calls); every observation is the same table up to column order,
  so the test compares columns by name. EVENT_BASED pads shorter traces with
  zero rows up to the longest trace; Minera returns the unpadded rows and the
  test pads them.
- `firstIndexAct@@a` and `lastIndexAct@@a` are -1 for an activity absent from
  the trace (other extra features default to 0). Minera used 0 and now uses -1.
- An explicit numeric event attribute missing from every event of some trace
  raises (`Exception`, "at least a trace without any event with event
  attribute").

The package is complete on its three selectors. Still partial: the internal
`variants.temporal_lazy` module and `util.locally_linear_embedding`.

## Profile-clustering bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-profile-clustering-bank.py` (seed 20261032, 300 seeded logs,
four hash seeds) records the sublogs of the public
`algo.clustering.profiles.algorithm.apply` (SKLEARN_PROFILES, default
clusterer) as trace positions, or the error. The fixture
`src/backend/tests/fixtures/profile_clustering_bank.txt` drives
`minera_profile_clustering_parity_tests` against the new
`reference_profile_clustering` (include/minera/clustering.hpp).

Reference behaviour found (black box, by comparing the public call with
scikit-learn 1.9.0 calls on the same features): the default clusterer is
k-means with two clusters, `random_state=0` and one k-means++ initialisation,
over the TRACE_BASED log-to-features rows with default parameters. Sublogs
come in ascending label order; a one-trace log raises ValueError. Minera
reproduces mean centring, k-means++ seeding (2 + floor(ln k) local trials)
from a Mersenne Twister seeded like numpy's legacy RandomState, and Lloyd
iterations that stop on repeated labels or a squared centre shift at most
1e-4 times the mean feature variance.

Contract: 280 logs match exactly and 13 raise as the reference does. In the
other 7, a nearest-centre decision sits on an exact distance tie (duplicate
or symmetric traces are common with one-hot features); the reference then
decides by the rounding of its OpenBLAS kernel (SkylakeX here), which no
portable summation order reproduces and which varies across machines. Native
flags such runs (`tie_dependent`), and the test then requires a k-means
fixpoint instead (each trace nearest to its own cluster mean), capped at 15
logs. One bank log also changes outcome with the hash seed (feature column
order changes the rounding). Custom `sklearn_clusterer` objects are outside
the contract.

## LLM log-abstraction bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-llm-abstractions-bank.py` (seed 20261033, 150 seeded logs,
four hash seeds) calls the public `algo.querying.llm.abstractions` modules
`log_to_cols_descr`, `log_to_dfg_descr`, `log_to_variants_descr`,
`log_to_fea_descr`, `stream_to_descr` and `logske_to_descr` (on the public
`discover_log_skeleton`) under 18 parameter sets, 2,700 calls in all. Each call
gets a freshly built log: the public columns, DFG and variants abstractions add
`case:` attributes to the events of the log they receive, so a shared log
would change later calls (Minera takes the log by const reference and has no
such side effect). The fixture
`src/backend/tests/fixtures/llm_abstractions_bank.txt` drives
`minera_llm_abstractions_parity_tests` against the functions of
`include/minera/llm_abstractions.hpp`; all 2,700 calls match byte for byte (68
raise, as the reference does).

Reference behaviour found (black box):

- Columns: the event table (event attributes, then `case:` trace attributes,
  one row per event) sorted by column name. Float columns (numbers with a gap
  or any float) and datetime columns print `empty:` and the five linear
  quantiles (Python float repr; pandas Timestamp repr at microseconds,
  truncating the interpolated float). Integer columns without gaps and string
  columns are omitted. Boolean and mixed columns with two or more distinct
  values print `(value; freq. n)` pieces by count then value, descending; a
  count tie between a string and a non-string value raises TypeError. Pieces
  of all columns are taken by count, then column name, descending, while a
  budget below `max_len`; the budget starts at the total length of the
  quantile lines and charges each piece plus, for a column's first piece, its
  `col  empty: n values:` head and eight more characters.
- DFG: arcs over each case ordered by timestamp, by frequency (cases with the
  arc under `relative_frequency`, shown as the truncated percent of cases)
  then arc, descending. Performance uses durations in seconds; `stdev` is the
  sample deviation, NaN prints `nan`, an unknown primary aggregation raises
  KeyError and a NaN or unknown secondary one is left out.
- Variants: activities in log order, case duration as last minus first
  timestamp, sorted by count, primary performance and variant, descending;
  `stdev` is the population deviation and has no value for a single case
  (left out as secondary, TypeError as primary, as are unknown names).
- Features: default TRACE_BASED log features; per feature the count of
  non-zero traces and the quantiles of the non-zero values, sorted by count,
  coefficient of variation (numpy population std over mean) and description,
  descending. Descriptions split the feature name at `@` (first part the
  attribute, last part the value) and successions at `#`.
- Stream: events (`case:` attributes appended) by timestamp, latest first with
  ties in log order, each line put in front of the earlier ones while the text
  is at most `max_len`; values use Python repr.
- Skeleton: the shared Log Skeleton header, relation pairs each preceded by a
  space, activity occurrences in first-appearance order.

Budgets (`max_len`) count code points and stop once the text so far exceeds
the limit (columns: once the budget reaches it). Contract: relation pairs in
the skeleton follow Python set order, which moves with the hash seed, so the
test compares each relation line as a set of pairs; native prints sorted
pairs. The reference types a mixed string/number attribute by the first member
of a Python set of its values, so with some small integers it raises
ValueError under some hash seeds; Minera one-hot encodes every value of such an
attribute when it occurs in every trace (the bank's outcome under all four
seeds). That rule is now in the native log-to-features inference, which also
keeps the log-to-features bank green. Stream key order is `concept:name`,
`org:resource`, `time:timestamp`, `lifecycle:transition`, the other event
attributes in input order, then `case:concept:name` and the trace attributes:
native events do not record the source order of their first-class fields.
`abstract_log_skeleton` now uses the same spacing for several or no pairs.

Empty traces have no rows in the reference event table, so the variants
description lists no empty variant and relative frequencies (variants and DFG)
divide by the non-empty cases. `/api/llm-context` and `minera_context` now
return these exact abstractions for `dfg`, `variants`, `event_stream`,
`log_attributes`, `log_features`, `log_skeleton`, `ocel_ocdfg` and
`ocel_features` (with lifecycle paths), and `abstract_declare` /
`abstract_temporal_profile` on the discovered models for `declare` and
`temporal_profile` (no character budget, as in the reference; `truncated`
compares with an unbounded call). `case`, `petri_net`, `ocel` and
`ocel_features` without lifecycle paths remain Minera summaries.
## ILP discovery bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-ilp-discovery-bank.py` (seed 20261025, two hash seeds, no
seed variation) records 1,169 public calls: `pm4py.discover_petri_net_ilp`
on seeded EventLogs (random walks, short random logs, tiny logs, sequences of
single/exclusive/concurrent blocks, empty logs and traces) and on DataFrames
whose rows interleave the cases and run backwards in time, and
`algo.discovery.ilp.algorithm.apply` (CLASSIC) with explicit
`CAUSAL_RELATION` dicts (including missing artificial nodes and unknown
activities) and custom artificial start/end names, for alpha in {1, 0.9,
0.75, 0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.25, 0, 2, -1}. The fixture drives
`minera_ilp_discovery_parity_tests` against `reference_ilp_net`
(include/minera/ilp_reference.hpp): all 353 `exact` calls reproduce the
reference net exactly (transition names and labels, place names, producers
and consumers, source/sink markings), all 795 `tied` calls pass the
optimal-rounding check below (360 of them are equal anyway), and the 21
errors match by class and message.

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- Each trace gets the artificial start (`▶`) and end (`■`) activities. The
  default causal pairs are the directly-follows pairs (a, b), a != b, of the
  wrapped log with no (b, a), in first-occurrence order (traces in log
  order; a DataFrame contributes its cases in first-row order and its rows in
  row order, timestamps unsorted). An explicit `CAUSAL_RELATION` is used in
  its key order. A causal graph without the start (checked first) or end node
  raises NetworkXError "The node ▶ is not in the digraph."; a pair naming an
  activity outside the log raises ValueError "'x' is not in list".
- One LP relaxation per pair (scipy; cvxopt and PuLP are not used: removing
  them changes nothing), over x_t, y_t in [0, 1] with the pair's producer x
  and consumer y fixed to 1. Rows come from the sequence encoding: for every
  retained prefix σ followed by a, σ·x − (σ+a)·y ≥ 0, and for every retained
  complete trace, σ·x − σ·y = 0. The objective sums the marking σ·(x − y)
  after every retained prefix of the distinct variants (duplicate traces do
  not weigh it). Alpha filter: per prefix occurrence vector, a continuation
  is kept when its trace count is at least (1 − alpha)·max over that
  prefix's continuations; a dropped continuation cuts the rest of the trace
  and its final row. Arcs are the variables above 0.5, so the net need not
  fit the log.
- Infeasible pairs and places equal to an earlier one are skipped; a new
  place is named after the current place count, so the first is "2" (after
  source and sink).
- Then the public murata reduction: places outside the initial and final
  markings, in name order, are removed when a place-flow LP (a_p ≥ 1,
  a_q ≥ 0, a P-flow whose pre-weights stay within its initial marking) is
  feasible. Then the public simple reduction: repeated passes over the silent
  transitions, first merging a single input place that feeds only that
  transition and has one producer into its output places, then a single
  output place fed only by it with one consumer into its input places. Both
  were pinned by calling the public functions on designed nets.

Contract decisions:
- 84% of the pair LPs in a first 200-log probe had tied optima, and the
  reference keeps its solver's vertex, rounding exact 0.5 values either way.
  The capture therefore classifies each call with the LP model above:
  `exact` when every pair's rounding is the same at every optimal point,
  else `tied`, and it fails unless every numbered reference place is the
  rounding of an optimal point of some contained causal pair's LP (all 1,148
  nets pass). Exact calls bind the whole pipeline (pairs, filter, LP,
  rounding, naming, both reductions). Tied calls require every numbered
  reference and native place to be such an optimal rounding
  (`reference_ilp_rounding_is_optimal`); native picks its own optimal
  vertex (dense simplex, Bland's rule, rows added lazily).
- `mine_ilp`, and with it the JSON, CLI and server adapters, now builds its
  net with `reference_ilp_net` (`src/backend/ilp_miner.cpp`); the older
  native options (boundaries, noise filter, integer regions) stay as
  documented extensions. LP ties make adapter nets differ from the reference
  in shape (for example one shared self-loop place instead of two) while
  every reference place stays an optimal rounding. The package is complete.


## OCEL LLM-abstraction bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-llm-ocel-abstractions-bank.py` (seed 20261034, 150 seeded
OCELs from the OCEL graph generator, four hash seeds) calls the public
`ocel_ocdfg_descr` (six parameter sets) and `ocel_fea_descr` (default, and
`max_len` 600 without header, once per object type), 1,794 calls in all, each
on a freshly built OCEL. The fixture
`src/backend/tests/fixtures/llm_ocel_abstractions_bank.txt` drives
`minera_llm_ocel_abstractions_parity_tests` against
`llm_ocel_ocdfg_description` and `llm_ocel_features_description`; all calls
match byte for byte (488 raise, as the reference does). Outputs do not move
with the hash seed.

Reference behaviour found (black box):

- OCDFG: the edges of all object types are sorted together by event-couple
  count, mean event-couple duration, object type and edge, descending. A line
  `  "a" -> "b" (frequency (number of events) = n, frequency (number of
  objects) = m, duration = x.xx)` is added while the summed line lengths do
  not exceed `max_len` (checked before each line); types print as
  `Object type: T` blocks in the order of their first kept edge. The duration
  still orders the edges without `include_performance`. Without
  `include_header` the text is just two newlines. With
  `compute_edges_performance` off the reference raises KeyError whenever the
  graph has an edge, whatever `include_performance` says.
- Features: the default object features filtered to the type (lifecycle
  length, duration, start and end timestamps, degree centrality, interaction,
  descendants, inheritance, cobirth and codeath graphs, lifecycle activities,
  per-type interactions and unique activities; no type indicators or attribute
  counts), described like the log features with positive values only. The
  reference describes the inheritance ascendants as "follow ... inheritance
  graph" and the inheritance descendants as "precede ... descendants graph";
  Minera prints the same text. An OCEL with an event without objects raises
  KeyError for every object type; native throws `std::out_of_range`.

The bank also corrected native object degree centrality (now counted over
interacting objects only and scaled as `degree * (1 / (n - 1))`).

## Seeded Monte Carlo bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-monte-carlo-numpy-bank.py` (seed 20261035) runs 240 seeded
public PETRI_SEMAPH_FIFO simulations after `numpy.random.seed`: 150 with
explicit stochastic maps over every public random-variable family (chains,
choices, two choices, parallel branches, loops, silent bypasses; positive,
negative and zero weights; shared resource capacities one to three) and 90
that fit their map from a seeded source log (two thirds with an explicit
arrival ratio, the rest inferred). Each call runs six times on freshly built
nets under four hash seeds, and every distinct outcome is kept (427). The
fixture `src/backend/tests/fixtures/monte_carlo_numpy_bank.txt` drives
`minera_monte_carlo_numpy_parity_tests`: with `numpy_legacy_seed` native
reproduces every trace (activities and microsecond timestamps), the case
execution times, their median and the total time for 426 outcomes.

Reference behaviour found (black box):

- All draws come from numpy's legacy global generator (`random` seeding has
  no effect). Native `rng::NumpyRandomState` (include/minera/random.hpp)
  implements the published numpy algorithms (MT19937 init_genrand, 53-bit
  doubles, polar normal with its cached value, legacy exponential and gamma)
  and matches numpy bit for bit.
- Per firing, in scheduler order: one `numpy.random.choice` over the enabled
  transitions with probabilities weight / sum (1 / n for a zero sum; negative
  probabilities raise ValueError), then the service time. The laws are
  `mu + sigma * z` (no draw when sigma is 0), `loc + scale * E`,
  `loc + scale * U`, `loc + scale * G(a)` and `loc + scale * exp(s * z)`; a
  negative value is redrawn.
- The enabled transitions reach the choice in Python set order, which follows
  object identity and changes between runs of one process. The test accepts an
  outcome when some transition order (`numpy_choice_order`) reproduces it.
- `total_cases_time` runs from the first event of the first case, not the
  earliest event of any case, to the latest event; native now does the same
  (all 370 earlier scheduler observations agree).
- Map fitting from a log: a hidden firing passes on the latest time of the
  tokens it consumes (a zero sample) unless that token came from the first
  event of the trace or the initial marking, in which case the hidden firing
  and its outputs stay untimed. Native fitting now follows this; the earlier
  stochastic-fit checks (64) still pass.

Contract: exact, with one pinned residual. In mc-081 (t0 forks p0 into
p1 and p2, A: p1 to p3, B: p2 to p4, C joins p3 and p4 into p5; one resource
per place; six cases arriving every 0.5 s) the first divergence is case 1's B
firing at t = 8.152 (relative to the 1,000,000 epoch). Native finds p4 at
capacity (case 2's B token has held it since 7.237) and takes the earliest
release time on p4's queue, 6.398 (case 0's C); it does not wait. The
reference records no wait and leaves 6.398 on the queue, so its case 3 B
(9.119) takes 6.398 and does not wait, while native's case 3 takes 10.257
and waits; cases 4 and 5 then wait until 10.257 and 10.428 in the reference.
Every later firing follows from that. A rule change that reproduces it (for
example counting capacity as `occupied > capacity`) breaks other bank
outcomes (mc-043), and no consistent occupancy rule found so far explains
both; the cause is not identified, so this is an open residual rather than a
proven limit. The test pins it as the only one.
The seeded mode is available natively and through the shared request parser:
`minera_playout --monte-carlo-numpy-legacy-seed` /
`--monte-carlo-numpy-choice-order` and the server's
`monte_carlo_numpy_legacy_seed` / `monte_carlo_numpy_choice_order`; the
Monte Carlo workbench JSON and the frontend do not expose it yet.

## Genetic discovery bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-genetic-discovery-bank.py` (seed 20261025, three hash seeds;
deterministic outputs are recomputed on the stored inputs under seeds 1 and 2
and must agree) records 5,742 calls into `docs/genetic-discovery-bank.json.gz`:
1,900 `get_src_sink_sets_for_wfnet`, 1,902 `matrix2petrinet` (2 KeyErrors),
400 partition edits (`add_singleton_partition`,
`remove_transition_from_partitions`), 260 `tournament` populations, 1,200
evolutionary operator outputs (`individuals`, `crossover`, `mutate`, `repair`)
and 80 `algo.discovery.genetic.algorithm.apply` runs (14 reference errors). The
fixture drives `minera_genetic_discovery_parity_tests` against
include/minera/genetic_reference.hpp with 0 failures.

Contract: sources/sinks, nets (place keys and transition multisets, markings,
errors), partition edits and tournament fitness (within 1e-12) and order are
exact. The operators and the GA loop are seeded-random, and they iterate sets
whose order follows object identity (memory addresses), not only the string
hash: two fresh reference processes with the same `random` seed and the same
PYTHONHASHSEED already disagree. No seed reproduces them, so their outputs are
bound by invariants (invariant-only, declared): every individual,
crossover and mutate output is well formed (keys are exactly T, partitions
nonempty, drawn from T, disjoint, not repeated, and y in some O[x] iff x in
some I[y]); mutate keeps the edge set and crossover edges are a subset of the
parents'; repair (which appends bare singletons, may duplicate and edits in
place) keeps mirrored links and nonempty partitions drawn from T. For apply,
the returned net must be the conversion of the matrix it encodes (T in
first-occurrence order in the log) and its fitness must equal the maximum of
the last `log_csv` row; generations are not monotone. Some runs raise
ValueError "Sample larger than population or is negative" or IndexError.

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- Sources/sinks: sources come from the output partitions only, sinks from the
  input partitions only. Walking T in order, each transition's partitions
  join the first graph that contains it (or a fresh graph headed by it), and
  graphs headed by one of those members are merged into it; the result is
  the graph heads in list order.
- matrix2petrinet: a shared place (X, Y) needs X in I[y] for every y in Y and
  Y in O[x] for every x in X, then is pruned to a fixpoint when a producer
  has an outgoing edge or a consumer an incoming edge no shared place covers,
  or when an uncovered output partition of a producer strictly contains Y
  (symmetrically for inputs). Uncovered partitions strictly inside a covered
  one vanish; the rest become o(x, Y) and i(y, X) places joined by one silent
  transition per uncovered edge. Place i feeds the sources, the sinks feed o.
- Fitness is 0.4 * average trace fitness + 0.6 * fitting-trace share under
  token replay; the tournament sorts stably by descending fitness. Replay
  breaks equal-length silent-path ties by place name, so the native replay
  receives the reference place names (frozenset reprs, set reprs for apply
  nets) and the observed arc order; the bank records both.
- Random non-mirrored matrices can make the reference token replay loop
  forever, so fitness cases use well-formed or GA-made matrices.

`mine_genetic` and its adapters are unchanged (follow-up: wire the reference
building blocks into the bounded miner).

## Interleavings dataframe merge bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-interleavings-merge-bank.py` (seed 20261025, hash seeds 0, 1
and 2, which agree) records 6,000 public calls of
`algo.discovery.ocel.interleavings.utils.merge_dataframe_rel_cases` into
`docs/interleavings-merge-bank.txt.gz`: 3,000 `directly_follows_dataframe`
and 3,000 `merge_dataframes`, 372 of them raising. Inputs are seeded
DataFrames with str or int case ids, null ids and activities, NaT, hour ties,
UTC, Europe/Berlin and naive timestamps in us or ns, extra int, float, str
and bool columns, an existing index column, custom and shuffled indexes,
custom keys and the INDEX_KEY and suffix parameters, plus relation tables
with unknown, null and duplicate pairs, an extra column or a missing key
column. `minera_interleavings_merge_parity_tests` compares every result as
its complete native table (columns, dtypes, index class and labels, every
cell) against `interleavings_directly_follows_dataframe` and
`interleavings_merge_dataframes` (include/minera/interleavings_merge.hpp),
and errors by class and message: 0 failures.

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- directly_follows_dataframe adds one start (`▶`, at
  `1677-09-21T00:12:43.145224193+00:00`) and one end (`■`, at
  `2262-04-11T23:47:16.854775807+00:00`) row per non-null case, in sorted
  case order. The index column numbers the start rows, then the events sorted
  stably by (case, timestamp) with nulls last, then the end rows. The table
  is sorted stably by (case, timestamp) again, and every row whose case has a
  next row is kept with that row's columns suffixed `_2`. Null-case rows
  never pair, and a NaT event sorts after the end row, so the end row pairs
  with it.
- Columns are case, timestamp, activity, the other input columns in input
  order (an existing index column keeps its place and is overwritten), and
  the index key, then the same columns with `_2`. A UTC timestamp column
  becomes `datetime64[ns, UTC]`; any other zone gives `object` with each value
  in its own offset. int64 columns become float64 and bool columns object
  (the boundary rows are NaN), and the `_2` copies of case and index are
  float64 unless the input is empty. The result keeps a RangeIndex only when
  the final sort is the identity and the kept labels are 0..n-1.
- Naive timestamps raise TypeError "'values' is not ordered, please explicitly
  specify the categories order by passing in a categories argument." as soon
  as one non-null timestamp and one non-null case exist.
- merge_dataframes builds both directly-follows tables (left first), then
  inner-merges the left one with the relations on case + LEFT_SUFFIX and the
  result with the right one on case + RIGHT_SUFFIX (a missing key column
  raises KeyError). Columns present in both directly-follows tables take the
  suffixes, other relation columns sit between the two sides, and the index
  is a fresh RangeIndex. The row order is pandas' inner-merge order, including
  the regrouping when a merge yields exactly one pair per left row (see
  "Case-relations merging evidence").

## Process-tree reduction bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-tree-reduction-bank.py` (seed 20261025, eight hash seeds)
records 6,000 public calls into `docs/tree-reduction-bank.txt.gz`, followed
(seed 20261103, 2026-11-03) by 3,027 `process_tree.utils.generic.fold` calls
(27 fixed trees and 3,000 seeded ones over every operator including
interleaving, some operators without children) and 2,001 TREE_TR_BASED
reductions of trees with interleaving nodes, including the public
`<>(a, X(b, tau))` on trace `a`, which gives `<>(a, tau)`. The original part:
`reducer.apply` with the TREE_TR_BASED variant, `tree_tr_based.apply` with a
custom ACTIVITY_KEY, and `reducer.apply` without a variant (which raises
"please specify the variant of the reduction to be used."), on seeded trees
(sequence, xor, parallel, loop and or nodes with one to four children,
activity and tau leaves) and traces. 680 calls give different trees under
different hash seeds; every observed outcome is kept.
`minera_tree_reduction_parity_tests` passes with 0 failures: every observed
outcome (tree or error) comes from `reference_reduce_process_tree` under
some order of the distinct leaves, and `reduce_process_tree` (the public
reduction and its adapters) is that function in breadth-first leaf order,
which matches the reference in all but 50 non-varying cases. The extra
cases pass with 0 failures as well (TypeError compares by class); before the
2026-11-03 fold rewrite the extended bank failed 2,088 calls.

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- The walk deduplicates structurally equal subtrees. It starts from the
  distinct leaves, each represented by its first breadth-first instance, in
  hash-seeded set order, and appends a visited node's parent when the parent
  is not yet present and all its children are (both structurally). A
  subtree whose leaf instance belongs elsewhere is therefore never visited,
  nor are its ancestors, and the result is the last visited node, which can
  be a proper subtree of the input.
- Footprints are computed for the visited nodes: tau is skippable; xor is
  skippable when a child is; a loop when its first child is (a visited loop
  with fewer than two children raises IndexError "list index out of range");
  sequence, parallel and or when all children are. There is no interleaving
  footprint: a visited node other than the root and the last one whose
  subtree holds an interleaving node raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is
  not subscriptable`. Native raises `ProcessTreeReductionError` of type
  TypeError there, with a message that names the interleaving node, rather
  than returning a tree the reference never gives (a computed tree would
  depend on the hash seed whenever the walk order decides whether the node is
  read). An interleaving root or last node folds normally.
- Every visited node that is skippable and shares no activity with the trace
  is replaced by tau in its parent; then the result is folded. The input
  tree is not changed.
- The fold uses the reference node equality: two childless nodes are equal
  when their labels are, so tau equals any childless operator (`X()`), and
  list removal takes the first equal child. Before a node's children fold,
  a sequence, parallel, xor or or node with tau children keeps one tau when
  nothing else is left; otherwise sequence and parallel remove one equal
  child per tau, and xor and or one per tau but the first. The children then
  fold and a one-child node becomes its child. Sequence, parallel and xor
  absorb same-operator children (or and interleaving do not); the subtree's
  sequence and parallel nodes then drop their taus and its xor and or nodes
  keep one (the last when only taus are left), and a one-child node again
  becomes its child. Only a loop of exactly two taus becomes tau
  (`*(tau,tau,tau)` stays); interleaving nodes are otherwise left alone
  (`<>(tau,a)` and `<>(a,<>(b,c))` stay); childless operators stay
  (`+()`), and the equality makes `X(a,X())` fold to `a`, `->(X(),tau)` to
  tau and `->(tau,X())` to `X()`. `fold_process_tree_reference` follows
  these rules; on seeded fuzz with childless operators about one tree in
  5,000 still differs (a childless operator next to taus inside a nested
  xor or or that its parent absorbs, which the reference also removes), and
  none without childless operators (0 of 20,000).

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- EventLog: get_groups_from_log counts, per group and resource, the events
  that carry the activity, resource and group keys (an event without the
  activity is skipped); get_res_act_from_log counts the events carrying
  both keys; get_resources_from_log counts every event and raises KeyError
  on one without the resource key. A None value is a key of its own; dicts

## Precision utils bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-precision-utils-bank.py` (seed 20261025, three hash seeds,
which agree) records 3,000 calls of `algo.evaluation.precision.utils` into
`docs/precision-utils-bank.txt.gz`: 1,000 `get_log_prefixes` calls on
EventLogs and DataFrames (string and integer case ids, shuffled rows,
activities containing commas, a custom key), 1,000 `form_fake_log` calls
(empty keys and parts) and 1,000 `__search` calls on synchronous products of
prefix trace nets with inductive-miner nets and seeded move costs (570 reach
no covering marking). `minera_precision_utils_parity_tests` compares them
against include/minera/precision_utils.hpp: 0 failures.

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- get_log_prefixes reads the activity of every event first (KeyError on an
  event without it), then maps each proper non-empty prefix, joined by ",",
  to the set of following activities and counts it once per continuation;
  both dicts follow first appearance. A None activity inside a joined
  prefix raises TypeError. A DataFrame is read with cases in sorted case-id
  order (numeric ids by value) and events in row order. A uint64 column
  keeps ids past INT64_MAX apart (`[2^63+1, 2^63, 2^63+1, 5]` gives
  `({'a': {'c'}}, Counter({'a': 1}))`), and so does the native reader now
  (before, such ids were read as doubles and merged). Declared: integer
  ids past the uint64 range or below INT64_MIN (an object column of Python
  ints, exact in the reference) still compare as doubles natively.
- form_fake_log splits each key on "," into one event per part carrying only
  the activity key; traces have no attributes.
- __search is a cheapest-first search from the initial marking over
  synchronous moves and invisible model moves (">>", None) only. A marking
  is closed when it leaves the queue; one that covers the stop marking is
  recorded instead of expanded, and the search ends at the first queued cost
  above the cheapest recorded one. It returns the recorded markings, or None
  when there are none.

Reference behaviour found (black box): each log is replayed by the public

## OCPN extensive playout bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-ocpn-playout-bank.py` (seed 20261025, four hash seeds)
mines 200 seeded object-centric logs (two or three object types, events
relating one to four objects) with the public `discover_oc_petri_net`,
converts them with `pm4py.objects.ocpn.factory.create` and records the public
`algo.simulation.playout.ocpn.algorithm.apply` (EXTENSIVE) under one and two
bindings per activity: RETURN_TRACES (sorted label/object sequences),
EXISTS_TRACE, the default OCEL and OBJECTS_UNIQUE_PER_TRACE (by their
trace-order independent content) into `docs/ocpn-playout-bank.txt.gz`. Calls
over 10 seconds are marked as timeouts (78 of 1,496); 13 logs make the
reference discovery raise. `minera_ocpn_playout_parity_tests` mines each log
with `discover_ocpn` and compares
include/minera/ocpn_reference_playout.hpp: 1,418 calls, 0 failures.

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- The playout uses one object per type, `<type>_0`, starting on its type's
  source place; a trace is complete when every object sits on its sink and
  nowhere else, and every complete firing sequence is returned.
- A visible activity is one transition shared by the type nets that have
  it. A binding involves every type whose arcs on the activity are not
  double, may involve each type with double arcs, involves at least one
  type, and needs each involved type net to enable the activity.
- Every transition, silent ones included, fires at most
  MAX_BINDINGS_PER_ACTIVITY times per trace.
- The OCEL lists the visible steps of every trace in trace order as
  `event_<n>`, one second apart from 10,000,001 seconds after the epoch,
  with the objects that appear (`<id>_<trace>` per trace when unique);
  without any trace it has no event columns.
- The trace order follows hash-seeded set iteration; the bank records the
  traces sorted. Fractional branching factors are drawn at random and are
  not part of the bank.

## OC causal net extensive playout bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-oc-causal-net-playout-bank.py` (seed 20261025, four hash
seeds) builds 800 seeded object-centric causal nets (one or two object types,
up to three activities, one or two marker groups per side, cardinalities 0..2
or unbounded, shared or own marker keys) through the public
`create_oc_causal_net`; the factory rejects 467 of them. The public
`algo.simulation.playout.oc_causal_net` EXTENSIVE apply runs under one and
two bindings per activity: RETURN_SEQUENCES (sorted canonical binding
sequences), the default OCEL and OBJECTS_UNIQUE_PER_SEQUENCE (trace-order
independent content) into `docs/oc-causal-net-playout-bank.txt.gz`. Calls
over 5 seconds are marked as timeouts, calls whose result depends on the hash
seed as varying. `minera_oc_causal_net_playout_parity_tests` compares
include/minera/oc_causal_net_reference_playout.hpp: 1,807 calls, 0 failures
(191 timed out or varying). Nets converted from mined OCPNs name their
activities differently under every hash seed, so the bank leaves them out.

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- The state is a multiset of obligations (from, to, type, object). Every
  given object starts with an obligation to START_<type>; a sequence is
  complete when none is left, and every complete binding sequence is
  returned.
- START_<type> consumes the start obligations of any non-empty set of its
  objects. Another activity picks one input group and, per marker, a set of
  obligated objects within the marker's cardinality; its objects of a type
  are the union of those sets and must not all be empty. It then picks one
  output group with a marker for every bound type and, per marker, a subset
  within the cardinality, so that each type's markers cover exactly its bound
  objects. Markers of one group with the same key and type take disjoint
  sets; key 0 is a key of its own. Equal bindings count once.
- Each activity binds at most MAX_BINDINGS_PER_ACTIVITY times per sequence.
- Errors: a type without START_<type> raises KeyError; unless no object is
  given, an activity other than START_<type> without input groups raises
  KeyError at the first search step (which one, when several, depends on the
  hash seed); an activity other than END_<type> without output groups raises
  KeyError once one of its input groups can be bound.
- The OCEL lists every binding except START/END ones as `event_<n>`, one
  second apart from 10,000,001 seconds after the epoch, with one relation per
  consumed obligation (an object consumed from two activities is related
  twice), renamed `<id>_<sequence>` when unique.

Safety limits (native, not in the reference): the reference-binding playout of
a causal net converted from a mined OCPN (`--oc-causal-net` CLI and
`model=causal_net` server requests with `event_binding=reference`) stops with
an error after 120 seconds of search, sequence expansion and log building,
and when its complete sequences would hold more than 2,000,000 events. The
event count is summed per memoized search state during the search, so the
limit fails fast, before any sequence is expanded. Both are
`OcCausalReferencePlayoutOptions` fields (`time_limit_seconds`, `max_events`;
zero is unlimited, the default for direct calls). Under the limits the output
is unchanged.

## Process-tree DP alignment bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-process-tree-dp-alignment-bank.py` (seed 20261025, four
hash seeds, no variation) records the public
`algo.conformance.alignments.process_tree` DYNAMIC_PROGRAMMING apply on 3,000
seeded trees (sequence, choice, parallel, loop; up to four levels; labels
a..e with repeats; tau leaves) with eight traces each (tree walks with and
without noise, random words) into `docs/process-tree-dp-alignment-bank.txt.gz`:
cost, alignment and fitness per trace. `minera_process_tree_reference_alignment_parity_tests`
compares include/minera/process_tree_reference_alignment.hpp
(`reference_process_tree_dp_alignments`): 23,915 of 24,000 traces match
exactly; the rest are pinned (below).

Reference behaviour found (black box, by fuzzing a Python model against the
reference until it agreed):
- n-ary sequence, choice and parallel operators are nested to the right
  first (`->(a, b, c)` is `->(a, ->(b, c))`); inclusive choice and
  interleaving raise NotImplementedError.
- Unit log and model move costs. A leaf syncs the first occurrence of its
  label with log moves around it, or logs every event and adds a model move;
  tau logs every event. A choice takes its first cheapest child.
- A binary sequence keeps the cheapest split and, among equal totals, the one
  with the cheaper left part (the first such split).
- A binary parallel aligns each child on the trace projected to the child's
  labels (an event may go to both children), adds a log move per event in
  neither, and lists exactly one move per event: the next move of the event's
  first child. All other moves, model moves included, are dropped from the
  alignment but not from the cost.
- A loop on an empty segment costs nothing. Otherwise it is a dynamic
  program over positions with states after a body (D) and after a redo (R):
  D[j] is the body on [0, j) or R[i] plus the body on [i, j); R[j] is a redo
  on [0, j) or D[i] plus a redo on [i, j) for i >= 1; the result is the first
  cheapest, by i, of the body on the whole segment, R[i] plus the body on
  [i, n), and D[i] plus a second body on [i, n) (so two bodies may end a
  loop without a redo between them).
- fitness = 1 - cost / (length + empty-trace cost), and 0 when both are 0.

Pinned divergences (reference cache artefacts the cache-free model does not
reproduce): 62 reference alignments whose log moves do not spell the trace
(an alignment of a neighbouring segment of the same length is reused, and
its cost with it), 18 equal-cost alignments with a different loop
decomposition, and 5 traces whose reference cost differs from the
cache-free optimum of the model. They all involve loops over segments of
four or more events with repeated labels.

## Pandas filters bank (2026-10-25)

The seven pandas modules `attributes`, `between`, `cases`, `ltl`, `paths`,
`timestamp` and `variants` (all under `algo.filtering.pandas`) are bound to a
seeded public-call bank, `docs/pandas-filter-bank.json.gz` (87,971 calls, hash
seeds 0-3). It is replayed by `minera_pandas_filter_bank_parity_tests`. Tables
compare exactly through the normalized event-table JSON. The domain, the
behaviour found and the limits are in
[pandas-filter-domain-parity.md](pandas-filter-domain-parity.md). All seven
modules are complete.

## LLM SQL utils bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-llm-sql-utils-bank.py` (seed 20261025, two hash seeds)
records 3,000 public `mask_non_alphanumeric` calls on seeded texts (ASCII,
control characters, letters and digits of other scripts, symbols, emoji,
non-ASCII spaces) and 3,000 `restore_non_alphanumeric` calls on masked,
mutated and handmade texts (1,049 raise) into `docs/llm-sql-utils-bank.txt.gz`.
`minera_llm_sql_utils_parity_tests` compares include/minera/llm_sql_utils.hpp:
6,000 calls, 0 failures, error classes and messages included.

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- Masking keeps every character for which `str.isalnum()` holds (Unicode
  letters and numbers; src/backend/python_unicode_alnum.hpp is generated
  from Python 3.11 by scripts/generate-python-unicode-alnum.py) and
  ` !"'()*+,-.<=>_`; any other character c becomes
  `ordabcchrordabc<ord(c)>ordabcchr`.
- Restoring splits at every `ordabcchr` and replaces each piece starting with
  `ordabc` by `chr(int(rest))`, keeping the other pieces; `int()` accepts
  surrounding whitespace, a sign, single underscores between digits and
  non-ASCII spaces and decimal digits, and raises ValueError (with the
  literal's repr, cut to 200 characters), the 4,300-digit ValueError,
  OverflowError beyond a C int, and chr's range ValueError.

## Temporal lazy log features bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-temporal-lazy-bank.py` (seed 20261101, polars 1.44.1, four
hash seeds, two runs each) records 1,575 `_freq_to_polars_duration` calls on
seeded and handmade strings (ASCII letters and digits, signs, separators,
non-ASCII letters, digits and spaces; 1,095 raise) and 3,000
`temporal_lazy.apply` calls on seeded LazyFrames into
`docs/temporal-lazy-bank.txt.gz`. The frames have one to eight cases of one
to five events, string or integer case ids and activities, null activities
and resources, UTC or naive microsecond timestamps, an optional start
column, custom column names, single-row, empty and column-missing frames, and
grouper frequencies over every unit with multiples including 0.
`minera_temporal_lazy_parity_tests` checks include/minera/temporal_lazy_reference.hpp:
0 failures, error types and helper messages included.

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- The helper rejects None and "" with one ValueError message. It strips
  Python whitespace, cuts at the first '-', and keeps the str.isdigit
  characters as written and the str.isalpha characters upper-cased. The
  letters must name S/SEC/SECOND, T/MIN, M, D, H, W, Q or Y/A, either as is
  or after dropping trailing S's and then trailing E's. Otherwise it raises
  ValueError ("cannot infer unit ..." when there are no letters, "... is not
  supported ..." otherwise). The result is the digits (or 1) plus a Polars
  unit. src/backend/python_str_classes.hpp is generated from Python 3.11 by
  scripts/generate-python-str-classes.py.
- Buckets use the Polars truncation of the start timestamp in wall time:
  weeks are aligned to Monday 1970-01-05; days, hours, minutes and seconds
  to the epoch; months, quarters and years to January 1970. A multiple of 0
  keeps the timestamp. Only buckets with events appear, and the counts are
  UInt32.
- Errors come in this order: missing case or time column
  (ColumnNotFoundError), the helper's ValueError, missing activity or
  resource column, then non-ASCII duration digits (InvalidOperationError).
- Case metrics are as in TEMPORAL. Ties in arrival and finish order go to
  the smaller case id. Seconds are microseconds × 1e-6, except two cases that
  use microseconds / 1e6: sojourn when the frame has a single case, and
  service when the frame has a single row. Nulls are left out of the
  distinct activity and resource counts, the rework count and the resource
  ratios, and a bucket without resources has 0 cases per resource.
- Polars' group mean is a Kahan sum divided by the count, and it sums the
  bucket's cases in a thread-dependent order: 326 of the 3,000 frames gave
  different last bits across runs. The test accepts a mean that equals the
  Kahan mean of the native case values in some order, trying every order of
  up to eight cases. 182 tables needed an order other than first appearance.

Outside the bank's domain: null case ids or timestamps, millisecond or
nanosecond and Date columns, time zones other than UTC, inputs that are not
LazyFrames (TypeError), and metric destination names that collide with
existing columns.

## Locally linear embedding bank (2026-10-25)

`scripts/capture-lle-bank.py` (seed 20261102, numpy 2.4.6 with
scipy-openblas 0.3.31, scikit-learn 1.9.0) records 1,500 `smooth` calls and
500 `apply` calls into `docs/lle-bank.txt.gz`. The smooth calls use arrays of
length 0 to 40 and box widths from -1 to 15; 53 raise. The apply calls use
logs of 1 to 120 traces with tied and out-of-order whole-hour timestamps;
28 raise. scikit-learn runs for real, and its LocallyLinearEmbedding and
NearestNeighbors are only watched, so the bank also holds the feature
matrix, the neighbour indices and the embedding.
`minera_lle_parity_tests` checks include/minera/lle_reference.hpp with 0
failures.

Reference behaviour found (black box):
- smooth is numpy's `convolve(y, ones(box)/box, 'same')`. A full overlap of
  at most 11 terms sums rounded products left to right. Partial overlaps,
  and full overlaps of 12 to 15 terms, use fused multiply-adds left to
  right (the OpenBLAS dot below 16 terms). Errors: a negative box raises
  "negative dimensions are not allowed", an empty y raises "a cannot be
  empty" and box 0 raises "v cannot be empty", even when the kernel is the
  longer array.
- apply sorts the events of each trace by timestamp, then the traces by
  their first timestamp, both stable. It embeds the TRACE_BASED features
  (str_ev_attr and str_evsucc_attr set to the activity), using the native
  log_to_features, which matches the reference's matrix exactly. The
  embedding is scikit-learn's standard LLE: 5 neighbours, reg 1e-3, the
  dense solver and one component. The smoothing box is floor(sqrt(n)) + 1.
  Fewer than 6 traces raise scikit-learn's ValueError.

Contract: dates, the feature matrix and the smoothing are exact. The
features are binary, so distances tie in every log, and scikit-learn breaks
those ties inside its tree search. The native search breaks them by row
index. The test therefore checks that the native neighbours lie at the
reference's distances, then replays the reference's neighbours. In the 307
logs where the second eigenvalue is isolated, the native embedding equals
the reference's up to sign within 1e-7. In the other 165 logs, the
reference's vector is an eigenvector of the native matrix for the same
eigenvalue. Dots of 16 or more terms (logs over 224 traces, or longer
smoothing boxes) depend on the BLAS SIMD kernel and are outside the bank.

comparisons, handoff `docs/PARITY_BROAD_AUDIT_962196AF_2026-10-27.md` on the
reviewer's machine) found wrong results that the green suite did not catch.

Checked on 11 source files (all six formats, SQLite type tables in mixed orders, keys outside the lists): the three writers match the reference; the event and object global scopes, which the reference fills with `__INVALID__` defaults after an OCEL 2.0 XML, SQLite, CSV or OCEL 1.0 XML read, now match too (see "Fresh sweep: stochastic maps and playout, OCEL global scopes, OCEL statistics and filters"). OCEL JSON reads up to 128 MiB (the server's payload limit, 32 Mi nodes) and a larger file is refused with `OCEL JSON file exceeds the 128 MiB OCEL limit` (XML likewise); the server refuses an import whose JSON would not fit the other OCEL routes, so every import it returns can be posted back. Performance: SQLite import reads each type table once (120k events 212.8 s → 2.8 s; 30k 12.7 s → 0.5 s), classic JSON indexes typedOmap qualifiers (30k 5.9 s → 1.1 s), both XML writers index events and objects (120k from XML 97.4 s / 103.0 s → 5.2 s / 4.2 s, read included). Fresh round trips in both directions (native write → reference read, reference write → native read → JSON → reference read) for OCEL 2.0 JSON, OCEL 1.0 JSON, OCEL 2.0 XML, OCEL 1.0 XML, SQLite and CSV: 0 diffs on the rich fixture (lists, quotes, newlines, mixed and missing types, O2O, changes, orphans) and on 8,000 generated events, against 374 before. Declared: native OCEL 2.0 XML also names each value's type (`type="…"` on the value element; the reference reader ignores it) so native round trips stay typed; OCEL 1.0 XML keeps fractional seconds, where the reference truncates them; OCEL 1.0 XML and CSV refuse to drop qualifiers, O2O/E2E links, object changes or globals unless loss is allowed (`--ocel-xml-allow-lossy`, `--ocel-csv-allow-lossy`, the frontend's loss allowance), where the reference drops them silently; SQLite type-table names are collision-free tokens (`event_t_create_…`) where the reference CamelCases the type (`event_Create`), which the map tables resolve for both readers; the CSV reader accepts unquoted list items (`[o1]`), which the reference skips; a native OCEL JSON that holds events or objects without relations carries `"minera:keepUnrelated": true`, so an OCEL from a CSV import (or a filter or playout result) keeps them on every later route, while files without the marker are read as the reference reads them (OC7). | `minera_ocel_tests`, `minera_ocel_xml_tests`, `minera_ocel_sqlite_tests`, `minera_ocel_csv_tests` |

Fresh comparisons match 0/400 random Polars frames with null, categorical and integer cases and null activities. | `minera_minimum_self_distance_parity_contracts_tests` |
| B1 | Batch detection (log, pandas and Polars adapters share it) follows the reference detector exactly. It builds one interval per event in input order and heapifies the list (Python heap order); adjacent overlapping intervals (next start strictly before the current end) merge in place with a stable re-sort; near intervals (gap at most the merge distance) merge by removing the pair and heap-pushing the union, repeating the scan until nothing merges. Because the list is never re-sorted there, input order matters and intervals farther apart than the distance can join (e.g. points at 0, 10, 1000, 5000 s with 300 s give {0, 10} and {1000, 5000}). Repeated events count once per batch. Any finite merge distance (negative merges only overlaps) and any minimum size (0 or 1 keeps every interval) are accepted, through the API, `/api` batch fields, the export CLI and the UI. Polars keeps a null resource as its own group (a null and a text resource of the same activity and batch count fail to sort, as in the reference) and rejects a non-string case column even when empty. Batches are listed by start (the reference lists them per type in its interval order). The pandas adapter reads a datetime column as its integer units over 1e9, as the reference does, so a microsecond, millisecond or second column (declared in the table dtypes) gives times scaled down by 1e3, 1e6 or 1e9 and NaT reads as -9223372036.854776; it drops rows with a missing activity or resource, keeps a missing case as `nan`, and fails when a kept batch holds a `nan` and a text case at the same times (the reference cannot sort them). Fresh pandas comparisons match 0/600 random frames. A Python model of the detector matched the reference helper on 3,000 random event lists (durations, repeats, negative distances), and fresh Polars comparisons match 0/1,000 random frames (null resources, integer and categorical cases, event ids, shuffled rows); the reference log and pandas variants give the same order-dependent results as Polars on 92 probe lists, and native runs one detector for all three. | `minera_batches_parity_contracts_tests`, `minera_temporal_behavioral_tests` |
| P3 | The Polars footprints adapter (`polars_lazyframes`) keeps a null activity as an activity and as a start or end activity (`activities_include_null` and the start/end flags on the native result), never in a directly-follows pair, and groups null case ids into one case that counts for start, end and minimum length but forms no pairs, as the reference does; the eager adapter still rejects both. The flags reach the analysis JSON, the footprints workbench JSON and the UI (shown as `null`) only when set. Fresh comparisons of dfg, sequence, parallel, activities, start/end activities and minimum trace length match 0/500 random Polars frames with null cases, activities and timestamps (and 0/400 without nulls), sorted and unsorted. | `minera_footprints_discovery_parity_contracts_tests` |

Declared exceptions (not equivalent, kept on purpose):

- **Weighted arcs in linear analysis (DC4).** Lifted on 2026-11-04: the
  marking equation now counts every arc object once, as the reference does
  (objectives 2/4/6 for the weight 1/2/3 sequence), see "Arc weights and
  parallel arcs across Petri code paths" below; `minera_petri_analysis_tests`
  pins the reference values.
- **Malformed OCEL (C3).** Native OCEL statistics reject duplicate ids and
  dangling relations that the public association helpers accept.
- **Streaming.** The streaming surface stays Partial and outside the 86/387
  catalog. S1 to S8 match on deterministic inputs. Not claimed: the
  reference's default thread pool (it can deliver events out of order; the
  comparisons use one worker), token-replay ties between duplicate labels or
  equally short silent paths (the reference picks by memory address),
  temporal profiles over string timestamps (the reference raises), XES events
  outside any trace (the reference attaches them to the previous trace,
  native drops them), and lifecycle/distributed orchestration.
- **Windows.** Windows build and CTest are configured in CI but not yet
  executed: runner jobs currently fail before their first step.

Not yet covered by fresh comparisons (no claim either way): Polars tables other than the DFG, minimum self-distance, batch and footprints adapters (P1-P3, B1), genetic evolution and wider ILP
parameters, decomposed
alignments. Every public pandas/Polars adapter variant (batches, footprints, minimum self-distance, performance spectrum, case relations, network analysis, roles, SNA, DuckDB knowledge) is selectable over HTTP and in the UI.

Declared (not equivalent, kept on purpose):

- **K5 (fixed 2026-10-31, no longer declared).** The reference JSON and XML
  importers keep each timestamp's clock fields and attach UTC, dropping the
  offset, so events order by wall-clock time, not by instant: "05:00+08:00"
  follows "01:00Z". Native ordered by instant, which reordered any log with
  offsets, not only offset-equivalent ties. Native now orders OCEL JSON
  (classic and 2.0) and classic XML by ISO 8601 wall-clock fields read like
  Python 3.11 `fromisoformat` (basic and week dates, any separator, hour-only
  and `,` fractions). OCEL 2.0 JSON and classic XML raise the reference
  message on an unreadable timestamp. OCEL 2.0 XML follows the reference's
  dateutil fallback: a fallback value keeps its offset and so orders by its
  UTC instant (`"2020-01-01T10:00:00+05:00 "` precedes `"...07:00:00"`), one
  without an offset is naive and raises next to aware values as pandas'
  sort does, and native reads the dateutil subset `YYYY/MM/DD`,
  `MM/DD/YYYY` (`/`, `.`, `-`), `Jan 2 2020`, `2 Jan 2020` and
  `January 2, 2020` with a clock and a Z/UTC/GMT/`+HHMM` offset; a text
  with no digit and no month or weekday word raises "String does not
  contain a date". Still declared: other dateutil shapes keep the file
  order of the whole log. The importers also store each event timestamp as
  the reference stores it (2026-10-31): a text with a non-zero offset, or
  one the native parser reads differently (week and basic dates, `,`
  fractions, dateutil shapes), becomes `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.ffffff]+00:00`
  holding the wall clock (ISO readings) or the UTC instant (SQLite, aware
  dateutil values). Timestamp filters, OCEL features, statistics and the
  JSON/XML/SQLite exporters therefore see the reference's values on
  mixed-offset logs (`"05:00+08:00"` falls in a 04:00-06:00 filter window
  and an object living from it to `"10:00Z"` lasts 18000 s). The exporters
  still write that text, not the reference writers' own spellings
  (`...Z` without fraction in JSON). Also still declared:
  classic OCEL JSON keeps the file order of the whole log on an unreadable
  timestamp instead of raising, because native adapters carry empty and NaT
  timestamps through it as transport. SQLite still compares UTC instants at
  nanoseconds, which the reference SQLite importer also converts.
  Tests: `minera_recheck_regression_tests` (`ocel_wall_clock_order`).
- **Stream events without a case id (live sessions fixed 2026-10-31).** The
  reference DFG, footprints, temporal and token-replay stream monitors skip
  an event with no case id (a None case id stays a value); Declare files it
  under "undefined_case". The live session now skips such events (for
  example from an XES trace without `concept:name`) instead of filing them
  under the empty case. Still declared: the one-shot streaming server routes
  pass `event->case_id` to the monitors and keep the empty case. The
  monitors' `receive(const Event&, case_id)` overloads keep taking the
  caller's case id, because the CSV stream passes a present empty one. Test:
  `minera_streaming_session_tests` (`events_without_case_ids_are_skipped`).
- **Pandas batch None case.** A None case id in a pandas batch is written as
  the text `"nan"`.
- **PNML zero marking key.** An explicit zero initial-marking annotation stays
  a key in native reached markings (`{"p0":0}` where the reference gives `{}`);
  counters and fitness agree.
- The earlier DC4, C3, streaming and Windows declarations stay in force.

## Recheck of 65572296: fixes and declarations (2026-10-28)

The recheck of 65572296 (reviewer handoff and evidence
`minera-recheck-65572296/`) reported nine fix groups (L1-L9). Each fix was
reproduced against public PM4Py 2.7.22 calls, the pandas rules below were
pinned by fuzzing a Python model of the reference until it matched on every
input, and every reviewer case is bound by `minera_recheck_65572296_tests`
(fixtures in `src/backend/tests/fixtures/recheck_65572296/`, the typed
batch/network table in `src/backend/tests/recheck_65572296_cases.inc`
generated by `scripts/generate-recheck-65572296-fixture.py`).

Shared Python scalar model (`src/backend/python_scalar.hpp`): a selected cell
is kept as its Python object (None, pd.NA, bool, exact int of any width,
float, str, Timestamp) until identity and order are decided. Equality and
`<` follow Python (`1 == 1.0 == True`, `"1"` is distinct, big integers are
exact, a number against a str raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between
instances of ...`). `groupby` over object keys follows pandas: groups are
keyed by Python equality, a group's label is the first equal value in the
column, groups are ordered numbers before strings (the reference's
`safe_sort`), and a level whose values are all non-bool int/float with at
least one float is inferred as float64. `str()` of a label follows Python
(`True`, `1.0`, `nan`).

| ID | Fix | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| L1 | Network analysis requires every selected column (`df[[...]]`): an absent name raises `KeyError: "['x'] not in index"` (all absent: `None of [Index([...])] are in the [columns]`). A first-class projection is a column only under the field it was read from; an XES trace's case key is a column only as `case:<key>` (its bare key is not the activity column). Calendar distributions read an explicit timestamp key the same way (absent keys raise). Streaming temporal passes an explicit activity key unchanged to the shared selector and reads an explicit timestamp key only from the literal attribute or a projection recorded from exactly that field, never a canonical alias of a timestamp imported under another name. | `minera_recheck_65572296_tests` (L1 network, calendar and streaming selector cases over the XES fixtures) |
| L2 | Batch event ids are typed scalars: `[1, 1.0]` is one event, `[True, 1, 2]` two, `[1, "1", 2]` and `[None, None, 2]` raise the Python TypeError (pandas and Polars nullable Int64 alike), and the minimum batch size applies after deduplication. Intervals are `(start, end, set)` tuples through `heapq.heapify`, union on merge, Python `sorted` after the first merge (proper-subset set order on ties) and `heappush` for the near merge. | same (J29/L2 cases) |
| L3 | Batch keys (case, activity, resource, event id) keep exact integers of any width; `9007199254740993` and `9007199254740992` stay distinct as case ids and as group keys, and mixed-number equivalence (`1`, `1.0`, `True`) still joins. | same (delta table, batches rows) |
| L4 | Network relation keys join by Python equality (`[1, 1.0]`, `[True, 1]` link; `[1, "1"]` does not); source, target and edge groups follow the pandas `groupby` model above with first-seen labels (`"1"`, `"True"`), so equal numeric keys form one count-2 edge and a number and its text stay two count-1 edges. | same (delta table, network rows) |
| L5 | Sequence-filter case identity for datetime cells is the exact instant (nanoseconds, offset-normalized): `2031-07-12T08:09:00Z` and `11:09:00+03:00` are one case for timestamp grouping and strict suffix filtering; distinct nanoseconds stay distinct; the grouped key dtype is `datetime64[us, UTC]` (ns when needed, `UTC+HH:MM` for one fixed offset; object when offsets differ, corrected by M8, or when naive and aware mix). | same (L5 cases) |
| L6 | Lexical integer cells beyond 64 bits (`18446744073709551616`, `18446744073709551617`, `-2**63-1`) keep exact identity through the shared key instead of a double fallback; a float cell of `2**64` stays distinct from the integer `2**64+1`. | same (L6 cases) |
| L7 | Calendar fields (year, month, day, hour, weekday, day of year) derive from the exact timestamp parts; `2031-12-31T23:59:59.999999999Z` bins to 2031/12/31, hour 23, Wednesday, and 9998-12-31T23:59:59.999999Z stays in 9998. | same (L7 table) |
| L8 | The frontend API and both streaming forms accept any finite temporal zeta (0, -1) and reject only non-finite text. | `streaming-workspace.test.ts` (vitest) |
| L9 | The open-cases table and CSV list the separate null case (`null_case`) as its own row, distinct from an empty-string case. | same |

Declared (not equivalent, kept on purpose):

- **Absent-column order.** When several selected network columns are absent,
  the reference lists them in Python set order, which varies across hash
  seeds; native lists them in selector order (out, in, source, target, edge,
  sorting, timestamp). A single absent column matches exactly.
- **TypeError operand order.** When a str is compared with a number in a
  batch event-id or interval sort, the reference's operand order
  (`'int' and 'str'` or `'str' and 'int'`) varies across hash seeds; native
  is deterministic and the test accepts either order.
- **K5, expanded.** Classic OCEL JSON now joins Standard JSON and XML:
  ties between offset-equivalent instants keep their file order while the
  reference orders them by its own tie rule.
- The 61ebeee0 declarations (pandas batch None case as `"nan"`, PNML zero
