  names the header already holds: `a,a,a.1` reads `a`, `a.2`, `a.1`), names
  are compared byte for byte (`x ` and `x` differ unless trimming), and a
  UTF-8 BOM is dropped only at the very start of the file (a BOM after a
  leading blank line stays in the first name, as pandas keeps it). Selectors
  pick the first column of a name (`activity`, not `activity.1`); the
  renamed ones are attributes. `case:x.1` is the trace attribute `x.1`. The
  OCEL CSV reader then selects columns as `pm4py.read_ocel_csv` does:
  `ocel:type:<T>` columns are object types (a duplicate `ocel:type:order.1`
  is type `order.1`), a bare `ocel:type:` column is ignored, and every other
  column, `ocel:eid.1` and unknown `ocel:` names included, is an event
  attribute; the object table's `ocel:oid.1` or `Unnamed: 0` columns are
  object attributes. Formerly both readers refused empty and duplicate
  names, and the OCEL reader refused unknown `ocel:` columns. The CSV
  stream reader (`csv.DictReader` semantics) keeps the header as written.
  `/api/mine`'s size scan counts the columns as the importer names them and
  drops a delimiter after a blank row a lone `\r` ends, as the importer
  does. Fuzz: a header model checked against `read_csv` on 8,000 random
  headers (0 mismatches); 800 random event-log CSVs (blank and repeated
  names, `Unnamed: N` and `a.1` already present, spaces, BOMs, leading
  blank lines, raw and trimmed) through `read_csv` + `format_dataframe`:
  1,592 read the same columns, cases and attributes, 2 both refuse and 6
  differ, all a BOM after a blank line that leaves no `timestamp` column,
  which `format_dataframe` refuses and native imports untimed (its
  `require_timestamp_column` default, unchanged); 1,000 random OCEL CSV
  headers through `pm4py.read_ocel_csv`: 913 the same, 87 the same except
  the declared added objects, 0 differ. The case-relations CSV reader,
  which still refused empty and repeated header names, follows since the
  next section.
- **An OCEL JSON object id listed under two types.** OCEL 2.0 JSON now reads
  it as `read_ocel2_json` does: one object at the first listing's position,
  with the last listing's type, attributes and O2O links; the object changes
  of every listing are kept in document order, each value converted by its
  listing's declared attribute type, and typed by the last listing. Classic
  OCEL JSON reads repeated object and event keys as `json.load` does (the
  last value at the first key's position), and an object change takes its
  object's type whatever its own `ocel:type` says (also without repeats:
  `"ocel:type": "zzz"` on an `order` object is an `order` change). Seven
  fixtures (repeated ids with and without attributes, O2O, changes and
  conflicting attribute types): events, objects, O2O and changes the same;
  object type counts, flattening by either type and the exports follow,
  except that OCEL 2.0 JSON `objectTypes` keeps the declared catalog (see
  the next section). Relations keep their event's list order; the
  reference's order there depends on `PYTHONHASHSEED` (see the next
  section, which replaces the "reversed" wording of this round). Declared: OCEL XML (2.0 and 1.0), SQLite and CSV
  still refuse such an id, now naming both types. There the reference keeps
  a row per listing (XML: objects `o1 order` and `o1 item`, relations typed
  by the last listing, `ot_count` counting both, OC-DFG edges for `order`
  while `activities_ot` lists only `item`, flattening by `order` empty;
  SQLite: three object rows, all typed by the last, flattening repeats the
  events, 8 rows for 5; CSV: `o1` as an `order` and an `item` object), which
  a native OCEL, keyed by object id, cannot hold.
- **Naive OCEL timestamps are stored as UTC.** `read_ocel2_json`,
  `read_ocel_json`, both XML readers and the SQLite reader store a time
  without an offset as UTC (`datetime64[us, UTC]`); native kept it naive, so
  a CSV written from such a log printed `2024-01-01` where the reference
  prints `2024-01-01 00:00:00+00:00`. Native now stores a naive event time
  as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.ffffff]Z` and a naive object change as
  `...+00:00` (the spellings the reference JSON writers use for event and
  change times, so a native JSON written back without a fraction is theirs
  byte for byte; a basic shape such as `20200101T100000` is spelled `...Z`
  too since the next section), and every exporter sees the UTC value: CSV
  `2024-01-01 00:00:00+00:00`, OCEL 2.0 XML `2024-01-01T00:00:00+00:00`,
  OCEL 1.0 XML `2024-01-01T00:00:00Z`, SQLite `2024-01-01 00:00:00+00:00`.
  An OCEL 2.0 XML dateutil value without an offset stays naive, as the
  reference keeps it; `pm4py.read_ocel_csv` keeps naive times naive and so
  does native. The OCEL 1.0 XML writer now appends `Z` to a naive time (a
  naive CSV log), as `pm4py.write_ocel_xml` does (`2024-01-01T00:00:00Z`;
  natively no suffix). Checked over a naive fixture (an event date
  attribute, fractions, a static and a changed object attribute) read by
  all seven readers and written by all six writers: every event, change and
  static time matches the reference writers' text, against 4 of 35 writer
  outputs before, except the declared spellings below. Declared, unchanged:
  the JSON writers write the stored text rather than the reference's
  `...Z` without fraction (a naive CSV log writes `2024-01-01 00:00:00`
  where the reference writes `2024-01-01T00:00:00Z`); OCEL 1.0 XML keeps
  fractions; SQLite type-table names. Unchanged here, fixed in the next
  section: date-typed attribute
  values stay text where the OCEL 2.0 JSON/XML and OCEL 1.0 XML readers
  convert them to UTC timestamps; an OCEL CSV log with a `+02:00` offset is
  written in UTC by both XML writers where the reference writes the wall
  clock (`+02:00` in 2.0, the wall clock with `Z` in 1.0), and a SQLite
  input whose event table holds `ocel:activity` cannot be written as CSV.
  Tests: `minera_core_tests` (`csv_header_names_follow_read_csv`),
  `minera_ocel_csv_tests` (`names_columns_as_pandas`,
  `refuses_an_id_under_two_types`,
  `writes_naive_json_and_xml_timestamps_as_utc`), `minera_ocel_tests`
  (`repeated_object_ids_contract`, `naive_timestamps_read_as_utc_contract`),
  `minera_ocel_sqlite_tests` (naive and repeated-id fixtures),
  `minera_recheck_regression_tests` (`ocel_wall_clock_order`).

## OCEL date attributes, CSV offsets, SQLite activity columns, relation order, case-relation headers and footprints fitness (2026-11-04)

Items left open or undeclared by the previous rounds, each reproduced first
against black-box PM4Py 2.7.22 (pandas 3.0.5) calls.

- **Date-typed OCEL attribute values.** Per reader: `read_ocel2_json`,
  `read_ocel2_xml` and `read_ocel_xml` convert the values of date attributes
  (OCEL 2.0 JSON: a declared type naming `date` or `time` in any case;
  OCEL 2.0 XML: one naming `date`, case-sensitive, so `time`, `timestamp`
  and `Date` stay text; OCEL 1.0: a `<date>` value) to `datetime64[us, UTC]`: the ISO wall clock with its offset
  dropped (`2024-02-01T08:30:00+02:00` is 08:30 UTC), a naive text as UTC,
  for event, static object and object-change values. `read_ocel_json`
  (even with `"date"` in `ocel:eventTypes`), `read_ocel2_sqlite` (also for
  `TIMESTAMP` columns) and `read_ocel_csv` keep the text. On a value
  `fromisoformat` refuses, both OCEL 2.0 readers fall back to dateutil:
  `read_ocel2_json` keeps a text dateutil cannot read either (`hello`,
  `Feb 30 2024`), `read_ocel2_xml` raises `String does not contain a date: X`
  for one without a date; the OCEL 1.0 XML reader raises `Invalid isoformat
  string: 'X'`. A dateutil value without an offset (`Feb 1 2024`,
  `01/02/2024 10:00`, a padded ` 2024-02-01`, which `fromisoformat` refuses)
  stays naive for events and objects in both 2.0 readers; `read_ocel2_json`
  stamps its change value UTC (`2024-02-01T00:00:00+00:00`), `read_ocel2_xml`
  keeps that naive too. `read_ocel_xml` converts each `<date>` element: a
  `<string>` under the same key stays a string (so a column can mix both).
  Native readers now do the same (`convert_ocel_date_value`): an event or
  object value is stored as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.ffffff]Z` (naive: no
  suffix), a change value as `...+00:00`, the OCEL 2.0 XML reader keeps a
  date text's surrounding white space for that reading, and the OCEL 1.0 XML
  reader converts per element and catalogues `<date>` keys as `date` for the
  writers. Its writer prints a date in a column that mixes dates with other
  values as the reference prints that object column:
  `<string key="d" value="2024-02-01T08:30:00+00:00"/>`. The native dateutil
  subset reads `YYYY/MM/DD`, `MM/DD/YYYY` (day first above 12, `/`, `.` or
  `-`), month-name dates, the basic `YYYYMMDD[THHMM[SS[.f]]]`, a clock after
  `T` or spaces, and `Z`/`z`/`UTC`/`GMT`/`+HH[[:]MM]` (an all-numeric date
  directly followed by `-HHMM` is a naive clock HH:MM, as dateutil reads it).
  Checked on 920 generated date strings in two seeds (ISO, dateutil and other
  shapes, padded, with and without offsets) through `read_ocel2_json`: every
  event, object and change value matches except the values that depend on
  the day the reference runs, declared next. Declared: dateutil fills a
  missing date part from today (`10:00`, `2024`, `Jan 2020`, `Monday`);
  native keeps those texts. dateutil reads `Z`/`z`/` UTC` after some shapes
  as the machine's local zone (`tzlocal()`); native reads them as UTC, which
  is the same instant only on a UTC machine (the check ran on one). The
  OCEL 2.0 XML reader keeps a date text native does not read that still has
  digits or a month word (`Feb 30 2024`: the reference raises `day is out of
  range for month`), so it never refuses a value dateutil may read. A
  dateutil value with an offset keeps that offset in the reference
  (`tzoffset(None, 7200)`) where native stores its UTC instant, as for the
  OCEL 2.0 XML reader; the change value (UTC there) matches. The writers print an attribute the catalog declares a date as the
  reference writes a datetime64 column: OCEL 2.0 XML
  `2024-02-01T08:30:00+00:00` (fractions kept), OCEL 1.0 XML
  `<date key="d" value="2024-02-01T08:30:00Z"/>`, CSV and SQLite
  `2024-02-01 08:30:00+00:00` value by value, the SQLite column typed
  `TIMESTAMP`. Checked on a fixture with offset, naive, date-only, fractional,
  unreadable and changed date values through every reader and writer: every
  date value matches except as declared. Declared: the JSON writers write
  the stored text (the reference drops fractions: `2024-02-02T08:30:00Z` for
  `.123456`), as for event times; OCEL 1.0 XML keeps fractions; classic OCEL
  JSON keeps its declared `date` types in the catalog, so a value read from
  it is written as a date by the XML, CSV and SQLite writers where the
  reference keeps the text and declares `string` (classic JSON is the
  native transport between routes, which must keep the declaration of a log
  read from OCEL 2.0); the writers take any catalog type naming `date` or
  `time` (any case) as a date, also after an OCEL 2.0 XML input, whose
  reader converts only `date`. Tests: `minera_ocel_csv_tests`
  (`date_attributes_read_as_reference`), `minera_ocel_sqlite_tests`
  (dated writer fixture).
- **OCEL CSV times with an offset.** `read_ocel_csv` keeps a `+02:00` column
  as `datetime64[us, UTC+02:00]` (mixed offsets raise there), and the
  writers print its wall clock: OCEL 2.0 XML `2024-01-01T10:00:00+02:00`,
  OCEL 1.0 XML `2024-01-01T10:00:00Z`, SQLite `2024-01-01 10:00:00+02:00`,
  CSV `2024-01-01 10:00:00+02:00`. Native XML and SQLite writers wrote UTC;
  when every event time shares one non-zero offset they now write that wall
  clock (CSV already did). Times that do not share an offset stay UTC.
  Declared, unchanged: the JSON writers write the stored text
  (`2024-01-01 10:00:00+02:00` where the reference writes
  `2024-01-01T10:00:00Z`). The classic OCEL JSON that routes pass between
  them (the `log` member of an `/api/ocel/io` import, posted back to an
  export) marks such a log `"minera:eventTimeOffset": true`, and the JSON
  reader keeps its event times as written when it sees the marker (without
  it, `read_ocel_json` stores the wall clock stamped UTC), so an API client
  that imports and posts that `log` back to an XML or SQLite export writes
  the same offset as the CLI. The marker (and `minera:eventActivityFirst`)
  is transport only: the files a user keeps (`minera_ocel --format
  classic|standard`, the `/api/ocel/io` JSON export download, the
  object-centric playout workbench's JSON artifacts) are written without
  them, so they read in native as `read_ocel_json` reads them. The
  frontend opens an import through its standard `open_log` (also the file
  it offers for download), which never carried either marker: in the
  browser an imported CSV with offset times exports XML and SQLite in UTC,
  as the reference does after reading that downloaded OCEL 2.0 JSON. Test:
  `minera_ocel_csv_tests`
  (`writes_offset_csv_wall_clock_in_xml`), `minera_ocel_sqlite_tests`.
- **SQLite to OCEL CSV.** `pm4py.write_ocel2_sqlite` writes an
  `ocel:activity` column into each event type table; `read_ocel2_sqlite`
  ignores it (the `event` table's type is the activity even when the column
  holds another value). The native reader kept it as an event attribute,
  so a reference-written file (naive or aware) could not be written as OCEL
  CSV (`event attribute collides with an OCEL CSV column: ocel:activity`)
  and the JSON writers listed the attribute. The column is now skipped, also
  in the type catalog; the round trip writes the reference's event table
  (`e1,2024-02-01 00:00:00+00:00,Create,v,['o1']`, aware
  `e1,2024-01-31 22:00:00+00:00,...`). Declared, unchanged: the reference
  object table of a SQLite input lists `ocel:type` after the attributes
  (`ocel:oid,status,ocel:type`), native writes it second. Test:
  `minera_ocel_sqlite_tests` (activity-column fixture, naive and aware).
- **Relation order within an event (declared).** Only `read_ocel2_json`
  changes it, and not by reversing: each event's relations come out in
  set-iteration order, which differs between `PYTHONHASHSEED` values
  (`o5,o2,o7,o1,o3,o8` in the file read as `835721`, `752831`, `328571`,
  `187235` under seeds 0 to 3; two relations come out in either order).
  `read_ocel_json`, both XML readers and `read_ocel2_sqlite` keep the file
  order, `read_ocel_csv` the order of the type columns, and all six writers
  keep the frame order, under every seed tried. Native keeps the file order
  everywhere, as no seed-free order exists to match. This replaces the
  "reversed" wording of the previous round.
- **Case-relations CSV header names.** Both relation readers
  (`parse_case_relations_csv`, `parse_case_relations_table_csv`, used by the
  CLI and server merges) now name columns as `pandas.read_csv` does, with
  the importer's `reference_csv_header_names`: `Unnamed: <i>` for an empty
  name, `a.1`, `a.2`, ... for repeats past names already present; the
  selectors take the first column of a name. Checked with `read_csv` +
  `case_relations.apply` (`,case_id_LEFT,case_id_RIGHT,note,note` merges with
  `Unnamed: 0` and `note.1` columns; `case_id_LEFT,case_id_RIGHT,case_id_LEFT`
  with `case_id_LEFT.1`). Declared: names are trimmed like the cells, so a
  name of spaces is `Unnamed: <i>` where pandas keeps `' '`. Test:
  `minera_case_relations_tests`.
- **Footprints fitness with zero dfg counts.** `fp_fitness` raises
  `ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero` when every dfg count of the
  log footprint is 0 (also with no relations) and when a non-empty dfg comes
  with no sequence, parallel or interleaving relation and no start or end
  activity, for a footprint and for a list of trace footprints; an empty dfg
  gives 1.0. Native returned 1.0 in both cases and now refuses with
  `std::invalid_argument` naming the ZeroDivisionError. Discovered footprints
  never have such counts, so `/api/mine` is unaffected; the footprints
  workbench reports the refusal in its `fitness.error` field. Tests:
  `minera_footprints_tests` (`fitness_zero_divisions_refuse`),
  `minera_footprints_workbench_json_tests`.
- **Prefixed OCEL attributes.** An OCEL CSV can carry attributes named
  `ocel:foo`, `ocel:eid.1` or `ocel:oid`. `write_ocel2_json` and
  `write_ocel2_xml` drop them (and their type declarations),
  `write_ocel_xml` drops them from objects and writes event ones on the event
  without the prefix, outside `vmap` (`<string key="foo" value="w"/>`, left
  out of `attribute-names`); SQLite, CSV and flattening keep them. Native
  writers now match these three. Declared: `write_ocel_json` drops object
  ones and writes event ones as keys of the event entry (`"ocel:foo": "w"`
  beside `ocel:vmap`), which `read_ocel_json` ignores; native classic JSON,
  the transport between routes, keeps both in the maps.
- **OCEL 2.0 JSON change-only attributes.** For a field without a static
  value, `write_ocel2_json` writes only its change entries; native wrote an
  extra `{"time": "1970-01-01T00:00:00Z", "value": null}` base entry (both
  for an OCEL 2.0 input whose last listing has no static value and for a
  classic input). It no longer does; a reader takes the first change as the
  base, as the reference reads its own export. Declared: with an object id
  listed under two types, `objectTypes` lists only the last type's
  attributes (`B{p}`) in the reference, while native keeps the declared
  catalog (`A{p}`, `B{p}`), as for every declared-only type; and the
  reference declares a change-only field `string` (`a` holding 5) where
  native types it by its values (`int`).
- **Classic JSON change times with an offset.** `read_ocel_json` stores an
  `ocel:objectChanges` time as its UTC instant
  (`2020-01-03T00:00:00+01:00` is 2020-01-02 23:00 UTC,
  `2020-01-03 00:00:00.5-02:30` 02:30:00.5), while its event times and every
  OCEL 2.0 reader keep the wall clock. Native kept the wall clock and now
  stores the instant (for offsets the native timestamp parser reads).
  Test: `minera_ocel_csv_tests` (`reference_writer_shapes`, which also
  covers the three items above).
- **Naive basic ISO times.** A naive OCEL 2.0 JSON or XML event time in a
  shape the native timestamp parser does not read (`20200101T100000`) was
  stored `...+00:00`; it is now `...Z`, the reference JSON writers' spelling
  (`2024-W01-1T00:30:00,5` too, `minera_recheck_regression_tests`).

Tests run (scratch build, each alone under a 4 GiB address-space limit):
`minera_footprints_tests`, `minera_footprints_workbench_json_tests`,
`minera_case_relations_tests`, `minera_ocel_csv_tests`,
`minera_ocel_sqlite_tests`, `minera_ocel_tests` (OCEL 2.0 JSON round trip of
a change-only field), `minera_ocel_xml_tests`,
`minera_recheck_regression_tests`, `minera_core_tests`,
`minera_ocel_filter_tests`, `minera_ocel_statistics_tests`,
`minera_ocel_transform_tests`, `minera_ocel_exact_filter_controls_tests`,
`minera_ocel_codeath_module_tests` and the three OC-DFG control and
performance suites all pass.

## Fresh sweep: transition systems, organizational mining, log statistics and OC discovery (2026-11-04)

Random logs (1-12 cases, 1-7 activities, ties, millisecond and sub-second
steps, shuffled CSV rows and out-of-order XES events) were run through
`minera_export`, `minera_ocel` and, for transition systems, the
`/api/discover-graph` route, and compared with pm4py 2.7.22 public calls. CSV
inputs are compared with `format_dataframe` frames (or the converted log where
the native variant is a log variant), XES inputs with
`read_xes(return_legacy_log_object=True)`.

Fixes:

- **Eventually-follows sorts each case by timestamp.** The reference
  (`discover_eventually_follows_graph` and
  `statistics.eventually_follows.log.get`) stably sorts every case by
  timestamp before counting position pairs, so a log whose events are out of
  time order counts in time order: A@5, B@1, C@3 gives B→C, B→A, C→A. Native
  counted in trace order (8 of 150 XES logs differed). Ties keep trace order
  and timestamps compare at microseconds, as Python datetimes do. Declared:
  the reference raises KeyError on an untimed event; native keeps the trace
  order of a trace that holds one. A completion attribute without a start
  attribute (`--eventually-follows-timestamp-attribute x`,
  `timestamp_key="x"`) is the reference's interval reading with the event
  time as the start: each case sorted by `time:timestamp`, a pair counted
  when the later event's time is at or after the earlier one's `x`
  (A(01, x 03), B(02, x 01), C(03, x 02) gives A→C, B→C); native ignored the
  attribute. Test: `minera_overlap_tests`
  (`eventually_follows_timestamp_order_reference`).
- **Start/end activity, attribute value and roles key orders.**
  `--boundary-activities` (and `/api/boundary-activities`) lists `starts` and
  `ends` in first appearance over the cases, as `get_start_activities` and
  `get_end_activities` do on both an EventLog and a `format_dataframe` frame
  (native sorted by name). `--attribute-statistics` (and
  `/api/attribute-statistics`) orders `entries`, and the `values` object
  with them, as the DataFrame's `get_event_attribute_values` and
  `get_trace_attribute_values`: descending count, equal counts in first
  appearance over the rows; with `keep_once_per_case` equal counts follow the
  sorted `[case id, value]` groups (case ids compare as text, so `k10` comes
  before `k9`). Native kept first-seen order. Roles: each activity's
  resources start in first appearance (EventLog, `--roles-variant log`) or
  by name (DataFrame, `pandas`), and a merge keeps the left role's keys then
  the right role's new ones; native listed every role by name. The
  similarity sums run in that same key order, which settles which of two
  equally similar pairs merges first (native merged a different pair in 2 of
  1,200 logs, e.g. `[A,E]` instead of the reference's `[D,E]` at
  0.7142857142857142 vs ...43). Tests: `minera_boundary_activities_tests`,
  `minera_attribute_statistics_tests`, `minera_role_discovery_tests`.
- **`get_activity_position_summary` entry point.** `minera_export
  --activity-position-summary <activity>` (with
  `--activity-position-summary-activity-key` and
  `--activity-position-summary-variant pandas|log`) emits `ACTIVITY_POSITION_SUMMARY` with
  `positions` as `[position, count]` pairs in the reference dict's order:
  descending count with ties in first appearance for the DataFrame a CSV or
  XES import gives (`pandas`, default), first appearance for an EventLog
  object (`log`). Positions are 0-based within the case's event order (CSV
  cases sorted as `format_dataframe` sorts them, XES events in file order);
  an absent activity gives `[]`, as the reference's `{}`. Test:
  `minera_boundary_activities_tests`.
- **Case arrival and dispersion averages follow the input's path.** For a
  CSV or XES input (`minera_export --case-arrival`, `/api/case-arrival` on a
  CSV or XES source) the reference is the DataFrame path
  (`pm4py.get_case_arrival_average` on a `format_dataframe` frame or on
  `read_xes`'s DataFrame): each gap is the whole seconds plus the
  microseconds times 1e-6 plus the nanoseconds left times 1e-9 (so 232001 us
  is 0.23200099999999998) and the mean is numpy's pairwise sum over the
  count. For an EventLog (a native table source, the time-analysis
  workbench) the EventLog path floors each gap to the microsecond and
  averages the exact quotients with `statistics.mean`. Four starts
  at 00:28:54.365, 03:21:57.038, 03:43:54.029 and 04:53:21.015 give
  5288.883333333334 on the DataFrame path and 5288.883333333333 on the
  EventLog path. Checked on 320 generated CSV logs with microsecond times
  and 320 with nanosecond times, each through both paths (the paths give
  different averages in 560 of the 640), and 40 XES files written from
  them: every arrival and dispersion average matches. Declared: a single-case log gives NaN on the
  DataFrame path, native 0.0. Test: `minera_case_arrival_tests`.

Matched without changes: transition systems (all views, both directions,
windows -2 to 10, occurrence data; 1,200 CLI logs, 150 more with the
resource as activity key and 120 server CSV logs), handover of work (beta 0
to 1), working together, subcontracting (n 1 to 4), log and pandas variants,
and roles (400 logs, plus 150 for role order);
local diagnostics from `org:group` (300 logs); OC-DFG with and without
business hours and OCPN (im, imd, token-based-replay annotation counters,
nets up to isomorphism; 700 OCELs); case durations, start/end activities,
variants as counts, rework, minimum self-distances and witnesses (300 logs
after the fixes, plus 75 CSV logs against the `format_dataframe` frame).

Order follow-up (800 logs, half CSV with shuffled rows, half XES with
shuffled trace order and 15% out-of-order events, numeric and text case ids,
ties; 1,200 more for roles, both variants): starts and ends 800/800 in order
(before 360/800 and 347/800); attribute `entries` 800/800 for activity and
resource, with and without `keep_once_per_case`, and trace attributes
800/800 (before 46-103 of 200 per cell); position summary 3,723/3,723
activity queries for `pandas` and 2,923/2,923 for `log` against the EventLog;
roles 1,200/1,200 exact (before 377/600 and 378/600, 2 with a different
merge); `--variant-statistics` already matched `get_variants_sorted_by_count`
in order (800/800).

Declared:

- **Set and multiset transition systems with equal-valued states made in one
  step.** When a step's source and target windows have the same set or
  multiset value and neither exists yet, the reference creates two states and
  keeps both in its state set only when their `repr` differ. A set's `repr`
  follows string hashing, so the number of root states, which of the two a
  later lookup returns, and how many transitions with equal endpoint values
  and label appear vary with `PYTHONHASHSEED` (l398: 35 states for 38 of 41
  seeds, 36 for 3; `A,C,A` twice under multiset forward window 2 gives 3 or
  4 transitions). Native keeps one root per value, takes the first-registered
  state and one transition per value triple. The sweep checks invariants for
  these logs: equal sets of state values and transition triples and equal
  transition occurrences merged by value.
- **Joint-activities weights to the last bits.** The reference is
  `scipy.stats.pearsonr` (SciPy 1.17.1) on the per-resource activity count
  vectors; its rounding could not be reproduced black-box (it is not the
  textbook two-pass formula, `np.corrcoef`, or the unit-vector dot product:
  `pearsonr(x, x)` is 0.9999999999999997 for x = 1,1,1,0,0,2). Native
  computes the two-pass formula; 39 of 79 logs differ by a few ulps
  (relative error below 1e-12), every other weight, NaN and error matches.
- **Empty OCEL.** On an OCEL without events (as the reference reader leaves
  it when no event has a relationship) `discover_ocdfg` and
  `discover_oc_petri_net` raise KeyError (`ocel:timestamp` or `ocel:type`);
  native returns the empty result.
- **Orders not claimed.** The analysis `variants` list (UI) is ordered by
  count with ties in first appearance, not by first appearance as
  `get_variants_as_tuples`; `--variant-statistics` follows
  `get_variants_sorted_by_count`. No native output claims the
  `get_variants`/`get_variants_as_tuples` order. On a `read_xes` DataFrame
  that order is not first appearance either (166 of 200 XES logs differ from
  the EventLog's).
- **EventLog `get_event_attribute_values(count_once_per_case=True)`.** The
  key order follows Python string hashing (`2,2,F,A,E,E` gives E,A,F,2 or
  E,2,A,F by `PYTHONHASHSEED`); native follows the DataFrame order above.

## Fresh sweep: BPMN, process trees and Petri utilities (2026-11-05)

Random process trees (depth 2-4, all six operators, taus, duplicate labels,
three-child loops, one-child operators, labels with spaces, `&`, `<`, quotes
and non-ASCII) and random nets (alpha, heuristics and inductive discoveries of
random logs with odd activity names, plus random nets with odd place and
transition names, arc weights 1-3, initial markings of 1-2 and optional final
markings of 1-3) were compared with pm4py 2.7.22 public calls. Nets are
compared as labelled multigraphs up to isomorphism (markings and arc weights
included).

| Entry point | Cases | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `convert_to_petri_net(tree)` | 400 trees | 400 isomorphic (silent-transition names too, except 6 interleaving trees the harness wrote as its own PTML) |
| `read_ptml(write_ptml)` of native PTML export | 236 trees | 236 equal |
| `convert_to_bpmn(tree)` language (native BPMN read back by the reference, traces up to 6 events) | 236 trees | 227 equal, 3 reference timeouts, 6 the declared one-child-sequence flow |
| EXTENSIVE tree playout (defaults, and max_trace_length 6 with max_loop_occ 2) | 800 runs | 800 equal after the fix below (557 languages, 243 both rejecting) |
| `read_pnml` / `write_pnml` round trip (odd ids, weights, final markings) | 350 nets | 350 isomorphic with equal names |
| PNML import markings and weights | 350 nets | 350 isomorphic |
| `check_is_workflow_net` | 350 nets | 350 equal |
| Maximal decomposition (`decomposition.decompose`) | 210 discovered nets | 210 equal (places, transitions, arcs, markings, labels) |
| `convert_to_petri_net(read_bpmn(write_bpmn(convert_to_bpmn(net))))` vs native `parse_bpmn` | 210 nets | 210 isomorphic |
| Petri EXTENSIVE playout, max_trace_length 3 and 5 | 350 nets x 2 lengths | 311 of 311 and 293 of 293 equal after the fix below (39 and 57 reference runs cut at 20 s); 32 and 33 differed before |
| Seeded `generate_process_tree` (BASIC, PTANDLOGGENERATOR), fresh bank seed | 900 cases (bank seed 20261105) | 875 generator calls, 1323 trees, 5 reference errors: 0 differences (`minera_random_tree_parity_tests` on the fresh capture) |

Fixes:

- **EXTENSIVE process-tree playout follows the reference construction.** The
  reference builds each node's words bottom-up (a choice unites its
  children, a sequence concatenates, a parallel shuffles, a loop repeats
  `do (redo do)^k` for k up to `max_loop_occ`, reading only the first redo
  child) and keeps a node's word w only when `|w| + minlen(root) -
  minlen(node) <= max_trace_length` and `|w| + maxlen(root) - maxlen(node)
  >= min_trace_length`, where a loop's maximum length is unbounded (it
  counts as one infinite unit plus its children's maxima, compared
  lexicographically) and a choice is not filtered. Its defaults are
  `max_trace_length` = the tree's shortest word length, `max_loop_occ` =
  `max_trace_length // 2` and `min_trace_length` = 1, and it raises on an
  interleaving operator anywhere, on an inclusive choice that is read (any
  position but a loop's third or later child), on a one-child sequence or
  parallel, and when its bottom-up walk over value-equal subtrees never
  reaches the root (deterministic across hash seeds: 262 trees x 6 seeds).
  Native enumerated the whole bounded language (defaults 1000 and 3), with
  no per-node filter, and accepted the trees the reference rejects.
  `ProcessTreePlayoutOptions::max_length` and
  `max_loop_occurrences` are now optional (unset = the reference default;
  the sampled variants keep `max_steps` and 3), the workbench JSON reads and
  writes them as `null`, and a `min_length` above `max_length` is accepted
  as by the reference. Test:
  `minera_process_tree_playout_tests`
  (`process_tree_extensive_reference_contract`, 34 captured cases).
- **Input-less transitions in Petri EXTENSIVE and STOCHASTIC playout.** The
  reference treats a transition without input places as always enabled
  (alpha nets of logs with a one-event activity contain them). Native
  EXTENSIVE and STOCHASTIC skipped them (basic playout already fired them):
  `c` consuming the source and `f` only producing the sink gives
  {(c,f),(f,c)} at max_trace_length 2, 3 and 4 in the reference, nothing in
  native. Test: `minera_playout_tests`
  (`inputless_transitions_are_always_enabled`). The source-log fit of
  STOCHASTIC playout (`fit_from_log`) replays with the same semantics: the
  reference's token replay fires an input-less transition (`f c` on that
  net replays fit, activating f then c) and its stochastic map weighs it
  (`get_map_from_log_and_net` on {cf, fc}: c 0.667, f 0.333); the native
  replay skipped it, so no trace replayed and every weight stayed 1. Now
  both traces replay: c 0.667, f 0.5 (activations over enablings along the
  replayed path; this fit is not the reference map, see "basic and
  stochastic Petri playout remain invariant checks"). OCPN playout refuses a type net with an input-less transition
  ("OCPN playout net contains a source transition"); discovered OCPN nets
  have none.

Declared:

- **Server bounds of process-tree playout (`/api/playout`, process tree).**
  Explicit `max_length` above 64, `max_loop_occurrences` above 100,
  `traces` or `max_steps` above 10000 and `max_traces`/`max_trace_cap` above
  10000 are refused with a 400 error envelope. EXTENSIVE resolves the
  omitted bounds first (`max_length` = the tree's shortest word length,
  `max_loop_occurrences` = half of it) and refuses those the same way, so a
  tree whose shortest word is longer than 64 needs an explicit `max_length`
  (the server forced 64 before max_length became optional). The server
  also caps the final EXTENSIVE words at `max_traces` (default 10000), the
  shortest first, and marks the result `truncated` (the JSON member; the XES
  download answers with the header `X-Minera-Truncated: true`, which the
  server lists in `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` with `X-Minera-Case-Count`
  and `X-Minera-Event-Count` so an allowed cross-origin page can read it, and
  the Conformance playout panel shows a note after the download). The reference
  caps the words of parallel, choice and loop nodes (see the next item) but
  not of a sequence, so a tree whose words multiply across a sequence can
  return more there. The
  native word budget (250,000 generated words) now stops a parallel cut's
  interleavings as soon as it is spent: two branches of 16 activities each
  (C(32,16) shuffles) finished in 1.2 s before the reference rewrite and
  ran unbounded after it; they finish in about a second again, truncated.
  Tree playout polls the client connection (the native `cancelled`
  callback) on `/api/playout` and the playout workbench. The sampled
  variants bound a trace at min(`max_steps`, 1000) visible events when
  `max_length` is omitted, as they did before it became optional. Test:
  `minera_process_tree_playout_tests` (`process_tree_playout_safety_bounds`).
- **EXTENSIVE tree playout `max_limit_num_traces`.** The reference caps the
  words of three node kinds (inferred black box on 2026-11-05):
  - a parallel node takes one word of every child (product order) and emits
    all their shuffles, the next symbol from the lowest child first; it
    counts every shuffle it emits, repeated ones included, of combinations
    whose length the node keeps, and stops after the limit (`+( 'a', 'a',
    'b' )` keeps 2 words with limit 2 to 4, all 3 from 5);
  - a loop stops collecting once it holds more than the limit of distinct
    words it keeps, so it returns at most limit + 1 (its rounds go breadth
    first; words its length bounds drop, such as words under
    `min_trace_length`, still seed later rounds but are not counted);
  - a choice unites whole children and checks the limit between them: once
    the union holds more than the limit, the later children are left out, so
    it can return many more than limit + 1 words (`X('e', ->(X(a,b),
    X(c,d)))` keeps all five words with limit 1; review X2-4);
  - a sequence is not capped.

  Native follows the same rules (the choice rule since review X2; it capped
  per word before). Before this fix choices and loops were never
  capped and a parallel node kept its first `limit` distinct words, so
  `*( X('a','b'), X('c','d') )` with `max_trace_length` 5 and limit 3 gave 42
  words where the reference gives 4. Native reports `truncated` when the
  result misses words of the uncapped language. A capped node whose lost
  words never reach the result (such as the redo of a loop that runs no
  round) leaves it false, and so does a node with exactly limit + 1 words.

  Which words a capped node keeps follows the reference's set iteration
  (string hash) order and changes with `PYTHONHASHSEED` (declared); native
  walks words in word order. So the count can differ when a capped node's
  words feed another capped node, as can the count of a parallel node whose
  shuffles repeat. Fuzz (trees read back from PTML, as native reads them;
  limits 1-8, `max_trace_length` 1-7, PYTHONHASHSEED 0-5): the count matches
  one seed on 439 of 441 trees; the other 2 are such nested caps, each one
  word off. Truncation agreed on all 439, and every native word is in the
  reference language. Uncapped runs give the same languages (354/354).
  Output order is a set's in the reference; native sorts by length, then
  lexicographically. Test: `minera_process_tree_playout_tests`
  (`process_tree_playout_choice_and_loop_caps`).
- **Frontend tree-playout query.** `processTreePlayoutQuery` still rejects a
  `min_length` above `max_length` before sending; the native request parser
  and core accept it.
- Not compared: BPMN layout coordinates (no parity claimed);
  `reduce_petri_net_invisibles` and `reduce_petri_net_implicit_places`
  (no native counterpart, as recorded above); `parse_process_tree` and
  `str(tree)` (no native counterpart; PTML was round-tripped instead); basic
  and stochastic Petri playout remain invariant checks, as before.

## Fresh sweep: attribute KDE, performance spectrum and XES float text (2026-11-05)

Targets were the user-facing entry points with no reference fuzz evidence:
`--attribute-kde` / `POST /api/attribute-kde` (numeric KDE and the date KDE
behind pm4py's events-per-time graph; only native "focused tests" before),
`--spectrum` / the timing workbench's spectrum variants (one fix, no fuzz),
and the XES writer's attribute typing (`--xes`, `--convert-only` and the
server XES downloads; typed round trips only). Inputs were random CSV
(shuffled rows) and XES logs with timestamp ties, sub-second and offset
times, int/float/bool/date/string attributes and missing cells, compared
against pm4py 2.7.22 (pandas 3.0.5, scipy 1.17.1) through the DataFrame path
(`format_dataframe(read_csv(...))`, `read_xes`), the EventLog path for the
LOG spectrum variants and `write_xes(read_xes(..., return_legacy_log_object=True))`
for the writer.

Fixes:

- **Attribute KDE follows `pm4py.statistics.attributes.pandas.get`.** The
  native estimator had its own grid (extra end points, inexact geomspace
  ends) and thinned date samples itself. It now calls the reference ports in
  `filtering_common`: numeric = `get_kde_numeric_attribute` (linspace and,
  for one-signed data, geomspace of `graph_points // 2` points, deduplicated,
  with the end nearest zero clamped to 1e-6 as the reference does, so
  all-positive data starting below 1e-6 (or all-negative data ending above
  -1e-6) gets the reference's grid; a single value spans +/-1% or +/-1); date = the column sorted, then
  `points_to_sample` positions (`floor(i*n/k)` when k >= n, otherwise
  `n // 2k + floor(i*n/k)` plus both ends), sorted, KDE on
  `linspace(min, max, graph_points)` of the picked seconds, x reported as the
  reference's datetime64[ns] grid. Dates are read as whole microseconds over
  1e6 (`Timestamp.timestamp()`). A key no event carries raises (the
  reference's KeyError); an empty date selection raises (IndexError there),
  an empty numeric one returns empty axes. 1,600 queries on 320 logs:
  numeric and non-default `graph_points` 1,278/1,280 equal within 1e-9 (2
  declared below), date 230/320 equal within 1e-9 and the other 90 within
  1.11x the conditioning bound `ulp(max x) / bandwidth` (before: date 16/640,
  numeric 664/1,280). A re-fuzz of the 1e-6 clamp on 161 logs (81 with
  one-signed values of magnitude 1e-9 to 1e-3, most starting below 1e-6), plus the inputs that had
  differed, was equal within 1e-9 on every query. Test:
  `minera_attribute_kde_tests` (`reference_values`).
- **Performance spectrum tie order and a missing error.** 1,280 queries on
  320 logs (four explicit variants, patterns of 2-4 activities with repeats,
  sample sizes 0-5 and default): LOG 320/320 (was 319), LOG_DISCONNECTED
  320/320 (was 298), DATAFRAME_DISCONNECTED 320/320 (was 303), DATAFRAME
  284/320, the other 36 declared below. Both LOG variants sort the log first:
  events by time and traces by their first pattern event, ties in log order.
  LOG_DISCONNECTED collects each trace's pairs as a Python set of `(i, i+1)`
  positions, so equally timed pairs leave in CPython set order (tuple hash,
  nine linear probes, perturbed jumps, growth to 4x used); native reproduces
  the set walk. DATAFRAME_DISCONNECTED gathers every case's longest
  subpatterns before shorter ones, so an equally early longer observation
  comes first, and with fewer pattern rows than pattern steps pandas raises
  "all arrays must be same length", which native now raises too. The
  320/320 LOG figures missed one case: the stable time sort broke ties by
  `input_order`, but treated `input_order == 0` as "not set" and fell back
  to the event's position, so a trace's first source row, tied in time with
  a later row, sorted after it. The tie-break now uses `input_order` for
  every event of a trace that carries one. A 160-log re-fuzz matched on all
  variants except two header-only CSVs in the DATAFRAME variant, where native
  raises "case-id column is missing" and the reference returns `[]`. That
  difference predates this sweep and is still open. Tests:
  `minera_performance_spectrum_parity_contracts_tests`
  (`performance_spectrum_reference_tie_order_contract`,
  `performance_spectrum_first_row_tie_order_contract`).
- **XES float text.** Typed float attributes were written with 17
  significant digits (`0.10000000000000001`, `2`, `9.9999999999999995e-08`);
  they are now Python's repr as `write_xes` prints them (`0.1`, `2.0`,
  `1e-07`). Same values, now the same text: 320/320 random XES round trips
  are equal attribute by attribute (before: 36 exact, 284 differing only in
  float text). Tests: `minera_xes_io_tests`, `minera_core_tests` (unchanged,
  passing).

Declared:

- **DATAFRAME spectrum sampling is random (declared).** Below the
  observation count the reference DATAFRAME variant keeps a random subset
  (two runs on one input give different points; no global seed is used);
  native keeps its deterministic spread. All 36 differences were subsets of
  the full observation list of the requested size.
- **Date KDE densities (declared).** The reference covariance goes through
  BLAS (`numpy.cov`'s matrix product); over epoch seconds a one-ulp change
  in the covariance moves the density by up to `ulp(max x) / bandwidth`
  (about 1e-8 for seconds-wide kernels). Grids and sample choice match
  exactly; densities are compared within that bound.
- **All-blank CSV column in the KDE (declared).** The CSV importer drops blank
  cells, so a column with no value reads like an absent key: native raises
  where the reference returns empty numeric axes (2 of 320 logs).
- **XES NaN, infinities and `<id>` (declared).** Native writes the xs:double
  tokens `NaN`, `INF`, `-INF` and keeps `<id>` attributes as `<id>`; the
  reference writes `nan`, `inf`, `-inf` and `<string>`. Values read back
  equal in both readers (320 further logs with these values: semantically
  equal, lexically different only there).
- **XES writing from a CSV DataFrame (declared).** `write_xes` of a
  formatted CSV DataFrame writes every column on every event with its pandas
  dtype (an int column with a gap as `<float>`, gaps as `nan`/`NaT`), the
  `@@index`/`@@case_index` columns, both the source and the canonical
  case/activity/timestamp keys and `origin="csv"`. Native writes each event's
  own cells as CSV text (`<string>`) under their CSV column names and no
  index columns, as documented in `xes_export.hpp`; every CSV input differs.

## Fresh sweep: stochastic maps and playout, OCEL global scopes, OCEL statistics and filters (2026-11-05)

Black-box sweep against PM4Py 2.7.22 in a separate virtual environment.

Fixed:

- **Stochastic map replay ends at an empty marking.** `get_map_from_log_and_net`
  drops a place from the replay marking once its tokens reach zero (an
  initial place listed with zero tokens stays until consumed) and stops the
  trace after a firing that leaves no listed place: that firing's activation
  and enablings count, its performance and every later firing do not.
  `fit_stochastic_map_with_report` now does the same.
- **Hidden-transition timing in the map.** Time moves on to the latest input
  token only when that token came from a later event than the first; a hidden
  firing records a 0.0 performance only when none of its timed inputs came
  from the first event or the initial marking.
- **Stochastic playout fitting is the map's.** `fit_stochastic_transition_weights`
  no longer runs its own breadth-first replay: it returns the activation
  weights of `fit_stochastic_map_with_report` (transitions the map lacks
  weigh 1.0, as in the reference). The input-less `f` with log `f c` now
  plays out c 2/3, f 1/3 (was f 1/2).
- **Stochastic playout loop.** In the exact final marking "stop" is one
  option of weight 1.0 beside the enabled transitions; `max_steps` caps
  visible events only (silent firings do not count); a silent livelock raises
  after max(1,000,000, 1000 · (max_steps + 1)) firings.
- **Server bounds of stochastic playout (declared).** Because silent firings
  do not count towards `max_steps`, the server's visible-event budget
  (traces · max_steps ≤ 1,000,000) does not bound the work: `/api/playout`
  and the playout workbench also cap every firing of a run, visible or
  silent, at 10,000,000, and stop when the client disconnects. A
  visited-elements run is held to a peak of about 512 MiB per request:
  - While it runs, its buffers (two elements per firing, each marking's
    place counts, counted by allocation as `playout_visited_bytes` does,
    a growing buffer with its old and new allocation) may not pass 512 MiB
    (`StochasticPlayoutOptions::max_visited_bytes`). It builds no event log
    beside them (it used to build and discard one, about 1.4 KB a visible
    event).
  - Before its JSON is built, the exact document size is counted without
    building it, and the result's bytes plus that size times the copies
    that live at once must fit in 512 MiB: 3 on `/api/playout` (the body,
    which is now written into one buffer of exactly its size; its UTF-8
    repair copy; the gzip output) and 5 on the playout workbench (its
    wrapped and concatenated response).
  - A run past a bound is refused with 400 ("the visited elements would hold
    more than … bytes", "… would exceed the server's 512 MiB response
    budget", "the run would fire more than … transitions"). Measured on a
    self-loop net, a run fits about 1.3 million firings on 2 places,
    940,000 on 20 and 390,000 on 100 through `/api/playout` (600,000,
    470,000 and 240,000 through the workbench), so a run that fills the
    1,000,000 visible-event budget on a larger net is now refused; long
    activity names in the `/api/playout` JSON lower these further. (The
    previous per-place firing cap budgeted only the elements: with the
    discarded event log and the JSON copies a capped run could peak well
    over 2 GB.)
  The library defaults (`StochasticPlayoutOptions::max_total_firings`,
  `max_visited_marking_entries`, `max_visited_bytes`, `cancelled`) set
  none, as the reference. (A net with a weight-500 silent self-loop and
  traces=100 once ran the server out of memory with visited elements;
  traces=1000 took 32 s.)
- **OCEL global scopes.** An event or object scope that a read did not declare
  is written with the reference defaults (`{"ocel:activity": "__INVALID__"}`,
  `{"ocel:type": "__INVALID__"}`) by the OCEL 1.0 JSON and XML writers; the
  OCEL 2.0 JSON reader declares every scope (empty), the classic JSON reader
  keeps the scopes it lists, and the OCEL 1.0 XML reader ignores `<global>`
  as `read_ocel_xml` does. Reference-generated globals (scope defaults, log
  `version`/`ordering`, `attribute-names`, `object-types`) no longer count as
  lossy for CSV and OCEL 1.0 XML, and the OCEL 2.0 JSON, OCEL 2.0 XML and
  SQLite writers do not echo them under `globals` / `ocel_globals` (an OCEL
  2.0 XML import exported again as OCEL 2.0 XML once gained the two
  `__INVALID__` globals from the classic JSON the routes pass along).
  Filters and splits keep the scope flags.
- **OCEL attribute filters on reserved columns.** `filter_ocel_event_attribute`
  on `ocel:activity` / `ocel:eid` and `filter_ocel_object_attribute` on
  `ocel:type` / `ocel:oid` select on those columns, as the reference does
  (they matched nothing before: 310 of 320 and 305 of 320 OCELs differed).

Match rates:

- Stochastic map (all distribution types, 697 random nets and logs with
  reference outcomes; 103 further reference runs exceeded 8 s and were not
  compared): 697/697 equal an observed reference outcome (37 only under a
  different duplicate-label or hidden choice, see below). The 32-case fixture
  checker (`scripts/check-stochastic-fit-reference.py`) passes all 64 checks.
- Stochastic playout (337 nets, 5,000 cases each, reference weights given):
  337/337 variant distributions agree (|z| < 4.5 per variant; 65 disagreed
  before). Weights fitted from the log equal the reference's in 317/337; the
  other 20 are duplicate-label or hidden choices.
- OCEL global scopes: 6 readers (OCEL 2.0 JSON/XML, OCEL 1.0 JSON/XML,
  SQLite, CSV) × 2 writers (OCEL 1.0 JSON, OCEL 1.0 XML): 12/12 equal.
- OCEL workspace routes (`/api/ocel/statistics`, `/api/ocel/filter`) on 320
  random OCEL 2.0 JSON files: object-type activities, objects per type,
  activity associations (none/start/end prefilter), object-type activity
  associations, edge associations with both performance lists, and the
  object-type, activity, event-attribute (string and int), object-attribute,
  object-type-attribute and time-range filters: 14 × 320 checks, all equal.

Declared:

- **Duplicate-label and hidden choices (declared).** When several transitions
  could replay an event, or several hidden paths enable it, the reference
  picks by the iteration order of a set of transition objects, which changes
  with the hash seed between runs; native picks deterministically. Native
  results equal one of the reference's observed outcomes.
- **Reference timeouts (declared).** 103 generated nets whose reference map
  took longer than 8 s were not compared.
- **Stochastic playout draws (declared).** Compared by distribution only (the
  reference draws from a set ordered by object identity). Native raises on a
  silent livelock where the reference does not return. Native names cases
  `case_1`, … on a 2026 clock (start, case and event intervals); the
  reference names them `0`, … from 10,000,000 s, one second per event.
- **Classic JSON `ocel:global-log` (declared).** Native writes the stored log
  globals; the reference recomputes the attribute-name and object-type lists.
- **Missing classic scope keys (declared).** The native classic JSON reader
  accepts a file without `ocel:global-event` / `ocel:global-object`, where
  `read_ocel_json` raises KeyError.
- **`fitting_max_states` (declared).** Still validated (must be positive) but
  no longer bounds fitting, which uses the map replay's own bounds.

Tests: `minera_stochastic_map_tests`, `minera_playout_tests`,
`minera_ocel_tests`, `minera_ocel_xml_tests`, `minera_ocel_csv_tests`,
`minera_ocel_filter_tests`.

## Fresh sweep: performance DFG, process-map numbers and Petri decorations (2026-11-05)

Targets: the process map's frequency and performance numbers (`/api/mine`
`edges`, start/end counts, `performance.edges`), the DFG performance variant
with every aggregation and both business-hour schedules
(`dfg_statistical_variants=performance`, `dfg_performance_aggregation`,
`dfg_business_hours[_slots]`), the pandas table DFG (`/api/dfg-dataframe`,
`get_dfg_graph`) and the replay decorations of the embedded Petri nets.
Inputs: 320 random logs, each as CSV (shuffled rows, 0/3/6/9 fractional
digits, ties, sub-second to multi-day gaps, a quarter with UTC offsets), XES
(a third with events out of time order) and a native EventTable (a third out
of order). CSV and XES were compared with pm4py 2.7.22's DataFrame path
(`discover_dfg`/`discover_performance_dfg` on `format_dataframe(read_csv)`
and `read_xes`, `get_dfg_graph`), the native table with the EventLog path.

Fixes:

- **Exact gaps.** Every duration was a difference of epoch doubles, losing
  about 1e-7 s (one microsecond in 2026 read 9.5e-7). Gaps now come from the
  exact instants: `timedelta.total_seconds()` on the EventLog path, pandas'
  `Timedelta.total_seconds()` (seconds + us*1e-6 + ns*1e-9) on the DataFrame
  path; also in Petri decoration waits. The gap is kept as whole seconds
  plus nanoseconds, so any two instants from year 1 to 9999 have an exact
  gap (an earlier bound on each instant dropped events after 2255 or before
  1685 from the map, waits outside 1843-2096 from decorations, and spans over
  292 years overflowed); a gap over 2**53 microseconds is divided once, as
  Python's int / int. pandas reads a CSV without sub-microsecond digits
  outside 1677-2262 as `datetime64[us]`; checked: year 1 → 9999 gives
  pm4py's 315537811200.0 on both sides.
- **Calendar-range gaps at nanosecond resolution (declared).** A CSV whose
  timestamps carry sub-microsecond digits and all lie in 1677-2262 is read
  by pandas as `datetime64[ns]`, and a gap of more than about 292 years
  (2**63 ns) overflows there: `1700-01-01T00:00:00.000000001` →
  `2250-01-01T00:00:00.000000003` makes pm4py's
  `discover_performance_dfg` raise `OverflowError: Overflow in int64
  addition`. Minera computes the exact gap (17356291200 s, the 2 ns below a
  double's resolution) and does not raise.
- **CSV events order at nanoseconds.** pandas sorts a case's events on the
  datetime64 values; the CSV importer now orders them on the exact instants
  (it compared epoch doubles, which merge events a few nanoseconds apart in
  2026, or microseconds apart in year 9999). A CSV with 9 fractional digits
  and sub-microsecond near-ties gave a different edge order and a 0 for a
  2.2e-08 gap.
- **Reference aggregation arithmetic** (`performance_arithmetic.hpp`).
  EventLog: Python `sum`, `statistics.mean`, `statistics.stdev`. DataFrame:
  Kahan sum, sum/count mean, Welford deviation, observations taken in case-id
  order (`DfgStatisticalOptions::dataframe_arithmetic`,
  `compute_performance_metrics(..., dataframe_arithmetic)`; set for CSV/XES
  sources, the CLI and the pandas table DFG, and for the performance DFG
  behind DFG performance playout and the stochastic map from a performance
  DFG, on the server, the CLI and `minera_playout`).
- **Business hours on the DataFrame path run on the UTC clock** (a CSV
  offset is converted; XES is read as wall-clock UTC), the EventLog path on
  each timestamp's own wall clock; week positions now come from integer
  microseconds.
- **pandas table DFG**: one observation gives a null deviation and
  `perf_aggregation_key=stdev` raises `'SeriesGroupBy' object has no
  attribute 'stdev'`, as in the reference.
- **Frontend**: `formatDuration` picks the unit after rounding (59.6 s was
  "60s", 3599 s "60.0m", 86399 s "24.0h"), shows sub-second waits in ms (was
  "0s") and a measured zero as "0s" (was "—", the no-data mark). The DFG
  variant and table DFG panels print seconds to 6 decimals (was 3, so 0.4 ms
  read "0s") and add Std dev and Sum columns, so every aggregation is visible.
  Checked in Chromium: a 0 s / 0.25 s / 3599 s chain reads 0s, 250ms, 1.0h.

Match rates after (before), 320 logs per entry:

| Entry | CSV | XES | native table |
|---|---|---|---|
| map frequency, start, end | 320 (320) | 234 freq, 320 start/end | 320 (320) |
| map mean/median/min/max/total | 320 exact (239-243) | 232-234 (177-181); 229/229 time-ordered exact | 320 exact (241-248) |
| variant mean/median/min/max/sum/raw_values | 320 exact (233-243) | 231-234 (50-180) | 320 exact (235-248) |
| variant `all` stdev | 74 (61), rest singletons | 56 | 320 exact (249) |
| business hours, both schedules | 320 within 1e-9 (303-306) | 218-250 | 320 within 1e-9 (317-320) |
| pandas table DFG, 8 aggregations + BH | 320 (0-243) | 320 (0-243) | — |

Petri decorations (`*_petri_net_decoration` vs token replay of the same net
with `single_element_statistics`): transition and place token counts 910/911
fitting nets, fit agreement 1,918/1,920, waits of places between visible
transitions 130/139.

Declared:

- **XES events out of time order (declared).** pm4py's DataFrame DFG sorts
  each case by timestamp for its edges but takes start/end activities in file
  order; Minera keeps XES file order for the whole map and DFG variants (as
  documented for XES elsewhere). All 91 differing XES logs have such traces.
- **Singleton and `stdev` deviations on CSV/XES (declared).** The DataFrame
  reference gives NaN for one observation and raises for
  `perf_aggregation_key="stdev"`; the map and DFG variant report 0 and
  Welford's deviation (the pandas table DFG follows the reference).
- **Business-hour values (declared).** Within 1e-9 relative, not bitwise
  (the reference works on float timestamps).
- **Decoration semantics (declared).** Minera decorates only traces whose
  every event is a net transition and replays cleanly (pm4py skips unknown
  activities: 2 logs), drops negative waits of out-of-order traces (pm4py
  keeps them: 8 places), times silent transitions at the next event (so
  places next to silent transitions are not compared), and a degenerate Alpha
  net with input-less transitions (1 log) counts differently.

Tests: `minera_dfg_variants_tests`
(`performance_arithmetic_follows_the_reference_paths`),
`minera_core_tests` (`performance_edges_follow_reference_arithmetic`,
decoration microsecond wait), `minera_dfg_dataframe_tests`
(`pandas_performance_arithmetic_contract`); frontend `types.test.ts`.

## UI downloads read back with pm4py (2026-11-05)

Every model and log download the frontend offers was triggered in Chromium
against a served build (a CSV with unicode, quotes and `& < >` in case ids,
activities and resources; an XES with int/float/boolean/date attributes and
`+02:00` offsets; an OCEL 2.0 JSON with typed attributes and qualifiers) and
read with pm4py 2.7.22: PNML, BPMN and PTML of every miner and of the model
file converter, all XES playouts, the log XES (both variants, gzip, inferred
metadata), the DFG, the filtered/cluster XES, the OCEL exports in all eight
formats, the OCEL filter/flatten/playout outputs, and SVG/PNG/PDF views.
Nets match the served decorations (places, transitions, labels), PTML trees
match the shown trees, typed XES attributes and OCEL JSON/SQLite types
survive, and names keep every character.

Fixed: a CSV log's XES downloads (`/api/xes`, the query-filter, LLM-cluster
and trace-cluster exports, the anonymization release) wrote the case id,
activity, timestamp and resource under the CSV column names (`case_id`,
`activity`, ...; a pm4py-style CSV even got a trace `case:concept:name`), so
`read_xes` returned no `case:concept:name`/`concept:name`/`time:timestamp`
and every pm4py discovery raised `KeyError`. For a CSV source these
downloads now write the case id, activity and timestamp under the standard
keys (`XesExportOptions::standard_keys`), as `read_csv`, `format_dataframe`
and `write_xes` do: another column already under one of those keys is
overwritten, as there (a CSV with `activity` and `concept:name` columns, and
`case_id` and `case:concept:name`, gives pm4py the activities and case ids
of the selected columns), and the resource and lifecycle columns keep their
names (`format_dataframe` does not rename them to `org:resource` /
`lifecycle:transition`). "Open filtered log" and "Open released log" reopen
the download with the default selectors, so the case id, activity and
timestamp are found. An XES source keeps its keys (a custom timestamp
attribute such as `clock` stays `clock`, as `read_xes` plus `write_xes`
keeps it), and native exports keep source keys. A table (typed EventTable
JSON) source keeps its keys too, also with custom selector columns: the
renaming happens in `format_dataframe`, which a DataFrame handed to
`write_xes` as it is never went through, so its columns are written under
their own names. Test: `minera_xes_io_tests`
(`standard_key_exports_rename_csv_projections`).

Declared:

- **CSV columns are not repeated (declared).** pm4py's `format_dataframe`
  adds the standard columns beside the CSV's own, so its XES also writes
  `case_id`, `activity` and `timestamp` (and the `@@index` and
  `@@case_index` helper columns) on every event, and a `origin` log
  attribute. Minera's CSV-sourced downloads write the selected cells once,
  under the standard keys; a reopened download has no `activity` or
  `case_id` event attribute, and its resource is found only when the
  resource column was named `resource` or `org:resource` (the default
  selector and its fallback); another resource column stays an attribute.
- **CSV attribute columns are XES strings (declared).** Minera's CSV log
  keeps attribute cells as text, so XES downloads write `<string>` where
  pm4py's `read_csv` would infer int64/float64/bool and `write_xes` would
  write `<int>`/`<float>`/`<boolean>`. XES and OCEL sources keep their types.
- **Workflow discovery's "adapted discovery source" XES (declared).** It is
  the exact discovery input and keeps the source keys, with the selectors to
  reopen it in `source_xes_options`; pm4py needs those keys passed to its
  functions (or the log XES download instead).
- **Process-tree playout traces carry no `concept:name` (declared).** As in
  pm4py's own `play_out` of a tree, so `read_xes` gives only `concept:name`.
- **Empty OCEL 2.0 JSON (declared).** A filter that keeps nothing downloads
  a valid empty OCEL; pm4py's `read_ocel2_json` raises `KeyError:
  'ocel:timestamp'` on an empty event list.
- **XES offsets.** Downloads of an XES source write each timestamp's own
  clock and offset; pm4py reads XES dates as wall-clock UTC, so it reads the
  download exactly as it reads the source file. Downloads of a CSV source
  write UTC (`+00:00`), as pandas-normalized pm4py does (`format_dataframe`
  converts offsets to UTC), so the download reads back to the CSV's instants
  (review V2).

## Model conversion matrix (2026-11-05)

Random source models (reference discoveries of random logs with odd activity
names, random process trees, random DFGs with self-loops, empty and foreign
boundary maps and zero counts, random POWL models with frequency leaves and
non-series-parallel orders) were converted by both sides. Nets are compared
up to isomorphism (labels, silent transitions, markings, arc weights); trees
by structure with the children of exclusive choices and parallels unordered.
"Both raise" counts as a match.

| Conversion (native entry point) | Cases | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `convert_to_petri_net(dfg, sa, ea)`, both variants (`minera_dfg --to-petri`, `/api/dfg-to-petri`, `/api/model-exchange`) | 550 DFGs x 2 | 1100/1100 after the fix (195 invisibles cases both raise); 218 of 600 differed before |
| `convert_to_process_tree(dfg, sa, ea)` and the tree of the invisibles net (`/api/model-exchange` dfg to ptml) | 320 DFGs x 2 | 637/640; 3 declared below |
| `convert_to_process_tree` of reference DFG nets (`--pnml-to-ptml`) | 729 nets | 729/729 |
| `convert_to_process_tree(net)` of tree, inductive, alpha and heuristics nets (`--pnml-to-ptml`, `net_to_tree`) | 1,000 nets | 1,000/1,000 (694 trees, 306 both raise); 116 of 400 differed before, one the declared hash-order case |
| `convert_to_petri_net(bpmn)` of `convert_to_bpmn(tree)` and `discover_bpmn_inductive` (`/api/model-exchange` bpmn to pnml) | 640 | 640 isomorphic |
| `convert_to_process_tree(bpmn)` (`--bpmn-to-ptml`, model exchange) | 640 | 640/640 after the fix (557 trees, 83 both raise) |
| `convert_to_process_tree(powl)` (`powl_to_tree`) | 650 | 650/650 after the fix; 20 of 100 differed before |
| heuristics net to Petri (`--pnml-miner heuristic` against `discover_petri_net_heuristics`) | 330 logs | 330 isomorphic |
| `convert_to_dataframe(log)` (`--log-convert to_data_frame`) | 710 logs | 710 equal (column order, cells, missing values) |
| `convert_to_event_stream(log)` (`--log-convert to_event_stream`) | 350 logs | 350 equal (event order, key order, values) |

Not exposed natively: `convert_log_to_ocel`, `convert_ocel_to_log` (the OCEL
flattening route is `ocel_flattening`, compared earlier) and DFG discovery
from nets. Skipped as matched in earlier rounds: tree to Petri, tree to BPMN,
Petri to BPMN to Petri and POWL to Petri.

Fixes:

- **DFG to Petri net takes the boundary maps as given.** The public call
  passes both maps, so nothing is inferred: an empty start or end map adds no
  boundary transition in activity-defines-place and raises in
  invisibles-no-duplicates (`KeyError` on the artificial activity; native
  `invalid_argument`). Native inferred boundaries from the graph and fell
  back to every activity. Activity-defines-place builds places only for
  activities on an edge and ignores boundary activities outside them (the DFG
  of the log `[<a>]` converts to a bare source and sink), while
  invisibles-no-duplicates keeps them. Every key counts whatever its
  frequency (native skipped zero counts). Test: `minera_dfg_conversion_tests`
  (`empty_boundaries_are_explicit`, `boundary_activities_outside_edges`).
- **Workflow net to process tree folds like the reference.** Nested
  sequences flatten (`->('a', ->('b', 'c'))` is `->('a', 'b', 'c')`), an
  exclusive choice keeps one tau (`X(tau, X(tau, 'a'))` is `X(tau, 'a')`),
  sequences and parallels drop taus, a loop of taus is a tau and a one-child
  operator is its child. A valid net with a single transition raises, as the
  reference does (`AssertionError` for a visible, `AttributeError` for a
  silent one); two or more transitions in a chain convert. The reference's
  tree-to-Petri conversion already folds silent steps, so the net of
  `->(tau, 'a')` is such a net. A loop whose do part ends in self-loops at its
  end place (activity-defines-place nets of DFGs with an `a -> a` edge) is
  now `->(rest, *(tau, cycles))`; the strict reducer rejected it as not
  block-structured. The same applies to BPMN to tree and model-exchange
  PTML. Test: `minera_powl_conversion_tests`
  (`workflow_net_to_process_tree_shapes_match_reference`, 55 captured nets,
  `scripts/capture-net-to-tree-shape-reference.py`).
- **POWL to process tree keeps frequency leaves.** `convert_to_process_tree`
  keeps a `FrequentTransition` as one leaf labelled `"<label>\n[1,<max or
  ->]"` when it is optional or self-looping, as its Petri-net conversion
  does; native expanded it into `X(tau, a)` or `*(a, tau)`. Tests:
  `minera_powl_conversion_tests`. Eight model-conversion workbench captures
  were refreshed with `scripts/capture-workbench-fixtures.py`.
- **POWL PTML downloads convert the POWL model.** POWL discovery's PTML
  (`/api/discover-workflow?family=powl`, `/api/ptml?miner=powl`,
  `minera_export --powl-ptml`) reduced the POWL's workflow net, which now
  raises for the one-transition net of a one-activity log; it converts the
  POWL itself, as `convert_to_process_tree(powl)` does (the leaf `'a'`; a
  residual partial order is layered, `a->c, b->c, b->d` giving
  `->(+('a','b'), +('c','d'))`, as the reference). Alpha and heuristics
  PTML still reduce their nets and raise on a one-transition net, as the
  reference. Tests: `minera_powl_conversion_tests`
  (`powl_ptml_converts_the_model_directly`),
  `minera_export_powl_ptml_one_activity_cli`.
- **PNML with places but no transitions.** The activity-defines-place net of
  a DFG without edges (the DFG of `[<a>]`) is a source and a sink place;
  `write_pnml` and `read_pnml` keep it, and the PNML reader now does too
  (it refused a net without transitions, so model exchange of such a DFG
  failed with 400 and lost the DFG data). A PNML without any place is still
  refused. Model exchange also reports a DFG net the reader cannot take back
  as `conversion_error` with the DFG data. Test:
  `minera_dfg_conversion_tests` (`boundary_activities_outside_edges`).
  Such a net now reaches the consumers, so two follow-ups:
  - Decomposed alignment of a net without transitions raises (400 on
    `/api/align-decomposed`): pm4py's `decomposed.apply` raises
    `ValueError: m must be a positive integer` on it, whatever the log,
    where native returned fitness 1 with no moves. A net with only silent
    transitions still aligns at cost 0 and fitness 1, as pm4py does. Test:
    `minera_decomposed_alignment_tests`.
  - Its PTML export (and `net_to_tree`) now says "workflow-net to process
    tree conversion requires a transition" instead of naming the POWL
    conversion; `net_to_powl` keeps the POWL wording (pm4py raises "not a
    WF-net" for both). Test: `minera_powl_conversion_tests`. The recorded
    workbench captures keep the old text.

Declared:

- **Loop shapes that follow hash order (declared).** When a loop place has a
  self-loop and another redo path, the reference reduces either the self-loop
  first (`*(*('c', tau), redo)`) or both redo paths as one choice
  (`*('c', X(tau, redo))`) depending on `PYTHONHASHSEED`; native always
  builds the choice. The languages are equal. Seen on 1 of 1,400 discovered
  nets and 3 of 640 DFG trees; each checked case gives both shapes across
  seeds 0 to 9.
- **Artificial DFG activity names (declared).** invisibles-no-duplicates
  defaults to `@@start@@`/`@@end@@` and refuses an activity with the same
  name; the reference uses `▶`/`■` and merges such an activity into the
  artificial one.

## Importer fuzzing: CSV timestamps, CSV parsing and XES frames (2026-11-05)

Fuzzed against `pandas.read_csv` + `pm4py.format_dataframe` and
`pm4py.read_xes` (DataFrame), 300 cases per category, seed 7 after fixes.
CSV parsing (9 categories, 2,700) and XES (9 categories, 2,700) differ only
as declared below, apart from 2 XES column-dtype cases (metadata and
duplicate keys) not yet examined.

CSV timestamps were not clean, as first claimed here: a review fuzz (seed
23, 3,000 multi-row columns) still found about 130 mismatching columns
(lowercase `utc` 83, `.`-separated dates with a nanosecond fraction 23,
hour-only offsets before trimmed padding 5, years such as `8 May 0001` 8,
large offsets past year 9999 6, other 5). After the follow-up fixes below, two new
3,000-column sets (seed 31 with the shapes above; seed 32 with 60% of the
cells from short-year, month-name, zone-case, `.`-date and large-offset
shapes) leave no mismatch except the declared ones: 70 and 152 columns
without any date that native keeps as text (declared below), and 6 cells
of seed 32 (year 0, and offsets past ±14:00 whose instant leaves years
1..9999 by more than the ±14:00 shift absorbs).

Fixed:

- **Timestamp resolution.** Cells that pandas parses through its ISO path
  keep nanoseconds; the shapes it hands to dateutil (lowercase `t`/`z`,
  `UTC`/`GMT` words, comma fraction, extra spaces, slash or text dates,
  AM/PM, weekday, an hour-only offset followed by whitespace) now truncate
  to microseconds, as the reference. `YYYY-Mon-DD` is accepted, and offsets
  beyond ±14:00 up to ±23:59 are converted to UTC.
- **Nanosecond range.** When any ISO cell has more than six fraction digits
  the column moves to nanoseconds, and a cell outside
  1677-09-21 00:12:43.145224193 .. 2262-04-11 23:47:16.854775807 (wall
  clock or UTC) leaves the column unconverted: the CSV importer refuses
  such a column, `format_dataframe` keeps it as text.
- **`timest_format`.** The format matches anywhere in the cell (leading and
  trailing text ignored), ISO-shaped formats keep their whole-cell quirks,
  and a cell shorter than the format (a case id `1` under `%d %b %Y`) no
  longer becomes 1900-01-01.
- **XES nested attributes.** For `iterparse` children kept in a dict, a
  repeated key keeps the first position with the last value; a later list
  attribute under a first-class key drops the earlier scalar selection; a
  nested `org:resource` keeps its document column position.
- **Timestamp follow-up (review).**
  - An hour-only offset before trimmed padding
    (`2024-07-05T05:10:33.6525764 +00 `) is a dateutil shape on the
    importer's fallback path too: microseconds, so a column with it and
    1500-01-01 imports instead of being refused as out of the nanosecond
    range.
  - The nanosecond rule counts the fraction after the seconds, not after
    the first `.`, so `2024.10.09 06:17:12.186788426` beside 1500-01-01
    leaves the column unconverted (CSV refused, `format_dataframe` keeps
    text).
  - Only uppercase `UTC` and `GMT` are zone names; `utc`, `Utc`, `gmt`
    fail as in pandas.
  - Years follow dateutil: a year joined by `-`, `/` or `.` with three or
    four digits is literal (`8-May-0001` is year 1, `075.08.22` year 75),
    one with one or two digits is two-digit; a year separated by white
    space is a number, two-digit below 100 (`8 May 0001` and
    `13 09 0001` are 2001). A first number that cannot be a day is the
    two-digit year (`40-03-03`, `40 Sep 28`, `0040 Sep 28` are 2040), a
    leading three-digit token is a year when joined or from 100 on, and
    plain space-separated numbers are ordered month-first unless the first
    cannot be a month (`009 08 05` is 2005-09-08).
  - A space-separated `YYYY MM DD` is on pandas' ISO path (nanoseconds
    kept); a cell that leaves the ISO path (lowercase `z`, `UTC`, AM/PM,
    ...) is read by dateutil as three numbers (`0040 09 14T14:41:11 z` is
    2040-09-14, `0001 09 28T11:46:53 z` is 2028-01-09).
  - An offset past ±14:00 whose UTC instant leaves years 1..9999
    (`9999-12-31T20:00:00-15:00`) is stored as the same instant at -14:00
    or +14:00 when that wall clock fits, instead of refusing the column.

Tests: `minera_core_tests` (`csv_timestamps_follow_pandas_resolution_and_offsets`,
`csv_events_order_at_nanoseconds`), `minera_dataframe_format_tests`
(`str_timestamps_follow_public_parsing`), `minera_xes_io_tests`
(`iterparse_nested_attribute_shapes`).

Declared:

- **Field trimming (declared).** `trim_fields` defaults to true; pandas keeps
  padding in string cells.
- **Year 0 and far offsets (declared).** pandas holds year 0
  (`0000-12-26`, `0000 06 17`) and an instant such as
  `9999-12-31T23:59:00-23:59` (UTC 10000-01-01); the native timestamp
  holds years 1 to 9999, so such a column is refused. A large offset that
  is kept is stored at ±14:00 or UTC, not with its own offset.
- **Invalid UTF-8 CSV (declared).** Latin-1 bytes are read; pandas raises
  `UnicodeDecodeError`.
- **Epoch and date-free timestamp columns (declared).** Kept as opaque text,
  as already documented; pandas gives an int64 or object column.
- **XES trace without `concept:name` (declared).** Native keeps a null
  `case:concept:name` column; the reference omits it.
- **XES `<values>` entry with child elements (declared).** Native reads it
  (its own writer emits such lists); `read_xes` raises `TypeError`.
- **Empty XES containers (declared).** An empty `<list>` is an empty
  container natively, `None` in the reference; a scalar whose only children
  are dropped is a plain value natively, `{'value': v, 'children': {}}` in
  the reference.
- **Uncovered timestamp shapes (declared).** Time-only cells (`10:00`, whose
  pandas result depends on the current day) and POSIX-inverted
  `UTC+02:00`/`GMT+2` offsets are not reproduced.

## Review U2: decorations of large concurrent nets, temporal and conformance JSON, top-k variants (2026-11-05)

Random logs were run through `/api/mine`, `minera_export` and
`/api/temporal-conformance` and compared with pm4py 2.7.22 public calls.

Fixes:

- **Petri decorations use the token replay's firings.** `decorate_model`
  took its firings from the clean silent-routing replay, whose routing to the
  final marking searched the marking graph breadth-first up to 4096
  markings. A net with k concurrent optional branches (the inductive and
  POWL nets of a random log: a parallel of `xor(tau, loop(a, tau))`) has
  about 3^k such markings, so from eight branches on every case came back
  undecorated, silently, while token replay fit them all (300 cases, 8
  activities: 0/300 decorated, reference and native token replay 300/300;
  5,000 cases, 20 activities: 0/5000 decorated in 9.8 s). The decoration now
  replays each variant with the forward token replay of `check_conformance`
  (the replay pm4py's frequency and performance decorations use) and
  decorates the variants it fits (no missing, no remaining tokens) with the
  transitions that replay activates, per event and for the final routing:
  300/300 and 5000/5000, the latter in about 0.4 s of replay. Transition
  counts equal the replay's activation counts. Token replay fires silent
  transitions greedily and can reject a variant that has a clean path (7 of
  150 cases on one POWL net of the fast-path bank), so variants it rejects
  still get the bounded clean replay, as before; the silent transitions it
  fires for a fitting variant can differ from that search's shortest routing,
  which moves silent-transition counts. Nets with inhibitor or reset
  arcs keep the clean replay; a variant whose silent search stops at the
  bound is counted in `capped_variants`, and after 16 such variants without
  one decorated the rest are skipped and counted too. The decoration JSON
  then carries `capped_variants` and a `message`; a decoration that covers
  no case says why (`message`), and the Petri net view shows it. Both fields
  are absent otherwise. Test: `minera_core_tests`
  (`decorate_model_fits_parallel_optional_loops`).
- **Zero-variance temporal distance.** `/api/temporal-conformance` printed
  the `sys.maxsize` distance of a zero-deviation pair as the double
  `9.2233720368547758e+18` (2**63); it now prints the reference integer
  `9223372036854775807`, as the streaming route already did. The batch log
  and dataframe conformance now set `zero_variance_sentinel` on such pairs
  (they left it false), so every serializer that honours it prints the
  integer.
  Fresh: 0/400 random logs, dataframe and log variants. Test:
  `minera_temporal_profile_parity_contracts_tests`.
- **Full-precision conformance fitness.** The `/api/mine` log-skeleton and
  Declare conformance printed `dev_fitness` with six significant digits
  (21/22 as `0.954545`); it is now the shortest round-trip double
  (`0.9545454545454546`). Test: `minera_core_tests`.
- **Top-k variants of zero.** `top_variants` (`--top-variants`, `/api/mine`
  `top_variants`, `LogFilterOptions::top_variants`) used 0 for "no limit";
  it is now optional, and 0 keeps no variant, as
  `pm4py.filter_variants_top_k(log, 0)` does. The frontend never sends 0.

Unchanged and matched on random inputs: log skeleton (noise 0-0.5) and
Declare discovery and conformance, temporal-profile discovery (CSV and XES);
variant and case filters on CSV and XES; token-replay diagnostics (two
differences where the reference depends on `PYTHONHASHSEED`); soundness and
Woflan; OCEL flattening from OCEL 1.0 JSON, 2.0 JSON and 2.0 XML; the prefix
tree.

## Review U1: CSV timestamp paths, A* bounds on non-ordinary nets, mine progress (2026-11-05)
