Fixes after a review of Round T, checked against `pandas.read_csv` +
`pm4py.format_dataframe` outputs only.

- **pandas' ISO path is tracked on its own.** The importer used one flag
  for "ISO spelling" and "pandas' ISO path". The ISO path also takes a
  one-digit hour, an hour alone and `HH:MM`, so a spaced `YYYY M D` with
  such a clock is literal (`0047 1 8 9:36` and `0047 01 08 19` are year
  47) and `2024-01-01 9:00:00.123456789` keeps its nanoseconds (beside
  1500-01-01 the column is refused, as the reference keeps it as text). A
  one-digit hour alone is no clock unless AM/PM follows (`2089-05-26 9`
  leaves the column text; `03/26/2089 9 PM` is 21:00). Trailing white
  space after a spaced date alone leaves the ISO path (`0060 3 20 ` is
  2060-03-20; `0060-03-20 ` and `0060 3 20 10:00 ` stay year 60).
- **Spaced dates that are no ISO date.** A spaced `YYYY MM DD` that is
  invalid read literally falls back to dateutil's order (`0024 11 31` is
  2031-11-24, `0012 13 05` is 2005-12-13); `2024 02 30` still fails.
- **Nanoseconds off the ISO path.** A `.` fraction whose digits 4-6 are
  `000` keeps its nanoseconds on the dateutil path too
  (`2024-01-01t10:00:00.12300045`, `... .123000456 UTC`), so such a column
  needs the nanosecond range; other fractions and every `,` fraction keep
  microseconds.
- **Year 0 on the dateutil path.** pandas holds year 0 only on its ISO
  path; a dateutil-shaped year-0 cell (`0000-05-26t17:01:52`,
  `0000-05-26 17:01:52 +01 `) leaves the column text, so the importer
  refuses it as for any unparsable cell.
- **A* model-run bounds.** The marking-equation bounds (the LP, its dual
  and the parent-plan bound) assume a firing adds the transition's
  incidence column. A reset arc, an inhibitor arc, or two weighted input
  arcs on one place (each checked on its own, so `b` with two weight-2
  arcs fires on two tokens) break that, and the pruned model-run search
  could prune a marking that reaches the final marking and call a fitting
  net unreachable. On such nets the search now uses no bound; a run it
  cannot finish within `max_states` is reported exhausted. Random nets
  (1,500 per generator mode, ordinary, weighted, negative-weight,
  reset/inhibitor, structured): ordinary nets' results and diagnostics are
  unchanged; on the affected nets some results move from unreachable or
  computed to exhausted.
- **Mine progress.** Native-dispatch stages are named (`Alpha miner`,
  `Inductive net: conformance`, ...); the OCEL discovery path no longer
  polls `/api/mine-progress`.

Fuzz: 10 sets of 3,000 multi-row CSV timestamp columns (seeds 202-204,
301-302, 401-402, 601-603), new importer vs Round T vs reference: no column
that Round T matched now differs; the remaining mismatches are the
declared year-0 and `9999-12-31T23:59:00-23:59` shapes.

Tests: `minera_core_tests`
(`csv_timestamps_follow_pandas_resolution_and_offsets`,
`mine_progress_names_native_families`), `minera_alignment_variants_tests`
(reset-arc and repeated-weight nets), frontend `mine-progress.test.ts`.

## Review V1: reachability on non-ordinary nets, decoration replay cost, CSV timestamp shapes (2026-11-08)

Fixes after a review of Round U, checked against pm4py 2.7.22 and
`pandas.read_csv` + `pm4py.format_dataframe` outputs only.

- **Reachability no longer stalls on non-ordinary nets.** Since Round U the
  pruned model-run search applied no marking-equation bound to nets with
  reset or inhibitor arcs or repeated weighted input arcs, which made it the
  same uniform-cost search as the first preflight. A net with an unbounded
  cost-0 silent pump (`source → τ → p1`, `τ: p1 → p1 + q`, `a: p1 → sink`)
  then exhausted both searches, and `final_marking_reachable` reported a
  reachable net as unreachable ("unsound") when it had an inhibitor arc on an
  always-empty place, a reset arc, or one dead transition with two weight-2
  inputs. Now:
  - inhibitor arcs keep the marking-equation bounds: they only restrict when
    a transition is enabled, and the firing still adds its incidence column,
    so the relaxation stays valid;
  - on nets with reset arcs or repeated weighted inputs (where the equation
    does not describe firing) the fallback is a breadth-first search over
    firing counts with the same state budget, which a cost-0 pump cannot
    stall (the four nets above are reachable);
  - the trace-alignment LP heuristic is off on the same nets (it was off only
    for reset and inhibitor arcs), so the state-equation A* aligns `<a, b>` on
    a net where `b` has two weight-2 inputs instead of reporting it exhausted;
  - the soundness check of `/api/mine`, active-source mining, the imported
    model route and `minera_export` keeps "the search stopped at its budget"
    apart from "unreachable" (`final_marking_reachability`); the model
    conformance JSON then carries `"reachability_exhausted": true` next to
    `"sound": false` (absent otherwise), and the frontend says the soundness
    check reached its limit instead of calling the model unsound, and still
    offers alignments (whose own state limit can be raised).
  Tests: `minera_core_tests` (`final_marking_reachability_keeps_exhausted_apart`),
  `minera_alignment_variants_tests`, frontend `alignment-uncomputed.test.ts`.
- **Decoration replay cost.** The Round U decoration replayed every variant
  through `replay_token_traces`, which also computes each row's enabled
  transitions at the reached marking; that was about two thirds of its time
  (50,000 random cases, 48,085 variants: Heuristics net 11.3 s, Inductive
  8.8 s). The decoration now takes the same rows without the enabled
  transitions (`token_replay_firing_sequences`): 4.6 s and 6.9 s (Alpha 1.6
  s, mostly the bounded search on the variants the replay rejects). Decorations
  are byte-identical to Round U on 56 random logs and nets (mined inductive,
  Heuristics and Alpha nets, process trees with duplicate labels) except the
  one trace of the next item; transition counts still equal pm4py's token
  replay activations over fitting traces on the mined nets. Reusing the rows of the
  `/api/mine` conformance replay was not done: that replay follows the
  request's token-replay options and per-miner activity keys, and records no
  per-event firings, so its rows are not the decoration's.
- **Activities outside the model.** The decoration skipped a trace that holds
  an activity the net lacks although the token replay (and pm4py) count it
  fit, since the replay skips such events (`e, d, b, d, b, d, a` against a net
  without `a`). It is now decorated with the other events' firings; the
  skipped event fires nothing. Test: `minera_core_tests`
  (`decorate_model_skips_activities_outside_the_model`).
- **CSV: fractions past 18 digits.** pandas' ISO path reads at most 18
  fraction digits; a longer fraction goes through dateutil and keeps
  microseconds (`2024-07-16T17:50:56.3650503944960724188` is `.365050`), as
  any dateutil fraction does, including the zero-microseconds rule
  (`.123000456496072418801` keeps `.123000456`). The importer kept
  nanoseconds.
- **CSV: offset minutes 60-99.** dateutil adds them to the hours while the
  offset stays below 24 hours (`+01:90` is +02:30, `-0099` is -01:39,
  `+23:60` fails); the fraction is then truncated to microseconds. The
  importer kept such a column as text.
- **CSV: mixed date separators.** Two different separators among `-`, `/`
  and white space read as dateutil reads them: `2024-12/07`, `2024 3/5`,
  `25-12/2024`, `07 12-2024` (month-first unless the first number cannot be
  a month), a leading four-digit year literal when joined (`0005-06/19` is
  year 5) and a number after a space (`0005 06-19` is 2019-05-06); a
  trailing year is joined by its own `-` or `/` after a space (`28 07-0057`
  is year 57) but a plain number after another joined separator
  (`15-04/0001` is 2001); a leading number above 31 is a literal year before
  a space (`57 7/0001` is 0057-07-01) and two-digit otherwise (`33-01 0011`
  is 2033-01-11). These cells are on dateutil's path (microseconds).
  Fuzz: 13,811 fresh one- to four-row columns (seeds 9101, 7331, 5150, 4242,
  8888, 6161-6464 and a separator matrix): every remaining mismatch is a
  declared year-0 shape or a `.` mix below. Test: `minera_core_tests`
  (`csv_timestamps_review_v1_shapes`).

Declared:

- **Date separators mixed with `.` (declared).** dateutil reads a token such
  as `12.07` as a decimal number, so mixes with `.` follow rules of their own:
  `07.12-2024`, `25-12.2024` and `07/12.2024` read day/month first as dates
  alone but are text with a clock; `2024.12 07` is 2024-07-01 and
  `2024 12.07` 2024-12-01; `2024-12.07` and `2024.12-07` are text. The
  importer keeps every such cell as text (a column of them stays text, and
  next to dates it is refused).

## Review V2: business-hour clocks, CSV XES offsets, BPMN markings, playout size (2026-11-08)

Fixes after a random-input sweep against pm4py (public API outputs only).

- **V2-1 Business hours on the DataFrame clock.** Case durations
  (`CaseStatisticsOptions`), service time (`ServiceTimeOptions`) and passed
  time (`PassedTimeOptions`) take `dataframe`: business hours then count on
  the UTC clock (a CSV offset converted, as `format_dataframe` converts
  it), as the DFG already did; off, each timestamp's own wall clock (the
  EventLog path). Passed time keeps its EventLog arithmetic
  (`DfgStatisticalOptions::business_hours_utc_clock`). The server sets it
  for CSV and XES sources, `minera_export` always. `06:30+02:00` to
  `08:00+02:00` with 07:00-17:00 hours: 3600 s on the wall clock, 0 s on
  the UTC clock (04:30-06:00), as pm4py's DataFrame functions give.
- **V2-2 CSV sources download UTC XES.** `XesExportOptions::utc_timestamps`
  writes each offset timestamp as its UTC instant with `+00:00` (the
  fraction digits kept); the server sets it with `standard_keys` (CSV
  sources). pm4py reads XES dates as wall-clock UTC, so `+02:00` read two
  hours off; the download now reads back to the CSV's instants. XES
  sources keep their own offsets (see "UI downloads read back with pm4py").
- **V2-3 BPMN and PTML imports: simplicity's marking.** An imported model
  without a PNML document now gives extended cyclomatic simplicity the
  conversion's initial marking (one token on its source, pm4py's
  `convert_to_petri_net` im), not one token on every input-free place,
  which a BPMN conversion leaves in dangling gateways or disconnected parts.
- **V2-4 BPMN-converted nets and alignment precision (declared).** Minera's
  BPMN conversion gives a net with the same labels, places, arcs and
  markings as `convert_to_petri_net`, but pm4py's alignment precision on
  its own conversion depends on internal names and iteration order: on
  `q17.bpmn` pm4py gives 0.41463414634146345 on its conversion (also after
  a PNML round trip), 0.41975308641975306 on Minera's exported net (Minera's
  value) and 0.4533 with transitions renamed. No black-box rule
  reproduces it, so the difference is declared.
- **V2-5 Single-case arrival and dispersion on the DataFrame path are
  NaN** (pandas' mean of no gaps), written as `null` like other NaN
  statistics; the EventLog path keeps 0.
- **Generalization summation order (S-1).** `evaluate_generalization` sums
  the fired transitions in the order they first fire, trace by trace, then
  1 for each unfired transition. In net order the sum differed in its last
  bits (repro `q76`: 0.36024727322755135 vs 0.36024727322755146). This order
  matched pm4py on 150 of 150 random nets (net order 122, `fsum` 113).
  The mine view's `compute_generalization` (conformance.cpp) still sums
  in net order.
- **Playout responses.** `/api/playout-workbench` sends generated logs as a
  compact native_state (`serialize_active_source_log_compact_json`):
  `legacy_view` is null, `defaults` hold the first trace's and event's
  fields, `activity_table` each activity once, and each event writes only
  `activity_ref` and the fields that differ. The frontend
  (`expandPlayoutEvents`) rebuilds every complete event for the
  generated-events table. The generated log's XES is opt-in
  (`export_generated_xes=true`); the frontend asks again with it when the
  XES is downloaded or opened, and refuses the XES if the repeated run's
  result differs. `/api/playout` visited JSON writes `transition_labels`
  once, and the typed adapters put `activity` back on each element, so
  the shown and downloaded JSON is unchanged. 10,000 cases of a
  5-transition sequence with 200-character names: response 97.7 MB (gzip
  1.40 MB) to 3.86 MB (gzip 0.17 MB), 22.1 MB with the XES; server peak RSS
  511 MB to 156 MB; time 2.1 s to 1.0 s. Recaptured fixtures: the 48
  unchanged entries are byte-identical, the 50 changed ones differ only in
  the encoding (checked by expanding them against the old responses), and
  every generated XES is byte-identical.

Fuzz against the new server: business-hour passed time and DFG on CSV logs with
offsets (60 logs), business-hour service time (80): no mismatch. BPMN
round-trip quality (60): only the declared V2-4 alignment precision. PNML
quality (60 + 80) and XES download round trips (60): no new mismatch. The
remaining fuzzer reports compare pm4py's in-memory net, not the PNML it
wrote; on the read-back net pm4py and Minera agree bit for bit. A
CSV with `+02:00` offsets downloads `+00:00` XES that `read_xes` reads back to
`format_dataframe`'s instants.

Tests: `minera_case_statistics_tests`, `minera_service_time_tests`,
`minera_passed_time_tests`, `minera_case_arrival_tests`,
`minera_xes_io_tests` (`csv_downloads_write_utc_timestamps`),
`minera_evaluation_tests` (`cyclomatic_bpmn_import_uses_conversion_source_marking`),
`minera_playout_tests`, `minera_playout_workbench_json_tests`
(`compact_generated_log_writes_each_event_once`),
`minera_active_event_source_tests`; frontend `types.test.ts`,
`playout-workbench.test.ts`, `playout-workbench-fixtures.test.ts` (recaptured).

## Review W1: two-digit years after a space, filtered XES clocks, drained pumps, playout XES (2026-11-08)

Fixes after a review of Round V, checked against `pandas.read_csv` +
`pm4py.format_dataframe` and pm4py 2.7.22 outputs only.

- **W1-1 Two-digit leading years.** A leading number above 31 before a space
  followed by a joined month and day is a literal year only when the day is
  written with more than two digits (`57 7/0001` and `57 7/001` are year 57);
  otherwise it is a two-digit year (`40 3/15` is 2040-03-15, `99 05/27 07:17`
  1999-05-27 07:17, `57 07/01` 2057-07-01). Round V read all of them as year
  00NN (128 of a 1,344-cell separator matrix). A year-first date joined by
  `-` or `/` and then another separator also takes a day of up to four digits
  with leading zeros (`2024-1/0015 10:00` is 2024-01-15 10:00, `2024/01 031`
  2024-01-31; `2024-01/1500` stays unconverted; 32 matrix cells were text),
  and so does a date of three numbers separated by white space alone, read in
  dateutil's order of three numbers (`2023 05 012` is 2023-05-12, `0012 05
  031` 2031-12-05, `99 05 012` 1999-05-12; 532 of a 1,350-cell spaced matrix
  were text, now 0 mismatches). Separator matrix: the 16 remaining cells are
  the declared shape below; fresh-seed fuzz of one- to four-row columns
  (seeds 8123, 6029, 3301, 5717, 9902): no unexplained mismatch. Test: `minera_core_tests` (`csv_timestamps_review_v1_shapes`).
- **W1-2 Filtered XES downloads of CSV sources write UTC.**
  `/api/log-query/export?format=xes` and `/api/log-cluster` (XES) set
  `utc_timestamps` with `standard_keys`, as `/api/xes` does; they wrote the
  source offset, which pm4py reads as wall-clock UTC. Test:
  `minera_server_traces_route_tests` (`MINERA_TEST_SERVER_PORT` pins its ports).
- **W1-3 Drained silent pumps.** `source → τ → source + sink`, `sink → τ`,
  `a: source + sink → sink` keeps the marking equation feasible on every pumped
  marking, so the pruned A* stops at its budget (equal-f ties go to the
  cost-0 pump). `final_marking_reachability` and `final_marking_reachable` then
  search breadth-first with the same budget, deadline and cancellation and
  find `τ, a`. Alignment preflights keep the A* outcome (their search counters
  and outputs are unchanged; 1,500 random ordinary nets byte-identical to
  Round V). Test: `minera_core_tests`
  (`final_marking_reachability_keeps_exhausted_apart`).
- **W1-4 Playout "Include generated XES".** The playout workbench has a
  checkbox for log-returning operations that requests `export_generated_xes`.
  When a re-run for a download returns a different log (only a wall-clock
  limit such as `max_execution_time_ms` makes that happen; seeds always
  default), the message points at the checkbox. Test: frontend
  `playout-workbench.test.ts`.
- **W1-5 Undecided reachability is not "unsound".** The POWL workflow-net
  conversion and the log alignment dispatcher (for nets outside its weighted
  easy-soundness check) say the reachability search reached its limit
  ("undecided") instead of "requires a reachable final marking" / "not easy
  sound". Test: `minera_petri_analysis_tests`.

Declared:

- **Space-first four-digit year with a three- or four-digit day
  (declared).** dateutil reads `YYYY M-DDD` / `YYYY M/DDDD` by value: for
  years 0001-0031 the long trailing number is the year (`0012 01-0015` is
  0015-12-01), for 0032-0100 it is the day (`0045 1-0015` is 0045-01-15), and
  from about 0999 the cell fails. The importer keeps such a cell as text.

## Review W2: DFG export filters, .dfg export of edgeless activities, IMf at noise 1 (2026-11-08)

Fixes and declarations after a random-input sweep against pm4py (public API
outputs only).

- **W2-1 DFG export filters run the reference port.** `GET /api/dfg` (and so
  the frontend's DFG export) and `minera_dfg` used the earlier native filters
  (`dfg_filter.cpp`, removed), which differed from
  `algo.filtering.dfg.dfg_filtering`: `contain_activity` kept every start
  activity that reaches the activity (log `ab,b`, `contain_activity=a`:
  reference starts `{a:1}`, native `{a:1, b:1}`), `paths_percentage` broke
  count ties differently (log `abc,ac,ab` at 0.5: reference ends `{c:2}`,
  native `{b:1, c:2}`), and a chained filter could refuse an activity the
  reference keeps (log `aba`, `paths_percentage=0&to_activity=b`: reference
  `{a>b:1}`, native "target activity is unknown"). Both routes now build a
  `DfgFilteringRequest` and call `apply_dfg_filtering_request`
  (`dfg_filtering.hpp`): noise cleaning (`clean_dfg_based_on_noise_thresh`,
  edges only), activities percentage, paths percentage, keep connected, to,
  from and contain activity, in that order. Reference errors keep their
  class: the server answers 400 and the CLI exits 1 with `KeyError: 'a'`
  (log `ca,cb`, `to_activity=b&contain_activity=a`).
  - The server passes the mined log's DFG with its real activity counts
    (`dfg_filtering_data_from_graph`), the `discover_dfg(log)` and
    `get_event_attribute_values(log, activity)` a reference user passes.
  - A `.dfg` file carries no activity counts. `dfg_filtering_data_from_dfg`
    gives each activity on an edge max(sum of its incoming edge counts, sum
    of its outgoing edge counts) and gives activities that occur only as
    start or end activities no entry. This is what the reference's public
    `pm4py.filter_dfg_activities_percentage` and
    `pm4py.filter_dfg_paths_percentage` (which take only dfg, start and end)
    use: across 1,500 random DFGs (3,000 wrapper calls) this rule
    reproduced every result, and in-sum, out-sum, in+out, boundary-inclusive
    sums, `dfg_utils.sum_activities_count` and constant counts did not. The
    CLI uses the same counts for keep-connected and the activity filters,
    which have no public count-free wrapper.
- **W2-2 `.dfg` export of edgeless start/end activities (declared).** When a
  start or end activity occurs on no directly-follows edge (a one-event
  trace, or a filter that removed its edges), `pm4py.write_dfg` raises
  ValueError (`'a' is not in list`; log `a` + `bc`). Minera's `.dfg` writer
  (`minera_export --dfg`, `GET /api/dfg`, `minera_dfg`) lists every edge,
  start and end activity and writes the file, which `pm4py.read_dfg` reads
  back to the same three dictionaries.
- **W2-3 IMf at `noise_threshold=1.0` depends on the hash seed (declared).**
  At noise 1 the reference's IMf tree changes with `PYTHONHASHSEED`: log
  `acac,c` gives `X( *( 'a', tau ), 'c' )` for 5 of 8 seeds and
  `X( tau, *( 'c', tau ) )` for 3; `caabdf,caabdff,cccbdffe,caabdf,ffdbeab,ecf,cef`
  gives four different trees over 10 seeds. Minera gives one deterministic
  tree, which was among the reference's outcomes in every checked case
  (seeds 17, 22 and 65 of the sweep, 10 hash seeds each). Below 1 (300 logs
  at 0 to 0.8, two hash seeds) the trees match exactly.

Matched in the same sweep, no change: heuristics miner to Petri net with
dependency, AND, loop-two, minimum activity and minimum edge thresholds (360
logs); transition systems over the three views, both directions and windows
0-5 (400 logs, apart from the declared Counter/set behaviour); Alpha+ within
`--alpha-plus-alternatives`, detached markings included (400); IMd from a
DFG (250); process tree to net to PNML to `--pnml-to-ptml` against
`convert_to_process_tree` (400 trees, exact strings); `minera_dfg
--to-petri`, both variants (250 x 2); `/api/dfg` noise cleaning (80 logs x 6
thresholds).

Fuzz against the new server: GET /api/dfg with random chains of all seven
filters (250 logs x 6 requests) and each filter alone (80 logs x 6 requests
per filter) against the reference functions with `discover_dfg` and
`get_event_attribute_values`: every response has the reference's edges,
start and end activities, and every reference error is a 400 with its class.
The `.dfg` byte order is not compared, because the reference writer orders
activities by string hash.

Tests: `minera_dfg_filter_route_tests` (server and CLI repros above, and the
`.dfg` count rule; replaces `minera_dfg_filter_tests`, which tested the native
filters), `minera_filtering_common_bank_parity_tests` (the reference port).

## Review X2: OCEL numeric attribute filters, choice caps in tree playout, `.dfg` labels, POWL (2026-11-08)

Random inputs were run through `/api/ocel/filter`, `/api/ocel/statistics`,
`minera_export` (POWL discovery, POWL nets and PTML, XES round trips, process
tree EXTENSIVE playout), `minera_tree_reduction` and `minera_dfg`, and compared
with pm4py 2.7.22 public calls.

Fixes:

- **OCEL attribute filters compare like pandas `isin` (X2-1).**
  `filter_ocel_event_attribute` / `filter_ocel_object_attribute` (the
  `event_attribute` and `object_attribute` routes) matched values by type, so
  the integer 4 the frontend sends as `i:4` never selected a cell pm4py wrote
  as 4.0 (it does whenever some event lacks the attribute). Booleans,
  integers and floats now meet numerically (1 == 1.0 == True), strings only
  equal strings, and null matches nothing new. Reproducer: events e1
  (`cost` 4.0) and e2 (no cost) on object o1 (`w` 2):
  `event_attribute&attribute_key=cost&attribute_values=i:4` keeps e1 and
  `object_attribute&attribute_key=w&attribute_values=d:2.0` keeps o1, as the
  reference does (native returned nothing). Fuzz: 4,544 filter calls on 400
  random OCELs (14 filter variants), 115 differed before, all on these two
  filters; 0 after (the declared missing-key KeyError aside). Test:
  `minera_ocel_filter_tests`.
- **EXTENSIVE tree playout: a choice checks the limit between children
  (X2-4).** The reference unites a choice child's whole word set and only
  then compares the union with `max_limit_num_traces`; native stopped after
  limit + 1 words. Log `a; b d; b e; c d; c e` (inductive tree
  `X('a', ->(X('c','b'), X('d','e')))`), max length 5, limit 1: the
  reference gives all five words under every hash seed, native gave two.
  Loops still cap per word (probed: `*(X(a,b,c), X(d,e))` with limit 1 gives
  `a`, `b`, which is the capped body choice). The section on
  `max_limit_num_traces` above is corrected. Fuzz (200 inductive trees of
  random logs, `max_trace_length` 1-8, limits 1-100000, `max_loop_occ` unset
  or 0-3, reference under PYTHONHASHSEED 0-9): the word count now matches
  in 198 of 200 (the other two are parallel nodes whose emitted shuffles
  repeat, as declared above); 176 outputs equal a reference outcome and
  the other 24 differ only in which words a capped node keeps. In 12 of them the
  reference keeps the same words under all ten seeds (generation order:
  `+(X(tau,*(a,tau)), ->(X(tau,b),*(c,tau)))`, max length 5, limit 1 gives
  `c`, native `b c`), so the declared set-order difference is not purely
  hash-driven; native keeps word order. Test:
  `minera_process_tree_playout_tests`.
- **`.dfg` writing keeps empty and padded labels (X2-5).** `write_dfg` writes
  every label on its own line as given and `read_dfg` strips it again; native
  refused empty labels and labels with surrounding whitespace ("activity
  labels must be non-empty and single-line"), so a pm4py-written file with an
  empty label read but could not be written back. Only a line break or NUL
  is refused now (`DFG: activity labels must be single-line and free of
  NUL`). The reader and the views already accepted such labels. Test:
  `minera_dfg_io_tests`.

Declared (not found in reasonable time; reproducers kept for a later round):

- **POWL `BRUTE_FORCE` with a filtering weight factor (X2-2).** Traces `b`,
  `b`, `c b`, `b a c`, `b a b` with `filtering_weight_factor` 0.3: the
  reference gives `PO[*(b, tau), X(tau, PO[X(tau,a) --> X(tau,c)])]`, its
  unfiltered model, while native filters the `b` sublog (`{b:4, bb:1}`) to
  `b`. TREE, MAXIMAL and DYNAMIC_CLUSTERING filter it in both. Probes show
  the reference filters BRUTE_FORCE children below sequence cuts,
  concurrency cuts and ordered partial orders that order the child, but not
  a child that is unordered in a partial order that orders its other
  children (13 of about 62 brute-force fuzz runs at 0.3 differ; no rule that
  explains all of them was found).
- **POWL `DYNAMIC_CLUSTERING` repair order (X2-3).** Traces `e c b f`,
  `f d c` (no filtering): the reference gives `X(tau,e) --> PO{c, f,
  X(tau,b), X(tau,d)}` under every hash seed, native `PO{c, f, X(tau,b),
  X(d,e)}`: after merging `{b,c,f}` native coarsens the never co-occurring
  `d` and `e` into a choice, while the reference merges `d` (followed and
  preceded by `{b,c,f}`, neither direction reaching the order ratio) into
  that group. Merging such pairs before choices breaks `x a b, x b a, x a c`,
  where the reference merges the choice first; about 1 in 300 random logs
  differ.

Matched without changes: OCEL filters other than the two above and OCEL
object-type statistics (292 calls); POWL discovery (all four variants, about
1,000 runs without filtering), POWL nets (239, isomorphic) and POWL PTML
(400); XES import/export round trips with lists, containers, nested values,
odd dates, globals and classifiers (400 logs; only the declared empty-list
and `<values>` differences); TREE_TR_BASED reduction (200, every native tree
among the reference's hash-seed outcomes); the `.dfg` reader on 400 mutated
files (only the declared negative and oversized counts).

## Review X1: `.dfg` boundary activities, reserved node names, greedy edge removal, exact XES export, CSV numeric dates (2026-11-08)

Fixes after a review of Round W, checked against pm4py 2.7.22 and
`pandas.read_csv` + `pm4py.format_dataframe` outputs only.

- **X1-1 Start-only and end-only activities on a `.dfg` input.** `minera_dfg
  --to-activity/--from-activity/--contain-activity` gives every start or end
  activity that is on no arc an activity count (the larger of its start and
  end counts) before those steps (`DfgFilteringRequest::count_boundary_activities`);
  the percentage steps keep `max(in, out)` over the arcs. A one-event trace
  `a` (`a` start and end, no arcs) now keeps `a` for `--to-activity a`,
  `--from-activity a` and `--contain-activity a`. CLI fuzz of the three
  steps against the reference called with those counts: 3,000 operations
  (900 with activities named `_S_START_`/`_S_END_`), 0 differences; the
  Round W CLI differed on 237 of 900.
- **X1-2 Internal start and end nodes cannot collide with activities.** The
  port's graph searches use node ids for the artificial start and end, so
  activities named `_S_START_` or `_S_END_` are ordinary activities: every
  filter gives the same result as with the activities renamed (declared
  below).
- **X1-3 Incremental greedy edge removal.** `remove_edges_greedily` keeps one
  adjacency structure with alive flags and a hashed edge index instead of a
  graph copy per trial; an edge on neither search tree is removed without a
  new search (removing it cannot disconnect anything). Outputs are
  byte-identical to Round W (4,500 random cases, the 3,944-edge and
  20,783-edge DFGs under five option sets). `--paths-percentage 0.3`: 3,944
  edges 3.0 s → 0.015 s (pm4py 0.38 s), 20,783 edges 110 s → 0.06 s (pm4py
  32 s); `--keep-connected 0.5` on 20,783 edges 0.07 s.
- **X1-4 Exact multipart XES export.** `POST /api/log-query/export` with
  `format=xes` (the exact-query multipart route) sets `standard_keys` and
  `utc_timestamps` for CSV sources as the plain route does (W1-2); it wrote
  native keys and the source offset.
- **Frontend.** `dfgExportQuery` sends `to_activity`, `from_activity` and
  `contain_activity` untrimmed (white space is part of the label); only an
  empty value is refused.
- **CSV numeric dates in dateutil's reading.** A cell that none of the
  shapes reads and that starts with three numbers joined by `-`, `/` or single
  spaces is read as dateutil does: a number joined by `-` or `/` is text, and
  one of more than two digits is the year with its century; in a token that
  mixes the two separators the last number stands alone; a standalone number
  is read by value and one above 100 is the year; more than one year fails;
  the order is year-first when the first number is above 31 or is the year,
  day-first when it is above 12, else month-first; a year below 100 without
  its century is two-digit (`2024-1/00015` 2024-01-15, `02 0007 2031`
  2031-02-07, `2057 004 22` 2057-04-22, `07-0016 24` 0024-07-16, `0012
  01-0015` 0015-12-01, `0999 1-0015` text). Numbers of more than five digits
  stay text. This supersedes the W1 declaration "Space-first four-digit year
  with a three- or four-digit day": those cells now read.
- **CSV clocks.** One-digit minutes and seconds read (also on pandas' ISO
  path). A fraction of a minute gives the whole seconds of 60 times the
  fraction and no sub-second part (`10:30.5` 10:30:30, `06:37.9` 06:37:54,
  `10:30.` 10:30:00; `10:30.Z` fails, `10:30. Z` reads). AM/PM takes hour 0
  (`0:30 PM` 12:30, `0 AM` 00:00) and may follow the offset or zone once
  (`3:08+05pm` 15:08+05:00, `3:08 UTC pm`; `3:08 Zpm` fails).

Fuzz: 12,500 random numeric-date cells (seeds 7001-7005) against pandas: 9
mismatches, 7 year-0 cells (declared under "Year 0 and far offsets") and 2
nanosecond-fraction cells before 1677, which pandas leaves unconverted and
the importer refuses under the existing nanosecond-range rule (the per-cell
harness compares before that column check); 3,357 cells that Round W read
wrongly now agree. Separator matrix (1,872 cells): 0 mismatches
(72 fixed). Server columns of two to five cells (750, seeds 501-503): 0
mismatches. `/api/dfg` filter chains against the reference (2,000 requests,
odd labels included): 0. `minera_dfg` percentage steps (3,000): 0.

Tests: `minera_dfg_filter_route_tests` (reserved names, one-event `.dfg`
cases, a 14,400-edge DFG within 60 s), `minera_server_traces_route_tests`
(exact multipart XES), `minera_core_tests` (`csv_timestamps_review_v1_shapes`),
`minera_filtering_common_bank_parity_tests`, frontend `api.test.ts`.

Declared:

- **Activities named `_S_START_` or `_S_END_` (declared).** The reference
  uses those strings as its artificial start and end nodes, so such an
  activity is merged with them: removing it raises `KeyError`, or the final
  prune drops it. On 1,000 random DFGs using those names the reference's
  activities-percentage, paths-percentage and keep-connected results differ
  from native in 638, 589 and 567 cases; to, from and contain agree (0).
  Native keeps them as ordinary activities.

## Review AA1: separators dateutil skips in CSV timestamps (2026-11-09)

A review of Round Z against `pandas.read_csv` + `pm4py.format_dataframe`
(public API outputs only) found one backend gap (the other AA1 findings were
frontend fixes):

- **AA1-5 Separators dateutil skips.** dateutil skips `;`, `/`, `'` and `.`
  between its tokens like a blank, so pandas reads `2024-01-05 03:15:34;`,
  `…03:15:34/`, `…03:15:34'`, `…03:15:34.p;` (15:15:34), `…03:15:34..pm`,
  `2024-01-05 1000./`, `…03:15:34Z.`, `; 2024-01-05 03:15`, `..2024-01-05`,
  `2024-01-05/` and `05.01.2024.`, which the importer kept as text. A cell
  that is no timestamp as written is now read once more, on dateutil's path
  (microseconds only), with such a run dropped at the start, turned into a
  blank at the end, and turned into a blank after the clock before a word or
  an offset (`03:15:34;pm`, `03:15/UTC`, `03:15:34..+05`, `03:15 . UTC`).
  After the clock the run needs a `;`, `/`, `'`, two `.` or a blank next to
  its `.`, so a lone `.` keeps the meridiem rules (`03:15:34.p` still fails),
  and a `.` right after a fraction joins that number (`03:15:34.5..` and
  `10:30.5.;+05` fail, as in pandas). Cells read as written are unchanged.

Declared (dateutil readings kept as text): a cell holding a `,` (dateutil
reads a `,` fraction or date by value: `03:15:34,5;` is 0001-01-05); a `-`
next to such a run or between the date and the clock (`01/05/2024-`,
`2024-01-05-03:15:34`); runs inside the date, between the date and the clock
or inside the clock (`2024-01-05;03:15:34`, `Jan 5;2024`, and `03;15:34`,
which dateutil reads as 15:34); a lone `YYYYMMDD` after a skipped run
(`;20240105`); a run after a clock without `:` when a later offset has one
(`1000'+05:00 pm`); a lone `.` between an offset and a word (`-05:00.pm`);
and two zones or offsets (as in review Z1).

Fuzz (per-cell readings through `reference_mixed_timestamp`, harness linked
against 028e35d's `libminera_core.a` with only the importer rebuilt, against
`read_csv` + `format_dataframe` on single-value columns): 5,376 cells with
separator runs at the start, the end, after the clock, between the date and
the clock and inside the date (`;`, `/`, `'`, `.`, `..`, `,`, `-` and blanks
in combinations, after 13 date, 14 clock and 16 zone/meridiem shapes): 2,954
fixed, 0 regressions, 0 new wrong values, 877 remaining mismatches all in the
declared classes above or in earlier declared classes. 12,000 random token
cells: 0 regressions, 0 new readings that differ from pandas (one fixed).
Tests: `minera_core_tests` (`csv_timestamps_review_aa1_skipped_separators`).

**Correction (review AB1-2).** The "0 new wrong values" above did not hold:
an independent fuzz (about 680k generated cells, compared with 813ffae^ and
with `read_csv` + `format_dataframe`) found 12 distinct cells the skip read
while pandas rejects them, all runs dateutil does not skip. These now keep
their text: a lone `.` before the only number of the cell (`.20240105`, a
decimal to dateutil); a run other than a single `;` or `'` between a lone
one-digit number and a meridiem (`2024-01-05 5/am`, `01/05/2024 5. pm`,
`5; am`; `5;am`, `05/am` and `5/Jan 2024` still read); a `/` at the end after
a slash date of two numbers (`2024 12/31/`; `2024/01/05/` still reads); a `.`
at the end after a dotted date led by a month name (`Jan.12.34.`;
`Jan.12.34;.` still reads); a cell ending in `:` (`03:15:34 am;+05:`); and a
cell with a decimal number outside the clock (`Jan-5.5/`, `/Jan/5.5`), whose
date shapes are not dateutil's. Declared: such a decimal cell that pandas
reads keeps its text (`/Jan 5.5` is 0001-01-05 to pandas). Refuzz of the same
generators plus two fresh seeds (about 1.1M cells, 53,759 that read
differently from 813ffae^): 0 new wrong values, and every cell the skip had
fixed still reads. Tests: the same test, extended.

## Review Z1: empty fractions before a zone, rounded int keys, isin list dtypes, padded NA cells (2026-11-09)

A review of Round Y against `pandas.read_csv` + `pm4py.format_dataframe`,
`get_event_attribute_values`/`get_trace_attribute_values` on `read_xes`
frames and `filter_ocel_event_attribute` (public API outputs only) found:

- **Z1-1 `.Z` after an empty fraction on dateutil's path.** An empty `.`
  fraction followed by a closing `Z` reads only on pandas' ISO path
  (`2024-01-05 09:32:02.Z`, `20570906 14:10:24.Z`, `2024-01-05 093202.Z`).
  On dateutil's path it fails, and Round Y read it: `2024-01-05  09:32:02.Z`,
  `2024-01-05 T09:32:02.Z`, `01/05/2024 09:32:02.Z`, `2024  1  5 09:32:02.Z`,
  `20240105t09:32:02.Z` and a closing `.z` anywhere now stay text. A blank or
  a word after it reads on both (`.Z pm`, `.z pm`, `.Z `, `. Z`, `.UTC`,
  `.+05`).
- **Z1-2 Rounded int keys in attribute statistics.** When a DataFrame column
  makes ints floats (Y2-3), each int is now keyed by its rounded double, so
  ints that round alike are one value: 2^53 + 1 and 2^53 on two of three
  events give `{9007199254740992.0: 2}` (Round Y listed the value twice). The
  once-per-case value level merges the same way (counts added, the earlier
  first group kept). 500 random XES logs (2,387 calls): 18 fixed, none
  changed for the worse; one difference remains (already in Round Y): once
  per case in an object column, `1e16` and the int 10^16 + 1, equal as
  doubles, sort in the opposite order of pandas' exact comparison.
- **Z1-3 The dtype of the isin list in OCEL attribute filters.** A values list
  of ints and floats only is float64, so against an int64 or float64 column its
  ints are rounded to doubles: an int64 column `[2^53 + 1, 2^53]` with
  `i:9007199254740993,d:1.5` keeps both events (Round Y: one). A list holding
  a bool or string is an object array and compares exactly, also against an
  int64 column (`[2^53 + 1]` with `b:false,i:0,d:9007199254740992.0` keeps
  nothing); an object column takes every list as given. 0 differences on
  2,809 random filter calls (25 fixed). Declared: `i:` values outside the
  signed 64-bit range are refused with an explicit error, while pm4py takes
  Python ints of any size.
- **Z1-4 Padded NA spellings.** Default trimming turned ` NA` / ` None ` into
  NA spellings, so Round Y dropped them from resource, lifecycle and extra
  attribute cells (and the case-id and activity columns dropped the row). They
  are now values (the padding is still trimmed, declared): resources ` NA`,
  `r1`, `NA` give `{NA: 1, r1: 1}` like pandas' `{' NA': 1, 'r1': 1}`.
  600 random CSVs with padded and unpadded NA spellings in the case-id,
  activity, resource and an extra column: 0 differences.
- **Z1-5 Empty `.` before AM/PM and after HHMM.** A lone `a`/`p` after an
  empty `.` fails only at the end of the text or before `Z`, `z`, a digit, `:`
  or `,` (`03:15:34.p +5`, `.p Z`, `.A Z`, `.a m`, `.p-05` and `03:15.p Z`
  read; `.p`, `.pz`, `.p5` fail). A basic `HHMM` clock takes an empty `.`
  (`2024-01-05 1000.`, `1000. pm`, `1000.+05`; `1000.5`, `1000.Z`, `1000.p`
  fail). An empty minute fraction followed by a closing `Z` fails, while a
  blank or word after it reads (`10:30.Z pm`, `10:55.Z `).
- **Z1-6** The decomposed alignment's per-trace `fitness` prints the shortest
  round-trip double, like its top-level fitness.
- **Z1-7** `/api/attribute-statistics` applies the DataFrame dtype rule (Y2-3)
  to CSV and XES sources only. A typed table source (`mining_input_format=table`)
  keeps each cell's type: its cells already hold the frame's values, and the
  reference keeps ints for an EventLog (`{1: 1, 2: 1}`) and for a nullable
  `Int64` column alike.

Declared (dateutil readings kept as text, in the classes of review Y1):
`.Z+05`, `.z+05` and `.Z +05` (two zones), `1:30 pm m` (a stray `m`),
`2024-01-05 T` and `20240105T` (a lone `T`).

Fuzz after the fixes: 5,897 random timestamp columns (pandas vs 2bb12ed vs
this tree, seeds 1-3): 0 regressions, 8 columns fixed, every remaining
mismatch a declared text reading; the 99,810-cell corpus of review Y1 changes
in one cell (`18 0008 0031T03:45.Z PM`, now read as pandas reads it). Tests:
`minera_core_tests` (`csv_timestamps_review_z1_shapes`,
`csv_na_spellings_in_attribute_cells_are_missing`,
`json_export_prints_quality_metrics_at_full_precision`),
`minera_attribute_statistics_tests`, `minera_ocel_filter_tests`.

## Review Y2: metric precision in the mine JSON, CSV NA attribute cells, DataFrame dtypes in attribute statistics (2026-11-08)

A random-input sweep of areas not recently compared (OCEL object graphs,
`discover_ocdfg`, `discover_oc_petri_net` with and without TBR diagnostics,
footprints conformance, log prefix utilities, start/end activities and
attribute values on CSV and XES) found three differences, all fixed:

- **Y2-1 Full-precision quality metrics.** The export and `/api/mine` JSON
  printed `footprints.metrics` (precision, log_fitness, perc_fit_traces),
  `conformance.<miner>.footprints` fitness/precision, token-replay fitness,
  precision, generalization and simplicity, alignment fitness, precision and
  per-variant fitness, and the embedded process-tree, DFG, edit-distance and
  decomposed alignment fitness, Declare rule support/confidence and decision
  accuracy, majority share and thresholds with the stream default of six
  significant digits (`33.3333` for pm4py's `33.333333333333336`). They are
  now the shortest round-trip double (`write_round_trip_double`); a
  non-finite value is `null`. Only the printed digits change. Test:
  `minera_core_tests` (`json_export_prints_quality_metrics_at_full_precision`).
- **Y2-2 NA spellings in CSV attribute cells.** `read_csv` reads `NaN`,
  `null`, `None`, `NA`, `n/a`, `#N/A` and the other default NA spellings as
  NaN in every column, and `get_event_attribute_values` does not count them.
  The batch CSV import now leaves a resource, lifecycle or extra attribute
  cell holding one missing (log and flat table), like a blank cell; stream
  readers keep the literal text. Reference: resources `NaN`, `null`, `r1`,
  `None` give `{'r1': 1}` (native counted four values). Test:
  `minera_core_tests` (`csv_na_spellings_in_attribute_cells_are_missing`).
- **Y2-3 DataFrame column dtypes in attribute statistics.** `read_xes`
  builds a DataFrame, whose column is float64 when it holds ints and a
  missing cell, or ints and floats, so the reference keys are floats:
  an int attribute on two of three events gives `{1.0: 1, 2.0: 1}`, a trace
  int on one of two traces `{3.0: 2}` and `2.5`/`1` gives `{2.5: 1, 1.0: 1}`;
  complete ints stay ints and a bool or string keeps the object column with
  every cell's type. Counting once per case groups by `[case id, value]`,
  whose value level holds the distinct keys, so ints beside a float there
  are floats too even in an object column whose bool merged into an int key
  (`1`, `True`, `0.5`, `3` gives `{1.0: 1, 0.5: 1, 3.0: 1}`; with `True` seen
  first, `{True: 1, 0.5: 1, 3: 1}`). `entries` (and the `values` map) now
  report those ints as floats (`1.0`, type `float`) for CSV and XES sources;
  `AttributeStatisticsOptions::dataframe_column_types = false` keeps each
  cell's EventLog type for a native log. Counts and order were already
  equal before; with the exact types, 0 diffs on 150 random XES logs. Test:
  `minera_attribute_statistics_tests`.

Documented (reference behaviour, no change): `footprints.metrics.log_fitness`
and `perc_fit_traces` follow `fitness_footprints` on an EventLog, which
averages the per-trace footprints (`fp_fitness` over the trace-by-trace
footprints, e.g. 0.873015873015873 on a six-trace log). On a DataFrame,
`fitness_footprints` returns one float from the whole-log footprint and its
extensive check instead (0.8757763975155279 on the same log); native reports
the EventLog dict.

Unchanged and matched on random inputs: OCEL object graphs (300 OCELs × 5
graph types), `discover_ocdfg` annotations and performance lists (300),
`discover_oc_petri_net` nets, double arcs and TBR place/transition counts
(400, nets compared up to isomorphism), footprints log_model, log_extensive
and trace_extensive results with fp fitness/precision on the inductive tree,
inductive net and heuristics net (150 logs), `get_prefixes_from_log`,
`get_log_with_log_prefixes`, `get_log_traces_until_activity` and
`get_log_traces_to_activities` (250 logs), start/end activities and
attribute counts on CSV and XES (130 logs).

## Review Y1: CSV minute fractions and dateutil clock shapes, OCEL large integers, literal DFG selectors (2026-11-08)

Fixes after a review of Round X, checked against `pandas.read_csv` +
`pm4py.format_dataframe`, pm4py 2.7.22 OCEL filters and its DFG filters
(public API outputs only).

- **Y1-1 Fractions of a minute in decimal arithmetic.** dateutil's seconds
  for `HH:MM.f` match `int(60 * (Decimal(minutes) % 1))` in Python's default
  28-digit decimal context (fitted on 700 probes, 0 misses): both the
  fraction and the product are rounded half-even to 28 significant digits,
  and a product that rounds to 60 makes the cell unreadable. The importer
  computed floor(60 x 0.f) exactly on at most 30 digits.
  `2024-01-05 10:07.01` + 28 sixes is 10:07:01 (was :00), `.016...67` with 31
  digits :01 (was :00), `.983333333333333333333333333333334` :59 (was :58),
  `10:07.` + 29 nines unconvertible (was 10:07:59).
- **Y1-3 dateutil shapes the importer kept as text.** Now read as pandas reads
  them: a basic `YYYYMMDD` date before a clock after `T`, `t` or white space
  (`20240105 11:07:52.123456789` keeps nanoseconds; a `,` fraction and a date
  alone stay text); basic clocks `HHMM` and `HHMMSS[.f]` (`2024-01-05 1107`;
  `1107.5` fails); a `T` after white space (`2024-01-05 T13:38`, dateutil's
  path); runs of spaces between the numbers of an all-numeric date
  (`2057  8 31`); one-digit offset hours and, after a colon, one-digit offset
  minutes (`+5` is +05:00, `+5:3` +05:03, `+0:30`; `+530` fails); `a`/`p`
  alone and dotted AM/PM whose `m` is lowercase (`3:08 p`, `p.m.`, `P.m.`,
  `p. m.`, `pm.`; `P.M.` fails); a repeated AM/PM applied again (`12:30pm pm`
  is 12:30, `12:08pm am` 00:08, `3:08pm pm` fails); a `.` with no fraction
  digits after the seconds (`09:32:02.`, `09:32:02.Z`; `.z` and a lone
  `.p`/`.a` fail, as after minutes). A bare one-digit hour cannot take AM/PM
  after two or more blanks, so `01 05 2024  1  pm  -12:00` (which Round X read
  as 2024-01-06 01:00 UTC) and `2024-01-05 1  pm` stay text (`11  pm`,
  `1:00  pm` read).
- **Y1-2 OCEL attribute filters and large integers.** The event and object
  attribute filters now follow the dtype of the reference frame's column: a
  column of integers only (int64) is compared as float64 against a float
  value (`9007199254740993` matches `d:9007199254740992.0`, `2^63-1` matches
  `9.223372036854776e18`); a column with a missing cell (a record without the
  key, or null) or a float holds every integer rounded to a double, which then
  compares exactly with the given value (`9007199254740993` there matches
  `i:9007199254740992` and not `i:9007199254740993`); a column holding a
  string or boolean compares like Python `==`. Small values are unchanged.
- **Literal DFG selectors.** `GET /api/dfg` and `minera_dfg` accept an empty
  `to_activity`/`from_activity`/`contain_activity` (the label `""`; the
  reference raises `KeyError: ''` when no activity has it), and the frontend
  sends it. `most_common_paths` labels keep their white space: only one space
  after a comma and one on each side of `->` are separator padding
  (`a -> b, c -> d` is unchanged; `a ->  b` names ` b`), in the server,
  `minera_dfg` (`parse_activity_pairs(text, true)`) and the frontend, which no
  longer trims the text. The log filters' succession syntax still trims.

Fuzz (single-cell columns, pandas path vs 9c6fad2 vs this tree): 14,563 random
numeric-date and clock cells (seeds 51, 52, 71, 72), a 6,160-cell AM/PM/offset
matrix, 3,000 value-edge numeric dates (seed 83) and 2,000 columns of two to
five rows (seed 61): no cell that 9c6fad2 read correctly differs now, and
every remaining mismatch is in a declared class (below or earlier: year 0,
`.` mixes, time-only cells, `GMT+05:30`). On the 99,810-cell corpus of review
X1 the importer's output is unchanged. OCEL: the 20 dtype cases of the review
against `pm4py.filter_ocel_event_attribute` and 4,640 filter calls on 300
random OCELs (review X2's fuzz), 0 differences. DFG: 1,200 `/api/dfg` calls
against pm4py's DFG filters with unusual labels, 0 differences.

Tests: `minera_core_tests` (`csv_timestamps_review_y1_shapes`,
`parse_activity_pairs_reads_the_arrow_syntax`), `minera_ocel_filter_tests`,
`minera_dfg_filter_route_tests`, frontend `api.test.ts`.

Declared (value-dependent dateutil readings, kept as text by the importer):

- **Date numbers of six or more digits (declared).** dateutil reads such a
  number as an `HHMMSS` clock and fills the date from the rest
  (`10 31 000001` is 0001-10-31 00:00:01, `0012  000006 14`
  0001-12-14 00:00:06).
- **Clock fields of three or more digits (declared).** Zero-padded fields such
  as `011:45`, `23:022:027` or a bare `013 pm` read by value.
- **More than one offset or zone (declared).** dateutil combines them
  (`+05:30 +01:90`, `Z+01:90`, `+1+1`).
- **Stray words and dots (declared).** A lone `t`, `T` or `m` word, doubled
  dots (`11:21..`), a `.` right after a bare hour (`01/05/2024 11.`), a third
  offset-minute digit (`+5:300` is +10:00). (`10:55.Z ` with a trailing
  blank reads since review Z1; doubled dots at the end, `11:21..`, read since
  review AA1.)

## Review AA2: structural reduction before the soundness reachability search (2026-11-09)

The soundness check of `/api/mine` (and of active-source mining, the imported
model route, `minera_export`, the POWL workflow-net conversion and the log
alignment dispatcher) calls `final_marking_reachability`. On a random CSV with
40 activities the inductive net (162 places, 202 transitions) has billions of
interleavings: the three capped searches (uniform-cost, marking-equation A*,
breadth-first) all stopped at their budget after 17.6 s and 4.6 GB, and the
POWL net after 10.6 s and 1.9 GB, so both were reported as "reached its
search limit".

- **Reduction first.** On an ordinary net (unit arcs, repeated unweighted
  endpoints as multiplicities, no reset or inhibitor arcs) the reachability
  search now first applies reduction rules that each keep "the final marking
  is reachable" exactly: removing transitions whose firing changes nothing,
  duplicate transitions and dead transitions (an input place nothing produces
  into, with too few initial tokens); removing duplicate places and places
  that are only tested; post-agglomeration (a transition that is the only
  consumer of its single input place, fused into that place's producers) and
  pre-agglomeration (a transition that is the only producer of its single
  output place, fused into that place's consumers). The proofs are in the
  comment above `ReachabilityReduction` in `conformance.cpp`. A net whose
  reduced initial marking equals its reduced final marking is reachable with
  no search: every process-tree translation (both variants) and POWL
  translation in the fuzz below reduces that way, in under 0.5 s for nets of
  90,000 transitions. A smaller residue is searched with the same three
  searches and a quarter of the state budget when at most two thirds of its
  places and transitions are left; when that stops at its budget
  the unreduced net is searched exactly as before, so no verdict the unreduced
  search decides can change (the undecided Heuristics nets of the fuzz keep 70-80%,
  so they skip the residue search: 10.9 s against 11.3 s before on the
  slowest). Nets
  with reset, inhibitor or non-unit weighted arcs skip the reduction.
  Alignment preflights (the `Aligner` outside reachability-only use) are
  unchanged, and cancellation is polled during the reduction and by both
  searches.
- **Measurements** (`/usr/bin/time -v`, the four mined nets'
  `final_marking_reachability` after importing the log): 30k events 17.6 s
  inductive + 10.6 s POWL, 4.63 GB peak, now 0.00 s each, 105 MB peak (the
  process; 1.1 s with the import); 500k events 17.9 s + 10.7 s, 5.65 GB, now
  0.00 s each, 1.68 GB (the imported log). Whole `/api/mine` (another process
  busy on a second core): 30k 48.0 s and 4.77 GB → 17.7 s and 3.22 GB; 500k
  117.5 s and 7.78 GB → 88.1 s and 6.21 GB. The responses are identical apart
  from `sound` turning true and `reachability_exhausted` disappearing for the
  inductive and POWL models.
- **Differential fuzz** (old vs new verdicts): 19,571 nets — inductive (IM,
  IMf, IMd; standard and transition-bordered), Alpha, Heuristics, POWL and ILP
  nets mined from random logs, random raw nets with weighted, reset and
  inhibitor arcs and explicit markings, and random block-structured nets with
  arc mutations. No decided verdict changed (13,734 reachable and 5,276
  unreachable before); 106 inductive nets went from exhausted to reachable (each confirmed by an
  independent random-walk witness), and one Alpha net from exhausted to
  unreachable (unbounded, confirmed by a Karp-Miller coverability graph in
  which no marking covers the final marking).

Tests: `minera_core_tests` (`final_marking_reachability_reduces_block_structured_nets`).

## Review AC2: packed model-footprint exploration (2026-11-09)

The "<model> net: footprints" stages of `/api/mine` (and every other
`check_footprints` caller) explore the net's markings breadth-first up to
`kFootprintCap` (200,000) expansions. On a random 500-case CSV with 25
activities in random order every miner's net is concurrent enough to hit that
budget: 3.7 s inductive, 1.6 s Heuristics and 1.1 s POWL, with a 1.1 GB peak.
The result is unchanged; only the cost:

- **Packed markings.** On a net with unit ordinary arcs (repeated endpoints as
  multiplicities, inhibitor arcs allowed, no reset or weighted arcs: every
  mined net) a marking is a row of fixed-width token fields in 64-bit words,
  one bit per place while the net stays safe and widened (2, 4, ... 32 bits,
  re-encoding the stored rows) when a place holds more. Markings get the same
  ids in the same breadth-first order and the same budget applies, so the
  expanded set, `exhausted` and a token-overflow error are those of the
  general path, which every other net still takes unchanged.
- **Nothing recomputed.** The visible labels enabled at a marking are found
  once, when it is met, the explored edges are kept instead of re-fired, and
  only the transitions listed under a marked input place are tested.
- **Memory.** Only the silent edges are stored as edges; a visible edge
  m -a-> m' is kept as the bit a in a per-marking row of entering labels,
  closed against m''s observable labels at the end (the seeds are closed in
  place). Storing every explored edge (review AD1) needed 8 bytes per enabled
  transition per expansion: a counter generator plus 500 visible self-loops
  peaked at 836 MB against the general path's 65 MB, and 1,500 self-loops
  ran out of a 2 GB address space where the general path answers. Now the
  extra is one label row per marking, and those nets peak at 68 MB / 550 MB
  against 65 MB / 522 MB (18 concurrent rings with 500 / 1,500 self-loops:
  270 / 683 MB against 280 / 655 MB), with the timings above unchanged.
- **Stopping when the answer is fixed.** The relation can only grow as more
  markings are expanded and never holds more than every pair of the live
  visible activities. Once more than 200,000 markings are known (so the
  budget will be hit and `exhausted` is true) and the relation of what is
  expanded so far already holds every such pair (the pairs seen directly are
  checked after each expansion, the closed relation at doubling checkpoints),
  exploring on cannot change the answer. This stop is only taken when no
  firing within the budget can overflow a token count.
- The log's directly-follows relation is collected as activity numbers and
  named once per pair.

Measurements (`/api/mine` stage times polled from `/api/mine-progress`; both
responses byte-identical apart from `run_id`): 500 cases x 25 activities,
footprints 3.75 + 0.01 + 2.20 + 1.56 s (inductive, Alpha, Heuristics, POWL)
= 7.5 s, now 0.06 + 0.00 + 0.16 + 0.12 = 0.34 s (whole request 8.7 s ->
1.5 s; the four `check_footprints` calls alone 1.1 GB -> 80 MB peak); 494k
events x 40 activities 8.98 + 0.15 + 0.35 + 3.02 = 12.5 s, now 0.15 + 0.08 +
0.29 + 0.28 = 0.8 s. A net that does not settle still runs the full 200,000
expansions, about 3x faster than before (the 25-activity inductive net with
the stop disabled: 1.0 s against 3.7 s).

Differential fuzz (old against new `check_footprints`, every field and every
exception): 7,212 nets from inductive (IM, IMf, IMd; both conversions), Alpha,
Heuristics, POWL and ILP nets on random logs, large concurrent miner nets,
random raw nets with weighted, reset and inhibitor arcs, out-of-range inputs,
explicit and near-`INT_MAX` markings, random block nets with arc mutations
and wide parallel nets: all identical (2,371 exhausted, 31 overflow errors;
on the packed path 1,264 runs to the full budget and 922 early stops).

`minera_server_mine_progress_tests` cancelled a mine inside the inductive
footprints stage, which now lasts tens of milliseconds; it now mines 2,000
cases of 20-60 events over 40 activities and cancels inside "Inductive net:
token replay" (about 4 s).

## Review AD2: faster `/api/mine` stages on a large log (2026-11-09)

No output changes: every `/api/mine` response is byte-identical apart from
`run_id`, both on a 494k-event, 40-activity CSV and on 22 smaller CSV/XES
responses. Changes, from the largest gain down:

- **Token precision searches, pipelined and threaded.** The ETConformance
  walk interns each distinct reached marking into a compact pool (zigzag
  varint keys, falling back to the full marking when a count is wide). Up
  to three worker threads (one per 2,048 markings, at most hardware - 1),
  each with its own `Replayer` and the caller's enabled-search budget, run
  the forward enabled-transition search on markings as soon as they are
  published. The main thread keeps walking and then helps search. Results
  are read back in prefix order, so the first exception raised is the one a
  single sequential pass raises. A search that fails stops later searches
  (markings past the failing id are skipped). Cancellation is checked by the
  walk and by the main thread's searches; the workers stop and are joined
  before the error propagates.
- **Log skeleton** is computed once per variant on interned activity ids
  (ids numbered in name order, so pair order stays lexicographic), with dense
  tables. Conformance prepares the model once. Same rules, the same error for
  a missing activity, the same deviation order.
- **Declare conformance** checks each variant on interned ids against the
  rule families in the original order, with per-activity position lists.
- **Model decorations** no longer build a wide `TokenInteger` for the
  `uint64` bound on every arc (an inline value is compared as an integer).
- **CSV import** reserves each case's events up front. Time ordering returns
  early when the events are already in order (sizeof(Event) is 1.4 KB, so
  moving every event cost time).

Tried and dropped: running the four decorations in parallel (slower, 10.4 s
against 7.3 s, because of malloc contention under the server's
`M_ARENA_MAX=2`), splitting token-replay firing sequences into chunks (about
1 s slower), and a deque for pending CSV rows (later stages slowed).

Measurements on the 494k-event log (stage times polled from
`/api/mine-progress`, idle four-core machine): whole request 80.8 s -> 40.9 s;
inductive token replay 31.3 -> 8.2 s, log skeleton 11.1 -> 0.48 s, declare
6.8 -> 1.8 s, decorations 7.0 -> 6.4 s, reading the log 4.2 -> 3.9 s. Other
stages are unchanged.

`minera_server_mine_progress_tests` now mines 5,000 cases instead of 2,000:
the threaded searches brought "Inductive net: token replay" on 2,000 cases
down to about 1 s, and this keeps it the longest stage (about 3 s). It passed
5 runs in a row.

## Review AE2: log skeleton and Declare on XES frames, self-pairs, ratios (2026-11-09)

Random logs (1-12 cases, 1-7 activities, numeric, text and odd case ids,
padded and empty names, shuffled rows, out-of-order events, XES traces that
share a case id and empty traces) were run through `/api/mine`,
`/api/discover-constraints` and the original log-skeleton and Declare
workbenches, and compared with pm4py 2.7.22 public calls on the
`read_csv` + `format_dataframe` frame and the `read_xes` frame. Results after
the fixes: own-model runs (600 logs, a third XES: discovery, conformance lists and
their case order, diagnostics and their order, `/api/mine` defaults) 0
undeclared differences; supplied models with self-pairs (450 logs) 0; Declare
ratios and multipliers inside and outside [0, 1] (400 CSV logs) 0; the only
remaining differences are 28 + 22 XES logs of AE2-10 (Declare only). A sample of other
`/api/mine` sections on 300 XES logs with shared ids (case counts,
start and end activities, variants as counts, rework, eventually-follows,
case durations) matches `read_xes` apart from the declared "XES events out of
time order" edges (106 logs); the tree before this change gave a different case count on 117 of them,
and the other sections differed with it.

Fixed:

- **AE2-1 XES traces that share a case id are one case.** `read_xes` gives
  one row per event, so pm4py's frame algorithms see traces that share
  `case:concept:name` as one case (their events in file order, the first
  trace's attributes; a key only a later trace holds is not taken) and never
  see a trace without events. The active-source import of an XES file (the
  log shape: `/api/mine`, `/api/discover-constraints`, the workbenches and
  other routes reading an imported XES source) now merges such traces and
  drops empty ones (`merge_dataframe_cases`). Traces with a null or missing
  id stay apart. Native log JSON is unchanged. (Review AF1 extends this to
  the table shapes of an XES upload, the routes and tools that import XES
  themselves, and `minera_export`; see AF1-1 and AF1-4.)
- **AE2-2 Case order of log-skeleton and Declare lists on XES.** pm4py's
  frame conformance (log skeleton, Declare) lists cases in the stable
  code-point order of their ids, as the CSV path already gave (its frame is
  sorted by case). On XES the `log_skeleton_conformance` and
  `declare_conformance` lists of `/api/mine` and `/api/discover-constraints`
  and the workbench conformance results now follow that order (each entry
  keeps its own case id and Declare `trace_index`), and log-skeleton
  discovery meets the cases in it, so `activ_freq` ties resolve as pm4py's.
  Diagnostics tables stay in file order, as `return_diagnostics_dataframe`
  gives them. Other sections keep file order.
- **AE2-3 Self-pairs in `response`, `precedence`, `succession`.** For a
  supplied rule (a, a), pm4py compares the last a with the last a (response),
  the first with the first (precedence), both (succession), so a case that
  contains a satisfies it; native needed a later (earlier) occurrence and
  reported a deviation. Native now uses the same comparisons (`<=`) for these
  three templates. Discovery never proposes self-pairs, on either side.
- **AE2-4 Empty diagnostics tables.** For a log without cases pm4py's
  diagnostics DataFrame of both conformance checks has no columns; native
  listed the column names. Native now returns no columns there.
- **AE2-5 Declare ratios outside [0, 1].** pm4py accepts any
  `min_support_ratio`, `min_confidence_ratio` and `auto_selection_multiplier`
  (a negative or above-1 value only changes which rules pass). The server
  (`declare_min_support_ratio`, `declare_min_confidence_ratio`,
  `declare_auto_selection_multiplier`), `minera_export` and the UI rejected
  values outside [0, 1]; they now accept any finite value with pm4py's
  results. The log-skeleton noise threshold keeps its declared [0, 1] range.

Declared:

- **AE2-6 Declare keys with an empty activity name.** pm4py's Declare
  discovery stores a binary rule (X, '') under the plain key 'X', and its own conformance then
  raises IndexError on that model. Native keeps the pair (X, '') in the model
  and checks it as a binary rule. Not reproduced.
- **AE2-7 XES without timestamps.** pm4py's frame algorithms refuse a frame
  without a timestamp column ("the dataframe should (at least) contain a
  column of type date"). Native mines an untimed XES log in file order, as it
  keeps CSV files whose timestamp column holds no date (see "CSV rows without
  a timestamp are dropped"): a deliberate extension.
- **AE2-8 Merged cases out of time order.** A case merged from traces that
  share an id keeps file order, as `convert_to_event_log` and pm4py's
  start/end activities give it; pm4py's DataFrame DFG sorts the case by
  timestamp. This is the declared "XES events out of time order" difference.
- **AE2-9 One deviation per pair.** A log-skeleton deviation is native's one
  entry per violated pair; pm4py groups a constraint's violated pairs in one
  tuple. Counts and pairs compare equal after expansion.
- **AE2-10 Shared ids on non-adjacent traces.** When the traces that share
  an id are not adjacent in the file, pm4py's frame variants
  (`get_variants`) and its Declare discovery and conformance read the wrong
  rows: each case as many rows as it has events, starting at its first
  row, so they take events of the traces that follow it (traces `14: x`,
  `30: b`, `16: ü`, ..., `14: b b` give case 14 the variant `x, b, ü`).
  Its log skeleton, start/end activities, DFG and `convert_to_event_log` see
  the merged case. Native uses the merged case everywhere (AE2-1). (Later
  rounds model the slices where pm4py's DataFrame functions read them: the
  LLM declare description in BH1-3, the top-k and coverage variant filters
  in BH1-4, and Declare discovery in `/api/mine` and discover-constraints in
  BI1-1.)

Tests: `minera_xes_io_tests`
(`dataframe_cases_merge_shared_ids_and_order_by_code_point`),
`minera_log_skeleton_tests` (`trace_order_decides_activity_frequency_ties`),
`minera_declare_tests` (`self_pairs_follow_reference_comparisons`),
`minera_request_params_tests`, frontend `app-logic.test.ts`. The workbench
fixture manifests with XES inputs replay unchanged, and
`minera_mining_fast_path_equivalence_tests` keeps its pins (it runs the
library on native logs, and discovered models hold no response, precedence or
succession self-pairs, so AE2-3 does not reach it).

## Review AF1: one DataFrame-path model for XES inputs (2026-11-09)

Review AF1 found that the AE2 merge reached only some XES consumers and broke
the per-row case attributes. Now every XES input that follows pm4py's
DataFrame path (`pm4py.read_xes` returns a frame) uses one helper,
`merge_dataframe_cases` (or `import_xes_dataframe_log`, which imports and
merges). Case-grouped algorithms see the frame's cases: traces that share
`case:concept:name` are one case and a trace without events is no case. A
merged case whose traces differ in their attributes keeps each event's own
trace cells in `Event::case_row_attributes`, the slot the CSV import already
fills, with nulls for keys its trace lacks. Row-wise consumers then read every
row as the frame holds it. An active XES source (`ActiveEventSource::from_xes_frame`) keeps
the merged log plus the frame's rows as its table (file order, each row's own
cells), and a filtered source keeps projecting those rows.

Compared with pm4py 2.7.22 on random XES logs with shared ids (adjacent and
not), empty traces, attributes that differ between merged traces and unsorted
numeric-looking ids:

| Check | Logs | Undeclared diffs (HEAD 78c8dce → now) |
|---|---|---|
| Case counts, `/api/attribute-statistics` (case column), the log-query `dataframe` table, `keep_`/`remove_case_attribute_values` | 150 | trace count 0 → 0; statistics 91 → 0; log query 95 → 0; filters 40 → 0 |
| Log-skeleton and Declare lists plus `activ_freq`, over 4 mine paths (log, literal selectors, dataframe, lazyframe) and `/api/discover-constraints` | 150 | 16 per path (on 60 logs) → 0 |
| `/api/token-replay` and `/api/replay-fitness` (counts, fitness values) | 100 | 75 / 72 → 0 |
| `minera_export` (case count, skeleton list and its case order, variants) | 120 | → 0 |
| Other `/api/mine` sections | 200 | only "XES events out of time order" edges |
| AE2 fuzz (XES third) | 240 | only AE2-10 (28 logs, Declare) |

CSV and table-JSON responses (`/api/mine`, `/api/discover-constraints` in four
variants, `/api/traces`, `/api/xes`; 260 logs, 3,120 pairs) are byte-identical
to HEAD. The XES workbench fixture manifests replay unchanged.

Fixed:

- **AF1-1 Row cells and file row order of merged XES cases.** The frame keeps
  each trace's `case:` cells on that trace's rows. The merge gave the whole case the
  first trace's attributes, so these all read the merged case's values instead:
  - `get_trace_attribute_values` / `/api/attribute-statistics` on a case
    column (`{first: 3}` where pm4py gives `{first: 2, second: 1}`);
  - `filter_trace_attribute_values` (`keep_`/`remove_case_attribute_values`):
    pm4py keeps a case when any row matches and drops it when any row has a
    removed value;
  - the log-query `dataframe` table, which held the case-grouped merged rows.

  They now read the rows' own cells (`case_row_attributes`), and the active
  source's table is the frame's rows in file order, as `read_xes` gives them.
- **AF1-2 Literal source selectors.** `/api/mine` with `mining_selectors_json`
  (the native active-source dispatch) merged the XES log but gave log-skeleton
  discovery and both conformance lists in file order. It now uses the case-id
  order of AE2-2 (`constraint_case_order`), also in its analysis presentation.
- **AF1-3 Flat shapes of an XES upload.** `mining_input_shape=dataframe` and
  `lazyframe` group the frame's rows in first-appearance order. pm4py's
  frame log skeleton and Declare list (and, for the skeleton, meet) the cases
  in case-id order. Mine family results, `/api/discover-constraints` and the
  workbench conformance vectors now follow that order (`log_skeleton_case_order`
  computes it for the call's own `case_id_key` groups). The stream shape keeps
  first-appearance order, as pm4py's event stream does.
- **AF1-4 Routes and tools that import XES themselves.** These now read the
  frame's cases, so case counts agree with `/api/mine`:
  - routes: `/api/token-replay`, `/api/replay-fitness`,
    `/api/discover-alpha-plus` (uploaded log), `/api/timestamp-interleavings`,
    the reference logs of `/api/compare-petri`, `/api/evaluate-emd` and
    `/api/align-edit-distance`, `/api/streaming-declare`, the uploaded logs of
    the process-tree, graph and Petri anti/multi alignment workbenches, the
    workflow and inductive input workbenches, the saved-DFG projection, and
    the imported source of the original LTL filter (`source_format=import`);
  - CLIs: `minera_cluster`, `minera_context`, `minera_playout`,
    `minera_log_util`, `minera_streaming_declare`. `minera_query` keeps the
    frame's rows as its table and merges a filtered export, as
    `write_xes(filtered frame)` does.
  - `minera_export` now merges an XES input too, and lists its log-skeleton
    and Declare conformance in case-id order, as the server does. This
    resolves the conflict with "Mining filters over imported logs", which
    already put its filter flags on the DataFrame path. The headless
    `--convert-only` round trip keeps the log as read, as
    `write_xes(read_xes(..., return_legacy_log_object=True))` does, and so
    does the importer contract (`--xes-return-legacy-log-object`,
    `--xes-return-pl-lazyframe`).

  These deliberately stay on the EventLog path or on the frame's rows:
  - the log filter bank (`/api/reference-log-filter`,
    `/api/reference-log-attributes`, and `/api/reference-ltl-filter` with
    `engine=log`). These are `algo.filtering.log.*` module calls on an
    EventLog object; the pandas and Polars engines filter the frame's rows.
  - PRIPEL's `trace_variant_query`, an EventLog parameter.
  - the importer-contract workbenches (edit distance, Bose, discovery), which
    record `import_xes_result` itself.
  - live-stream and stream-reader XES batches, which are event streams.
  - the case-relation merge (server and `minera_export --merge-case-relations`), whose
    table is the frame's rows, one per imported event.
  - the `minera_query` exact-report path, which records the module calls on
    the log as imported.

Declared:

- **AF1-5 XES traces without a case id.** pm4py's frame algorithms refuse a
  frame with a missing `case:concept:name` cell ("the case ID column should
  not contain any empty value"). Native keeps each such trace as a case of
  its own and lists it with an empty id, which sorts first in the case-id
  lists. Such files are not rejected.
- **AF1-6 Per-case token-replay and alignment lists on XES.** Resolved by
  Review AG2 (AG2-1): these lists now follow pm4py's case-id order on XES.

Tests: `minera_xes_io_tests` (`dataframe_cases_keep_row_case_cells`),
`minera_active_event_source_tests` (`xes_frame_source_keeps_frame_rows`),
`minera_log_skeleton_tests`, `minera_attribute_statistics_tests`,
`minera_log_query_tests`, `minera_core_tests`,
`minera_exact_filter_discovery_json_tests`, and
`minera_mining_fast_path_equivalence_tests` (251 outputs, pins unchanged).

## Review AG2: case-id order of per-case lists on XES, cancellable log loading (2026-11-09)

Fixed:

- **AG2-1 Per-case token-replay and alignment lists on XES (was AF1-6).**
  pm4py's frame diagnostics (`conformance_diagnostics_token_based_replay`,
  `conformance_diagnostics_alignments` with a Petri net or a process tree, on
  a `read_xes` frame) list the cases in the stable code-point order of their
  ids ("1" < "10" < "9"), and `fitness_token_based_replay` averages the
  per-case values in that order. Native listed them in the log's case order,
  file order for an XES log. They now follow the case-id order, with the
  existing case-order machinery:
  - `/api/token-replay`, `/api/replay-fitness` and `minera_export
    --token-replay-model` (with `--token-replay-result` or the fitness
    result) replay the frame's cases in that order (`order_cases_by_id`, the
    order `case_id_order` gives). Their results carry no case ids, so the
    list and the float sums now equal pm4py's exactly.
  - The session lists keep their log order and are written in the case-id
    order by `AnalysisConstraintCaseOrder` (`constraint_case_order`), every
    entry keeping its own `trace_index` and `case_id`: the
    `token_replay.trace_diagnostics` of every model in `/api/mine` (the log,
    literal-selector and flat shapes, as for the log-skeleton lists) and in
    `/api/check-model`, the `process_tree_alignment` of `minera_export`, the
    `traces` of `/api/align-process-tree`, and `minera_export
    --token-replay-include-trace-diagnostics`. A list of another length (the
    results of a projected or filtered log) keeps its order.
  - `/api/evaluate` with `evaluation_family=replay_fitness` evaluates an XES
    session's cases in that order, so its per-trace `trace_diagnostics` and
    the token-based `average_trace_fitness` follow pm4py.
  An event-stream session (`mining_input_shape=stream`) keeps first-appearance
  order, as pm4py's event stream does. CSV inputs are already sorted by case
  and native JSON logs follow the EventLog path; both are unchanged.

  These stay as they were: the workbenches' `log` adapter (an EventLog, file
  order as `convert_to_event_log` gives it; their `dataframe` and `lazyframe`
  adapters already gave the case-id order), the process-tree alignment
  workbench (its trace list indexes its echoed `input_log`), and the variant
  lists of `/api/align`, `/api/align-decomposed` and the replay results,
  which have no pm4py counterpart. The edit-distance and decomposed
  alignments keep log order, as pm4py's `apply` on a `read_xes` frame does
  (file order), and the anti- and multi-alignments give one result. (This
  said the DFG alignment had no public frame function to compare with; it
  has, `algo.conformance.alignments.dfg.algorithm.apply` on the frame lists
  case-id order, and `/api/align-dfg` follows it since Review AH1, AH1-5.)

- **AG2-2 Cancelling a mine while a big log loads.** The byte read of an
  upload was cancellable (64 KiB slices), but the work after it was not: the
  CSV importer's typing and grouping passes and the ActiveEventSource build
  (about 3 s for a 21 MB CSV), and the whole XES parse and source build. The
  read-cancel hook of `/api/mine` (`source_read_cancel_hook()` in
  `source_read_cancel.hpp`) now reaches them through `cancelled` callbacks
  that follow the library's convention (`CancellationCheck`, polled every
  4,096 rows, events or XML tokens, and once between passes):
  `CsvImportOptions::cancelled`, `XesImportOptions::cancelled`,
  `LogConversionOptions::cancelled` (log, table and stream conversions) and a
  `cancelled` argument of `ActiveEventSource::from_csv` and `from_xes_frame`.
  An unset callback never cancels; outputs are unchanged (the CSV and XES
  regressions below are byte-identical).

  Cancel latency, from `/api/cancel-mine` until `/api/mine-progress` reports
  the mine stopped, with the cancel sent 0.5 to 9 s into "Reading the event
  log" (same machine, before → after):

  | Input | Before | After |
  |---|---|---|
  | 500,000-event CSV (21 MB) | 0.30–2.79 s (late cancels 1.6–2.8 s) | 0.29–0.68 s |
  | 500,000-event XES (89 MB) | 0.89–9.04 s | 0.09–1.13 s |

  Polling itself answers within 0.25 s (the longest unpolled step is
  `merge_dataframe_cases`, 0.24 s on this XES); the rest of the remaining
  latency is releasing the partly built log on the way out (about 0.7 s for
  the 500,000-event XES source).

Compared with pm4py 2.7.22 (public API only) on 257 random XES logs with
shared ids (adjacent and not), unsorted numeric-looking ids and empty traces:
the order differences of `/api/token-replay`, `/api/check-model` trace
diagnostics (log and literal-selector mines), the discovered models' trace
diagnostics and `/api/align-process-tree` (22, 22, 22, 8 and 20 of the first
60 logs at HEAD 8387b79) are 0 now; `minera_export --token-replay-model` 16
of 40 → 0. Value differences of the native discovered models and process-tree
alignment fitness against pm4py's own models are unchanged from HEAD (they
compare different models), as is the declared "XES events out of time order"
edge. `/api/evaluate` alignment-based `average_trace_fitness` differs from
pm4py in the last bit on 3 of 257 logs, before and after: it sums per
variant, not per case.

CSV and table-JSON responses are byte-identical to HEAD: `/api/mine`,
`/api/discover-constraints` (four variants), `/api/traces` and `/api/xes`
(260 logs, 3,120 pairs), and `/api/mine` with trace diagnostics,

`/api/evaluate` fitness variants, `/api/token-replay` and
`/api/replay-fitness` (120 logs, 1,680 pairs). The XES workbench fixture
manifests replay unchanged, so no fixture was recaptured.
