## Review BG1: re-review of round BF, XES file order in the remaining frame routes, and long fractions and clock-first dates (2026-11-12)

Round BG re-reviewed BF (`python::sort` for long lists, `frame_rows`,
`reference_clock_first` and `reference_six_digit_date`, the SNA pandas
sequence order and joint activities' NaN drop) and swept every frame route
that still read an XES upload's rows by case with interleaved uploads
(`ilwrap.py`, `ilwrap2.py`: the sweep's XES files rewritten so that trace
names repeat apart from each other). The device check on the Mac was
skipped (the round's thread had no device linked). Findings, all fixed:

- **BG1-1 Attribute statistics on XES uploads in file order.**
  `/api/attribute-statistics` counted the frame's cells case by case;
  pandas' `value_counts` lists equal counts, and keeps the first of values
  that are equal (`1`, `1.0`, `True`), in the frame's row order, which for
  an XES upload is `read_xes`'s file order. A column `['p', 'q', 1, True,
  'r']` in file order is `1` (int) twice, then `p`, `q`, `r`; by case it
  was `True` (bool), `p`, `r`, `q`. Once per case, a case's rows need not
  be adjacent any more, so a (case, value) pair is counted once wherever
  its rows are. Interleaved sweep (`statsweep.py --xes`, seeds 5000 to
  5119): 170 order and 14 value differences of 4,018 requests before, none
  after.
- **BG1-2 Case statistics grouped by another column on XES uploads.**
  With `case_statistics_case_id_key` naming a column other than the trace
  name (the activity, an event attribute), a group holds rows of several
  traces, and pandas' first and last rows of the group are those of the
  file. Grouped by the activity, rows `a@10:00` (c1), `a@08:00`, `b@09:00`
  (c2), `a@12:00`, `b@07:00` (c1 again) give `b` from 09:00 to 07:00 and
  `a` from 10:00 to 12:00; by case Minera gave `b` from 07:00 to 09:00
  and `a` from 10:00 to 08:00 (`axsweep2.py --xes` interleaved: 18 of 900
  requests before, none after). The other frame loops that read rows in
  order took `frame_rows` too: passed time, cycle time, service time,
  local diagnostics, the roles pandas variant and the SNA pandas
  variants' regrouping, sortable-value check and resource names.
- **BG1-3 The LLM event stream and column descriptions on XES uploads.**
  `read_xes`'s frame lists a column where the file's rows first hold its
  key, and lists its rows in file order. The event stream (each row a dict
  in column order, latest first, ties in row order) and the column
  descriptions (value counts in row order) now read the rows in file
  order, so a key first seen in a later `<trace>` element of a case comes
  later (`llmsweep.py --xes` interleaved: 6 event-stream and 2
  column-description differences of 101 before, none after).
- **BG1-4 Fractions longer than six digits off the ISO path.** pandas
  (dateutil) keeps nanoseconds of a `.` fraction only when its fourth to
  sixth digits are `000` and the clock is `H:MM:SS` with two-digit minutes
  and seconds: `Jan 5 2020 10:30:15.123000789` keeps `.123000789`,
  `Jan 5 2020 10:30:15.123456789` is `.123456`, and one-digit seconds or
  minutes (`10:30:5.123000789`), a basic `103015.123000789` clock and a
  comma fraction keep microseconds. Minera applied one rule to every
  long fraction.
- **BG1-5 Comma fractions.** A comma fraction after a basic date reads as
  after `YYYY-MM-DD` (`20240105 11:07:52,5` is 11:07:52.5; Minera refused
  it), and a comma fraction needs two-digit seconds: `Jan 5 2020
  10:30:5,5`, `05/01/2020 10:30:5,5` and `20240105 11:07:5,5` are NaT in
  pandas (Minera read them).
- **BG1-6 A clock before a month-name date.** BF1-4's clock-first reading
  now also takes month and weekday names (`10:30 Jan 5 2020`, `10:30:15
  Jan 5, 2020`, `7:05 PM Mon Jan 6 2020`, `10:30 5 January 2020`), a zone
  or offset between the clock and the date (`10:30 UTC Jan 5 2020`,
  `10:30 +01:00 Jan 5 2020`, moved to the end as dateutil applies it) and
  a comma fraction after two-digit seconds (`10:30:15,5 Jan 5 2020`). As in
  pandas, exactly one month name is taken (`10:30 Jan Feb 2020` fails),
  and so is one zone.

Re-review of BF without further findings: `python::sort` against CPython
3.11 comparison by comparison (`seqfuzz2.py`, 1,200 lists of 64 to 4,000
items with inconsistent and raising relations); the SNA pandas variants
and joint activities on interleaved and plain uploads; resource profiles,
local diagnostics, network analysis, roles, root cause and the
features on interleaved uploads; BF's date shapes on CSV uploads through
`/api/mine` and the attribute KDE (`pdsweep3.py`).

Declarations:

- A CSV timestamp column whose cells are all plain numbers stays int64 or
  float64 in pm4py's frame (`format_dataframe` converts only text
  columns), while Minera keeps such cells as opaque timestamps (a retained
  native deviation for timestamp columns with no date cell). The attribute
  KDE on `time:timestamp` of such an upload is then an empty numeric
  estimate and `IndexError` for the date estimator, where pm4py estimates
  the numbers and raises `AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute
  'replace'` (`pdsweep3.py` seed 3059, a one-row upload).
- Clock-first and other dateutil shapes pandas reads that Minera leaves
  unparsed (a column holding one stays text, a timestamp column refuses
  the upload as before): partial dates that pandas completes from today's
  date (`10:30 Jan 2020` is the 12th today, `00:00 Dec 31` this year), a
  day followed by a dot (`00:00 05. Sep 2020`), month abbreviations with
  a dot (`7:5am 05 Mar. 2020`), two zones or offsets in one cell, comma
  joins after one-digit seconds or before blank-separated numbers
  (`00:5,5 29 2020`) and one-digit-minute clocks before a month and year
  (`00:5 Sep 1999` is 1999-09-01 00:05). These make about 24 percent of
  the deliberately wide clock-first fuzz (`numdate7.py`), 5 percent of the
  long-fraction fuzz (`numdate6.py`) and 1.5 percent of BF's clock-first
  fuzz (`mixfuzz5.py`), with no cell read differently.
- The trace- and event-based features and the LLM features on uploads
  with a column of mixed types (`mix`) still depend on Python's set order
  (declared since BC1); on interleaved uploads 4 of 180 feature requests
  matched none of 10 hash seeds, and a rerun of the same seed matched.

## Review BH1: re-review of round BG, the LLM model descriptions on uploads, and variant filters on XES frames (2026-11-12)

Round BH re-reviewed BG (attribute and case statistics in `frame_rows`
order, the LLM frame view, the long-fraction, comma-fraction and
clock-first date rules) and swept the frame loops BG left: the LLM
descriptions of the log skeleton, the temporal profile and the declare
model, the mining filters, the features' event-based rows and the temporal
profile route, with interleaved XES uploads (trace names that repeat apart
from each other), plain XES uploads and CSV uploads. The device check on
the Mac was skipped (the round's thread had no device linked). Findings,
all fixed:

- **BH1-1 The LLM log-skeleton description's activity occurrences.** On
  an upload pm4py discovers the skeleton on the DataFrame, whose activity
  counts list the activities of the first case by sorted case id (in the
  frame's row order), then the others in `value_counts` order (count
  descending, ties in row order); `abstract_log_skeleton` prints each set
  of counts sorted as text (`d: 0, 12, 2`). Minera listed the activities
  in the traces' order and the counts in ascending numbers (`d: 0, 2,
  12`). A native log keeps the EventLog order (first appearance over the
  traces). Before: 22 of 40 interleaved and 9 of 40 CSV uploads differed.
- **BH1-2 The LLM temporal-profile description on uploads.** pm4py's
  DataFrame discovery pairs each row of a case with every later row of
  that case after a stable sort by timestamp (a case whose rows are apart
  and out of time order in an XES upload has other pairs than its trace in
  file order), takes a duration from pandas' `Timedelta` parts (days times
  86,400, plus seconds, microseconds times 1e-6 and nanoseconds times
  1e-9, so 4.505 s is `4 + 505000e-6` where epoch seconds give
  4.505000114 and print as 4.51), the mean as pandas' compensated sum over
  the count and the deviation as Welford's sample deviation (0 for one
  pair). A missing timestamp raises `the timestamp column should not
  contain any empty value.`. Before: 2 of 40 interleaved uploads differed.
- **BH1-3 The LLM declare description on uploads.** pm4py's DataFrame
  declare discovery reads each case as the frame's rows from the case's
  first row on, as many as the case has, without sorting: with `x[a]`,
  `y[c]`, `x[b]` in file order, `x` is read as `a, c` and `y` as `c`
  (`Exactly 1: c`, `Existence: c`, `Non Succession: ('c', 'a')`, `Non
  Chain succession: ('c', 'a')`). Minera read each trace's own rows.
  Before: 36 of 40 interleaved uploads differed (templates and pairs
  compared as sets, as their order follows the hash seed).
- **BH1-4 Top-k and coverage variant filters on XES uploads.**
  `filter_variants_top_k`, `filter_variants_by_coverage_percentage` and the
  maximum coverage filter count and rank variants over the same slices as
  BH1-3 (each case read from its first row on, as many rows as it has),
  then keep the cases whose own variant is among the chosen ones: with
  `x a`, `y a`, `x b`, `y b`, `z c`, `w d` in file order the slices are
  `(a, a)`, `(a, b)`, `(c)`, `(d)`, once each, so the top variant is `(d)`
  and keeps `w` (Minera kept `x` and `y`, whose own variant `(a, b)`
  occurs twice), and a minimum coverage of 0.4 keeps no case. Minera's
  `top_variants`, `variant_min_coverage` and `variant_max_coverage` now
  count the slices of the surviving rows on a frame (`frame_rows`); CSV
  frames are sorted by case, so their slices are the cases' own rows.
  Before: 84 of 129 interleaved top-k and coverage requests differed.

Re-review of BG without further findings: attribute statistics and case
statistics, passed, cycle and service time and case arrival on interleaved
uploads; the LLM abstractions on interleaved uploads; the date fuzzers
(`mixfuzz5.py`, `mixfuzz6.py`, `mixfuzz7.py`), which read no cell
differently from pandas; the features, root cause and the temporal profile
route on interleaved uploads; the mining filters other than BH1-4
(endpoints, prefixes and suffixes, directly- and eventually-follows,
lengths, admitted variants) on interleaved and plain uploads.

Declarations:

- A comma directly after a clock and before a dotted or dashed date
  (`07:00,13.5.2020`, `00:00:00,01.13.99`) is a date to pandas and stays
  unparsed in Minera, like BG1's clock-first shapes (a column holding one
  stays text, a timestamp column refuses the upload). These are part of
  the refusals counted below; no cell is read differently.
- The open choice from BG1 stays declared: a CSV timestamp column of plain
  numbers is int64 or float64 in pm4py's frame and opaque timestamps in
  Minera.
- The features and the LLM log features on uploads with a key of mixed
  types (`mix`) still follow Python's set order (declared since BC1): on
  interleaved uploads 20 of 180 feature requests and 28 of 60 LLM
  log-features requests matched none of 10 hash seeds or raised on one
  side only, all on that key.

## Review BI1: re-review of round BH, `/api/mine`'s declare and temporal profile on uploads, and the row-changing filters on XES frames (2026-11-12)

Round BI re-reviewed BH (the LLM log skeleton, temporal profile and declare
descriptions, and the top-k and coverage variant filters on XES frames) and
took its targets: `/api/mine`'s own `declare`, `log_skeleton` and
`temporal_profile` sections on uploads, the discover-constraints route, the
temporal profile of the behavior route, and the mining filters that change a
case's rows (event projections, prefixes and suffixes, between, the activity
split, consecutive and timestamp grouping, lengths and endpoints) before a
variant filter, on interleaved XES uploads (trace names that repeat apart
from each other), plain XES uploads and CSV uploads. The device check on the
Mac was skipped (the round's thread had no device linked). Findings, all
fixed:

- **BI1-1 Declare discovery on uploads in `/api/mine` and
  discover-constraints.** BH1-3 fixed the LLM description only. pm4py's
  DataFrame `discover_declare` reads each case as the frame's rows from the
  case's first row on, as many as the case has (`x[a]`, `y[c]`, `x[b]` in
  file order read `x` as `a, c` and `y` as `c`), and `/api/mine`'s
  `declare` section and `/api/discover-constraints` on an upload read each
  trace's own rows. Both now discover on those slices
  (`discover_declare_as_uploaded`; a native log keeps its traces). CSV
  frames are sorted by case, so their slices are the cases' own rows.
  Before: 59 of 60 interleaved uploads differed in `/api/mine` and 20 of 20
  in discover-constraints.
- **BI1-2 The EventLog temporal profile's mean and deviation.** pm4py's
  EventLog discovery takes `statistics.mean` and `statistics.stdev` of each
  pair's durations in epoch seconds: both are exact (the sum and the sum of
  squared deviations as fractions) and rounded once. Minera kept a running
  Welford mean and deviation, which differs in the last digits (`a -> b`
  after 180.1 s, 60 s and 420.5 s gives `220.19999996821085` and
  `183.56489316812252`, Welford `220.19999996821088` and
  `183.5648931681225`). The profile now keeps the exact moments of each
  pair (sparse 64-bit words that grow only as far as the durations' bits
  reach) and rounds the mean and the deviation once; a single duration
  gives a deviation of 0 and a non-finite one NaN as before. This reaches
  native logs, the behavior route with `variant=log` and every caller of
  `discover_temporal_profile`. Before: the behavior route's log variant
  differed in the last digits on most uploads.
- **BI1-3 `/api/mine`'s temporal profile on uploads and the behavior
  route's DataFrame variant.** On an upload pm4py discovers the profile on
  the DataFrame (BH1-2's arithmetic: each case's rows stably sorted by
  timestamp, cases by sorted id, durations from pandas' `Timedelta` parts,
  a compensated mean and Welford's deviation). `/api/mine`'s
  `temporal_profile` section on an upload now uses that arithmetic when the
  options are the defaults (activity `concept:name`, one timestamp column,
  no business hours) and the EventLog algorithm otherwise. An upload with
  a missing timestamp, on which every pm4py DataFrame discovery raises
  `the timestamp column should not contain any empty value.`, keeps the
  EventLog algorithm, which skips the event, like the route's other
  sections. The
  behavior route's `variant=dataframe` uses the same arithmetic when its
  source and target timestamps are one column and no business hours are
  set. Before: 48 of 60 plain XES, 40 of 60 CSV and 48 of 60 interleaved
  uploads differed in the last digits, and the behavior route's DataFrame
  variant on most uploads.
- **BI1-4 The activity split on XES uploads.** pm4py's DataFrame
  `activity_split` labels the cases in sorted id order, each from its slice
  of the frame's rows (its first row on, as many as it has), and hands the
  concatenated labels to the frame's rows in row order. On an XES upload
  whose trace names are not in sorted order (`c2`, `c10`, `c1`) or repeat
  apart, a row can take another case's label: `c2[a, b]`, `c10[a, c]`,
  `c1[b, a]` with cut activity `a` and CUT_MODE `this` give
  `c1##@@0: row 0`, `c1##@@1: row 1`, `c10##@@1: rows 2, 3` and
  `c2##@@1: rows 4, 5` (Minera gave each case its own rows). The split's
  sub-cases keep each row's own case attributes when the rows they gather
  came from different cases. Later variant filters count the split frame's
  slices (BH1-4). Before: 40 of 312 interleaved and 17 of 233 plain combined
  requests differed through the split.
- **BI1-5 `filter_between` on interleaved XES uploads.** pm4py's DataFrame
  `filter_between` marks each case's slice in sorted id order, and a later
  case's mark replaces an earlier one's on the rows both slices cover; the
  marked rows keep the frame's order. With `x a`, `y a`, `x b`, `z a`,
  `y c`, `x b`, `w a`, `z b`, `y b` in file order and `a .. b`, `x`'s slice
  (rows 0 to 2: `a, a, b`) marks rows 0 to 2, `y`'s slice (rows 1 to 3:
  `a, b, a`) marks rows 1 and 2, and the result is `x##@@0: row 0` and
  `y##@@0: rows 1, 2`. Minera read each trace's own rows (`x##@@0: rows 0,
  2`, `y##@@0: rows 1, 4, 8`, `z##@@0: rows 3, 7`). Uploads whose cases are
  adjacent (CSV, XES without repeated trace names) are unchanged. Before:
  23 of 312 interleaved combined requests differed through `between`.
- **BI1-6 Consecutive activity grouping on interleaved XES uploads.**
  pm4py's DataFrame `consecutive_act_case_grouping` merges only rows that
  are adjacent in the frame (same case and activity as the row before), so
  `x a`, `y a`, `x a`, `x a` keep `x`'s rows 0 and 2 (`first`) or 0 and 3
  (`last`) and `y`'s row 1; Minera merged `x`'s three rows. Before: 24 of
  312 interleaved combined requests differed through the grouping.

Re-review of BH without further findings: the LLM log skeleton, temporal
profile and declare descriptions on interleaved and CSV uploads, and the
mining filters (BH1-4's variant filters among them) on interleaved and plain
XES uploads. The timestamp case grouping already merged only adjacent rows.
`/api/mine`'s `log_skeleton` section already matched on every upload.

Declarations:

- When an earlier filter (between, lengths, endpoints) leaves no row and a
  later filter runs, pm4py raises `the case ID column should be of type
  string.` on the empty frame; Minera returns an empty log (48 combined
  requests in the sweeps below).
- `/api/variant-statistics` counts each merged case's own variant, as the
  EventLog variants do; pm4py's `get_variants` on an interleaved frame
  counts the slices of BH1-4. Not changed in this round.
- The open choice from BG1 stays declared: a CSV timestamp column of plain
  numbers is int64 or float64 in pm4py's frame and opaque timestamps in
  Minera.

## Review BJ1: re-review of round BI, Declare and temporal conformance on uploads, and the segment filter's between on XES frames (2026-11-12)

Round BJ re-reviewed BI (the Declare discovery and temporal profile on
uploads, the exact EventLog moments, the activity split, between and
consecutive grouping on XES frames) and took its targets with interleaved
XES uploads (trace names that repeat apart from each other), plain XES
uploads and uploads with fractional seconds. The device check on the Mac
was skipped (the round's thread had no device linked). Findings, all fixed:

- **BJ1-1 Declare conformance on uploads.** pm4py's DataFrame
  `conformance_declare` lists one result per case by sorted id, each case
  read as its slice of the frame's rows (from its first row on, as many as
  it has; BI1-1's slices), while its diagnostics table
  (`return_diagnostics_dataframe=True`) reads the merged cases in the
  frame's order. With `x b`, `y c`, `x a`, `w b`, `y c` in file order and
  `existence(a)`, the list gives `w` and `x` (slice `b, c`) one deviation
  each and `y` (slice `c, a`) none, and the diagnostics give `x` (`b, a`)
  none and `y` and `w` one each. `/api/mine`'s `declare_conformance` and
  discover-constraints' conformance list read each trace's own rows; they
  now read the slices (`check_declare_conformance_as_uploaded`), and the
  diagnostics table keeps the merged reading. Before: 5 of 5 interleaved
  uploads differed in `/api/mine`.
- **BJ1-2 The DataFrame temporal conformance's case order.** pm4py's
  DataFrame conformance lists the cases in the order of their first rows
  (an XES upload's frame in file order: `q`, `p`, `r` stay in that order),
  and its EventLog conformance does the same with the traces. Minera's
  DataFrame variant (the behavior route's `variant=dataframe`,
  `/api/temporal-conformance` with `temporal_variant=dataframe`, and the
  table, stream and lazy-table inputs of `conform_temporal_profile`) listed
  them by case id. Within a case the order already matched. Before: the
  order differed on 6 of 6 interleaved and 4 of 6 plain XES uploads (CSV
  frames are sorted by case, so both orders agree there).
- **BJ1-3 The DataFrame temporal conformance's durations.** pm4py's
  DataFrame conformance takes a duration as the pandas `Timedelta` between
  the two timestamps (days times 86,400, plus seconds, microseconds times
  1e-6 and nanoseconds times 1e-9, as BH1-2's discovery), not as the
  difference of epoch seconds its EventLog conformance takes: 0.1 s to
  6:00.314369 is `360.214369` where epoch seconds give
  `360.21436905860901`, and the distance follows. Without business hours
  Minera's DataFrame variant now computes the `Timedelta`; with business
  hours it keeps the EventLog arithmetic. Before: 35 of 40 uploads with
  fractional seconds differed in the elapsed times or distances (2 more
  in the last digits only).
- **BJ1-4 The segment filter's between on interleaved XES uploads.**
  `segment_between_starts`, `segment_between_ends` and
  `segment_between_separator` run pm4py's DataFrame between filter with
  activity lists and a separator, which marks the slices as BI1-5 does: by
  sorted case id, a later case's mark replacing an earlier one's on the
  rows both slices cover, with BI1-5's reopening when the start and end
  lists are equal. With `x a`, `y a`, `x b`, `z a`, `y c`, `x b`, `w a`,
  `z b`, `y b`, starts `a, c`, end `b` and separator `_`, the result is
  `x_0: row 0` and `y_0: rows 1, 2` (Minera read each trace's own rows).
  BI1-5 reached only `between_*`; `filter_between` of the segment filter
  now marks the slices when the frame's cases are not adjacent. Before: 3
  of 58 interleaved requests differed.

Re-review of BI without further findings: the sub-cases of the activity

## Review BK1: re-review of round BJ, Declare on the frame's slices in every upload route, and temporal profiles with a start column, on streams and with other keys (2026-11-12)

Round BK re-reviewed BJ (the Declare conformance list on the frame's case
slices, the DataFrame temporal conformance's case order and `Timedelta`
durations, the segment filter's between on XES frames) and took its
targets with interleaved XES uploads (trace names that repeat apart from
each other), plain XES uploads, uploads with fractional and nanosecond
timestamps, and random toy logs with a completion and a start column. The
device check on the Mac was skipped (the round's thread had no device
linked). Findings, all fixed:

- **BK1-1 XES booleans and plus-signed floats.** `pm4py.read_xes` keeps a
  `<boolean>` as `True` when its value is `true` in any letter case and as
  `False` otherwise (`1`, `yes`, an empty or missing value), and a
  `<float>` with a leading plus (`+1.5`) as the number. Minera kept the
  file's spelling as the attribute's text next to the right typed value,
  so the routes that hand an upload on as a table (the Declare workbench's
  `dataframe` and `lazyframe` shapes, `/api/mine` with
  `mining_input_shape`) refused it with `dataframe JSON: boolean value
  disagrees with typed_value` or `invalid or out-of-range numeric cell`.
  The importer now keeps the text of the value pm4py reads (`true`,
  `false`, `1.5`). The line-by-line, chunk-regex and Rust XES variants
  keep their exact `true` test.
- **BK1-2 Declare on the frame's slices in the remaining upload routes.**
  BI1-1 and BJ1-1 read each case of an XES upload as its slice of the
  frame's rows (from its first row on, as many as it has) in `/api/mine`'s
  `declare` and `declare_conformance` sections and in discover-constraints.
  The Declare workbench's conformance list (`operation=conformance` and
  `conformance_view`, every shape but the event stream; an XES upload
  reaches pm4py as the frame, as AE2-2's case order already assumes) and
  `/api/mine` with `mining_input_shape` (the `declare` and
  `declare_conformance` family results, every shape but the event stream)
  read each trace's own rows. Both now read the slices
  (`discover_declare_frame_slices`, `check_declare_conformance_frame_slices`
  for logs, tables and lazy tables); the workbench's diagnostics table
  keeps the merged cases, as BJ1-1's. Before: `/api/mine` with
  `mining_input_shape` differed in both sections on all 23 interleaved
  uploads tried.
- **BK1-3 The DataFrame temporal profile with a start column.** With
  `START_TIMESTAMP_KEY` naming another column than `TIMESTAMP_KEY`,
  pm4py's DataFrame discovery and conformance sort each case's rows by the
  start, then the completion timestamp, then the row, and pair each row
  with every later row that starts at or after its completion, the
  duration being the `Timedelta` from the completion to the start. Minera's
  DataFrame variant (the behavior route's `variant=dataframe` and
  `lazyframe`, `/api/temporal-conformance`) sorted each case by
  completion and, for discovery, took the EventLog algorithm's pairs and
  arithmetic. With `p`: `a` 50/40, `b`
  20/10, `c` 60/55, `d` 45/45 (completion/start, seconds), pm4py pairs
  `b-a` 20, `b-d` 25, `b-c` 35, `a-c` 5 and `d-c` 10. The EventLog
  conformance also decides whether a target starts before the source
  completes on the exact (nanosecond) timestamps, as pandas compares them.
  Before: on 60 random toy logs, discovery differed on 22 and conformance
  on 26 (DataFrame and lazy-table variants alike); on 15 XES uploads with
  nanosecond start and completion columns, the DataFrame conformance
  differed on 12.
- **BK1-4 The temporal profile of an event stream.** pm4py reads an
  `EventStream` through its EventLog: the cases in the order of their
  first events, each case's events in stream order (unsorted), the
  EventLog algorithm's arithmetic. Minera grouped the stream into a table
  and ran the DataFrame algorithm (each case sorted by time, `Timedelta`
  durations). With case `1`: `a` at 10 s, `b` at 5 s, `c` at 20.25 s in
  stream order, pm4py pairs `a-c` 10.25 and `b-c` 15.25 only. Both
  discovery and conformance of the stream input (the behavior route's
  `variant=stream`) now run on that EventLog. Before: the stream
  conformance differed on 14 of 15 XES uploads with fractional seconds (and
  in the last digits on the 15th).
- **BK1-5 `/api/mine`'s temporal profile with other keys.** BJ1 declared
  that a non-default activity or timestamp key kept the EventLog algorithm;
  pm4py's DataFrame discovery runs on the named columns (text activities,
  date timestamps; BK1-3's sort and pairs with a start column), and
  `discover_temporal_profile_as_uploaded` now does so. The resource and
  the lifecycle, first-class fields of a read log, were not found as an
  activity key (`org:resource`) by the EventLog algorithm. The section's
  activities are now registered in the response's activity list as the
  minimum self-distances' are, where BJ1 declared a refusal of an activity
  outside the directly-follows graph (a resource name, an empty resource,
  which pm4py keys a pair by).
- **BK1-6 Variant statistics on uploads.** `/api/variant-statistics` and
  the CLI's variant statistics count the variants as `get_variants` on the
  frame does, each case read as its slice (BI1 had declared the merged
  reading). With `x b`, `y c`, `x a`, `w b`, `w c`, `y a` in file order
  the variants are `b, c` twice (`x` and `w`) and `c, a` once. Before: 28 of
  30 interleaved uploads differed.

Re-review of BJ without further findings: the Declare conformance list and
diagnostics table after the mining filters and with
`conformance_activity_key` (discover-constraints), the DataFrame temporal
conformance's case order with nanoseconds and separate columns, the
segment filter's between combined with prefix, suffix and the mining
filters.

Declarations:

- The Declare workbench's `stream` shape: pm4py's `conformance_declare`

  `EventStream`; Minera returns the merged cases' results.
- The business-hours temporal profile of a frame whose cases give no pair

## Review BL1: re-review of round BK, the DataFrame temporal profile with missing cells, CSV uploads with a start column and other activity columns, and pm4py on event streams (2026-11-12)

Round BL re-reviewed BK (XES boolean and float text, Declare on the frame's
slices in the workbench and with `mining_input_shape`, the DataFrame
temporal profile with a start column, the stream's temporal profile, the
keyed upload profile, the variant statistics' slices) and took its targets
with random toy logs whose events lack a start, a completion or an
activity, XES uploads with a start column, other activity keys and traces
without a name, CSV uploads with a start column and blank cells, and
pm4py's other functions on an `EventStream`. The device check on the Mac
was skipped (the round's thread had no device linked). Findings, all
fixed:

- **BL1-1 The DataFrame temporal profile with missing cells.** pm4py's
  DataFrame discovery and conformance (the behavior route's
  `variant=dataframe` and `lazyframe`, `/api/temporal-conformance`) read a
  missing cell as NaN or NaT and never raise for it: a row without an
  activity leaves the groups, a row whose start is NaT sorts last and pairs
  only as a source (with an `@@index`, BL1-2), one whose completion is NaT
  sorts after the equal starts and pairs only as a target, and the
  conformance lists every case, even one whose rows cannot pair. Minera's
  table adapters refused such uploads by default (`temporal profile:
  selected dataframe timestamp is missing`), and the lenient path dropped
  the rows without a completion. Before: on 80 toy logs with a quarter of
  the events missing a start or a completion, discovery and conformance
  refused 69 (both table adapters); after: 80 equal.
- **BL1-2 CSV uploads with a start column.** A CSV upload reaches pm4py
  through `format_dataframe`, which copies the upload's timestamp column
  over `time:timestamp`, drops the rows without a case, an activity or a
  timestamp, sorts each case's rows by the timestamp (then file order) and
  numbers them in `@@index`; pm4py's DataFrame algorithms
  pair a row with every row of a higher `@@index` that starts at or after
  its completion, whatever the start order, and read a blank start as NaT.
  Minera paired by the start order only (`frame_index_rows` on
  `TemporalProfileOptions` now carries the CSV reading; a table's own
  `@@index` column is followed too). With `s`: `a` 30/25, `b` 12/2, `c`
  5/20, `d` 40/40 (completion/start, seconds), pm4py pairs `c-a` 20, `c-d`
  35, `b-a` 13, `b-d` 28 and `a-d` 10. Before: on 100 CSV uploads,
  `/api/mine` differed on 19, the behavior route refused 57 and differed on
  4 more, the conformance differed on 61; after: 300 equal.
- **BL1-3 `/api/mine`'s keyed temporal profile with missing cells.** BK1-5
  kept the EventLog algorithm whenever a cell of the named columns was
  missing; pm4py's DataFrame discovery reads them as BL1-1 describes, and
  `discover_temporal_profile_as_uploaded` now does. Before: on 60 uploads
  (interleaved, fractional seconds, 3 % of the starts missing), 31 differed
  and 8 differed in the last digits; after: 60 equal.
- **BL1-4 Other activity columns in the keyed temporal profile.** With a
  number, boolean or date column as the activity key (an `<int>`
  `org:resource` with an event without it becomes a float column), pandas
  groups the values that are `==` (1, 1.0 and `True` alike) and pm4py keys
  each pair by them; Minera kept the EventLog algorithm. The DataFrame
  discovery now runs on them, each activity named by `str()` of pm4py's key
  (`1.0`, `True`, `2020-02-02 00:00:00+00:00`). Before: on 60 uploads with
  number, boolean and mixed activity columns, 33 differed (names, and
  values where cells were missing); after: 49 equal and 11 raise in pm4py
  only (declared below).
- **BL1-5 Traces without a name.** An XES trace without `concept:name`
  gives frame rows without a case. pm4py pairs rows by merging the frame
  with itself on the case column, where NaN meets NaN, so all such rows
  form one more case: discovery counts its pairs, and the conformance lists
  it at its first row. Minera dropped those rows (the table adapters, and
  `/api/mine` read each trace as its own case). Before: on 60 toy logs with
  30 % of the traces unnamed (and missing cells), the table adapters refused
  51; after: 58 equal and 2 raise in pm4py only (no trace named, declared
  below).
- **BL1-6 No start column.** When the frame has no start column at all (no
  event of the upload carries the key), pm4py's DataFrame algorithms take
  the completion column as the start; a missing completion column raises
  `KeyError`. Minera refused with `temporal profile: selected dataframe
  column is missing` (the table adapters) or kept the EventLog algorithm
  (`/api/mine`).

Re-review of BK without further findings: XES typed values through the
table transport (odd int, float, boolean and date spellings, `tfuzz.py`),
Declare on the slices in the workbench and with `mining_input_shape`, also
after the mining filters, the start-column sort with business hours
(`tptoy.py --bh`), the stream's temporal profile, the variant statistics
with other activity keys. New area, pm4py's functions on an `EventStream`
(`/api/mine` with `mining_input_shape=stream`, `streamfam.py`): the DFG,
the minimum self-distances, the transition system and the temporal profile
read the stream through its EventLog and match Minera.

Declarations:

- `/api/mine` with `mining_input_shape=stream`: pm4py's
  `discover_log_skeleton` (`UnboundLocalError`), `discover_declare`
  (`TypeError: string indices must be integers`) and
  `discover_process_tree_inductive` (`AttributeError: 'EventStream' object
  has no attribute 'loc'`) raise on an `EventStream`; Minera answers as for
  the log.
- `/api/mine`'s keyed temporal profile where pm4py's DataFrame discovery
  raises: a completion key the frame does not have (`KeyError`), and an
  activity column whose paired values mix dates and numbers (pandas cannot
  sort the groups: `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of
  'datetime.datetime' and 'float'`). Minera keeps the EventLog algorithm so
  that the rest of the response stands.
- An XES upload where no trace has a name: pm4py's frame has no case
  column and the DataFrame temporal profile raises `KeyError`; Minera
  answers with all rows as one case. A CSV start column that is blank in
  every row: pandas reads it as floats and pm4py raises `TypeError`;
  Minera returns an empty profile.
- The CSV timestamp columns of plain numbers and "roles to diagnostics
  groups" (round AT) are still with Philipp.

## Review BM1: re-review of round BL, the DataFrame DFG adapters on uploads, XES traces without a name and CSV uploads on the DataFrame shapes (2026-11-12)

Round BM re-reviewed BL (the DataFrame temporal profile with missing cells,
CSV uploads with a start column, the `mark_frame_index_rows` call sites)
with fresh seeds and took its targets: pm4py's DataFrame DFG adapters
(`df_statistics.get_dfg_graph`, `get_partial_order_dataframe`,
`get_concurrent_events_dataframe`, `/api/dfg-dataframe`) on CSV and XES
uploads with a start column, blank cells, sub-second and nanosecond times
and traces without a name; `/api/mine` with `mining_input_shape=dataframe`
and `lazyframe` on XES traces without a name and on CSV uploads. The device
check on the Mac was skipped (the round's thread had no device linked).
Findings, all fixed:

- **BM1-1 The DataFrame DFG adapters on a CSV upload.** pm4py reads a CSV
  upload through `format_dataframe`: the rows without a case, an activity
  or a timestamp dropped, the others sorted by case id, then the upload
  timestamp, then file order, with `@@index` and `@@case_index` (a CSV's
  own columns of those names are overwritten). `/api/dfg-dataframe`
  (pandas) read the upload's table in file order, so the partial order
  followed the wrong `@@index`. It now reads that frame
  (`csv_frame_table`). Also: a blank start cell is NaT (Minera refused it
  as an unparsable time); a NaT target start gives a NaN flow, which pm4py
  clamps to 0; and the pandas errors are raised where pm4py raises them:
  a start column without any value (`'>=' not supported between instances
  of 'float' and 'Timestamp'`), starts but no directly-follows pair
  (`cannot subtract DatetimeArray from ndarray[object]`), the partial order
  without any start (`Invalid comparison between dtype=datetime64[us, UTC]
  and ndarray`, `ns` for a nanosecond frame), and concurrent events with
  starts but no case of two candidate rows (`Invalid comparison between
  dtype=timedelta64[us] and int`). A row without an activity never pairs
  there, and without column reduction neither does a row with any null; an
  empty frame keeps the start column's type (a start read from the
  completion column is a datetime column, a CSV start blank in every row a
  float one). The older `minera_dfg_dataframe_tests` case of one row
  without an activity expected no pair; pandas raises, and the test now
  expects that.
- **BM1-2 Sort order.** With `sort_timestamp_along_case_id=False`, pandas
  sorts by the case only with numpy's unstable introsort (`nargsort`
  quicksort), so a case of more than 16 rows leaves in that order, not the
  file's; Minera kept the file order. The stable sort puts the rows without
  a case last, as pandas does with NaN.
- **BM1-3 Nanosecond and float times.** A frame with a value of more than
  six fractional digits is `datetime64[ns]`, and the adapters compare
  completions and starts at nanoseconds there (Minera compared
  microseconds, so `00:02:50.000000001` equalled `00:02:50`). The
  concurrent overlap is the difference of `Timestamp.timestamp()` floats
  (each rounded to six decimals); `frame_times::epoch_seconds` now divides a
  nanosecond time correctly rounded before that rounding.
- **BM1-4 Rows without a case in the self-merge.** On an XES frame with
  unnamed traces, pandas' merge on the case column matches NaN with NaN, so
  the partial order and concurrent events pair rows of different unnamed
  traces; Minera dropped them.
- **BM1-5 The temporal profile on a CSV with its own `@@index` (re-review
  of BL1-2).** `format_dataframe` overwrites the column, so the frame's
  index orders the pairs; Minera used the CSV's column (`own_index` now
  needs no frame timestamp). Found with `tpcsv2.py --ownidx`, which adds
  such a column of random numbers.
- **BM1-6 XES traces without a name on the DataFrame shapes.** `/api/mine`
  with `mining_input_shape=dataframe` or `lazyframe` on an interleaved XES
  upload with unnamed traces failed as a whole (`presentation_error:
  Declare conformance must contain one result per trace`): the Declare
  frame slices dropped the rows without a case. They now keep their place,
  each such trace its own case (37 of 40 uploads failed before, none
  after).
- **BM1-7 CSV uploads on the DataFrame shapes.** pm4py's DataFrame
  functions read the sorted frame of BM1-1; `/api/mine` with
  `mining_input_shape=dataframe` or `lazyframe` gave its families the
  upload's table in file order, and Declare, Declare conformance, the log
  skeleton and its conformance, alpha and the transition system depend on
  the row order. A CSV upload and the same upload with its rows already in
  the frame's order (the same frame for pm4py) gave different results in
  16 to 19 of 20 uploads for these families; against pm4py, Declare was
  equal on 1 of 5. The families now read the frame's rows
  (`prepare_csv_frame_view`).

Declarations:

- pm4py's high-level DataFrame functions (`discover_declare`,
  `discover_log_skeleton`, `discover_temporal_profile`, and every other
  `discover_*` but `discover_footprints`) refuse a frame with an empty case
  id (`the case ID column should not contain any empty value.`), such as an
  XES upload with unnamed traces; Minera answers with each unnamed trace as
  its own case, as its log does.
- `/api/dfg-dataframe` on an XES upload where no trace has a name: the
  frame has no case column and pm4py raises `KeyError`; Minera answers (the
  performance graph raises its own error). An XES upload without any start
  attribute: both raise, with different messages.
- Concurrent events on a CSV upload whose start values sit only in rows
  `format_dataframe` drops (an empty frame with a datetime start column):
  pandas raises its `timedelta64` comparison error, Minera returns no pair.
  (Fixed in review BN1-6: the frame declares its columns' dtypes.)
- The CSV timestamp columns of plain numbers and "roles to diagnostics
  groups" (round AT) are still with Philipp.

Verification (scripts in the project files under `review-harness/round-bm/`):

| Check | Comparisons | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `/api/dfg-dataframe` on CSV uploads, the pandas graph (frequency and performance), partial order and concurrent events (`dfgdf.py`: during the round about 3,000 uploads with blank and `NA` cells, fractions, nanoseconds, no start column, other aggregations, windows, sort and strictness options; final run on fresh seeds: 100 `--blank --frac --extra`, 100 `--blank --ns --nostart --extra`, 100 `--blank`) | 1,200 (final) | before: the partial order on the file's `@@index`, blank starts refused, the four pandas errors missing, ns compared as us; final: 1,174 equal, 26 raise on both sides with the same message |
| `/api/dfg-dataframe` on XES uploads with unnamed traces (`dfgxes.py --nocase --extra`: about 360 during the round; final run 60) | 240 (final) | 220 equal or raising alike; 20 on the 5 uploads where no trace has a name (pm4py `KeyError`; declared) |

| `/api/mine` DataFrame shapes on CSV uploads with blank cells and shuffled rows vs pm4py on `format_dataframe(read_csv)` (`minecsv.py`: 60 as DataFrame, 60 as LazyFrame with start and resource columns) | 480 | before: Declare 1 of 5 equal; after: 480 equal (Declare, its conformance, temporal profile, log skeleton) |

| Re-review of BL: `tpcsv2.py --ownidx` (80), `--blank --dual --ownidx` (80), `tptoy2.py --miss --nocase` (60), `tpkeys.py --il --frac --num` (60) | 680 | before: the CSV's own `@@index` ordered the pairs; after: equal except pm4py-only errors (an all-blank start column, no trace named, mixed date and number keys; declared) |
| Full ctest, script tests, frontend typecheck and tests, fixture replay | 471 tests, 406 script tests, 10,729 frontend tests, 2,673 responses of 16 manifests | 471 pass, 406 pass, 10,729 pass; 2,667 responses unchanged, 6 active-source CSV fixtures on the DataFrame and LazyFrame shapes rewritten (BM1-7: their families now read the frame's order, e.g. `A` at 10:00 before `B` at 10:01 where the file lists `B` first) |

`minera_review_bm1_tests` binds the DataFrame DFG adapters on a CSV frame
(a blank start, the four pandas errors, the case-only introsort, a
nanosecond partial order, a `Timestamp.timestamp()` overlap, rows without
a case in the self-merge), the temporal profile on a CSV's own `@@index`,
and the Declare frame slices with rows without a case (values taken from
pm4py black-box on the same inputs).

## Review BN1: re-review of round BM, CSV uploads on the session routes and workbenches in the frame's order, batches, heuristics and the DFG adapters on CSV frames (2026-11-12)

Round BN re-reviewed BM (the DataFrame DFG adapters on uploads,
`csv_frame_table`, `prepare_csv_frame_view`, the Declare frame slices) with
fresh seeds and took its targets: every other route that hands a CSV
upload to a pm4py DataFrame function (the analysis, timing, constraint,
graph, workflow and conversion routes on the session, the original Declare
and log skeleton routes, the token-replay and alignment workbenches), the
interval statistics (`overlap`) and batches with a start column, the DFG
adapters without column reduction, and the heuristics miner keyed by a
CSV's own columns. The device check on the Mac was skipped (the round's
thread had no device linked). Findings, all fixed:

- **BN1-1 Session routes and workbenches on a CSV upload read the file's
  order.** pm4py reads a CSV upload through `format_dataframe` (BM1-1),
  whose rows are sorted by case id, upload timestamp and file order. The
  session routes `/api/analyze-behavior` (minimum self-distances, pandas
  and Polars), `/api/discover-timing` (batches and performance spectrum,
  DataFrame and LazyFrame variants), `/api/discover-constraints`,
  `/api/discover-graph` (transition system), `/api/discover-workflow`,
  `/api/log-convert`, the literal-controls route and the original Declare
  and log skeleton routes, and the token-replay, alignment and replay
  duration workbenches on the DataFrame, LazyFrame and stream shapes, read
  the upload's table (or its stream) in file order. A CSV upload and the
  same rows already in the frame's order (the same frame for pm4py) gave
  different answers. They now read the frame (`session_selected_view`,
  `cached_source_view`, `adapter_source_table`, `csv_frame_stream`; a
  session builds it once and its copies share it).
- **BN1-2 The frame's date columns.** `format_dataframe` converts the
  timestamp column and every other column of date texts to
  `datetime64[us, UTC]`, or `datetime64[ns, UTC]` when any cell, including
  those of rows it then drops, has more than six fractional digits; the
  pandas batches divide the column's integers by 1e9 (seconds over a
  thousand for a microsecond column). The frame now declares these dtypes
  (Minera's pandas batches on a CSV upload read seconds).
- **BN1-3 The batches' default event id.** Without an event-id key the
  pandas and Polars batches take the frame's `@@index` column, when it has
  one, as the event id, so two rows alike in every other value stay two
  events; Minera made them one. The table adapters now do the same, and a
  CSV upload's batches read the frame with its index columns.
- **BN1-4 Batches with a start column.** pm4py takes an event that starts
  after it completes as it is (all three variants), and the pandas batches
  read a blank start (NaT) as the smallest datetime (`-9223372036.854776`);
  Minera refused both (`start timestamp is after completion`, `configured
  start timestamp is missing`). A blank resource cell is NaN there: the
  pandas batches drop the row, the Polars ones group it under a null
  resource; Minera grouped it under `""`. The older
  `minera_temporal_behavioral_tests` case expected the inverted event to
  be refused; it now expects pm4py's batch (one concurrent batch of the
  five events, the inverted one kept as it is).
- **BN1-5 The heuristics miner on a CSV upload's table shapes.** The table
  read as events keeps the activity column as the first-class activity
  under its own name; the heuristics miner and the model decoration keyed
  by that name (`act`) refused every event (`event is missing activity
  attribute 'act'`), so the heuristic family (and the footprints bundle
  after it) failed on every CSV upload mined as a DataFrame or LazyFrame.
  They now read it, as pm4py reads the frame's column.
- **BN1-6 The DFG adapters on CSV frames (re-review of BM1-1).** A frame
  emptied by `format_dataframe` (every row without a case) keeps the
  column types read before the drop: its start column is a datetime
  column, so the partial order is empty and the concurrent events raise
  pandas' `timedelta64` comparison error, with the unit of the dropped
  rows' digits; Minera treated it as a start column without values (the
  float-column error, BM's declared case). Likewise a frame whose rows'
  start values all sat in dropped rows: the performance graph clamps the
  NaT flows to 0 where Minera raised the float-column error. Without
  column reduction pandas
  drops a row with a NaN in any column, and a blank or NA cell of a CSV's
  other columns is NaN there; Minera read it as a value, so the concurrent
  events kept pairs pm4py drops.

Declarations:

- The `overlap` family runs pm4py's three interval statistics (interval
  events, cases, concurrent activities) as one analysis, so an error in
  one fails the family. pm4py's interval-event statistic raises on an
  event that starts after it completes and its interval-event and case
  statistics on a blank (NaT) start (`NaTType does not support
  timestamp`), while its case and concurrent statistics accept the
  inverted event and its concurrent statistic compares a NaT start as
  false. Minera refuses the event for the family (`overlap: start
  timestamp is after completion timestamp`, `overlap: invalid start
  timestamp`).
- With field trimming (`trim_fields`, the default) a whitespace-only CSV
  cell is blank, so the DFG adapters without column reduction drop its
  row; pandas keeps the text `" "`.
- The batches' log variant on a CSV upload groups a blank resource under
  `""`; pm4py's log holds NaN there and groups it under `nan` (an XES
  event without the attribute raises `KeyError`).

Verification (scripts in the project files under `review-harness/round-bn/`;
"before" is round BM's server on the same scripts):

| Check | Comparisons | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Metamorphic file order on the session routes (`metaroute.py`: MSD, correlation, temporal profile, constraints, batches, spectrum, transition system, footprints, alpha, heuristic, inductive, POWL, conversions, DFG; 25 uploads as DataFrame with a resource column, 20 as LazyFrame, 20 as stream) | 1,885 | before (20 uploads): 177 of 580 differed (batches, constraints, conversions, MSD, spectrum, transition system, workflow discovery); after: 1,798 the same, 87 raise alike |
| Metamorphic file order on the workbenches (`metawb.py`: token replay, alignments, Declare and log skeleton conformance on every shape, 20 uploads) | 320 | before (10 uploads): 140 of 160 differed (every shape but the log); after: all the same |
| Metamorphic file order on the whole `/api/mine` response (`metamine.py`: 20 as DataFrame, 15 as LazyFrame with a start column and pandas batches) | 35 responses | every field and family the same |
| Batches vs pm4py (`batchcsv.py`: 30 plain, 30 with blank cells, 30 with a start column and blanks, 30 with a start column and nanoseconds; pandas, Polars, log) | 360 | before (90 uploads): 92 of 270 equal; after: 322 equal, 38 raise on both sides (Polars and log on a blank start) |
| Minimum self-distances vs pm4py (`msdcsv.py --blank`, 30 uploads, three variants) | 90 | before (20 uploads): 43 of 60 equal; after: all equal |
| Heuristics net vs pm4py (`heurcsv.py --blank`: 30 as DataFrame, 20 as LazyFrame; DFG, dependencies, start and end activities, occurrences) | 250 | before (20 uploads): every upload refused; after: 245 equal, 5 on one upload pm4py refuses (no case left; declared in BM) |
| `/api/dfg-dataframe` vs pm4py (`dfgdf.py`: 140 `--blank --extra`, 40 `--blank --ns --extra`) | 720 | 693 equal, 27 raise alike (the one difference, a start column whose values sat in dropped rows, is fixed and bound in the test) |
| `/api/dfg-dataframe` without column reduction (`dfgnored.py`: 100 with a start column, 30 without; NaN cells in extra columns) | 520 | before (30 uploads): 9 concurrent-event lists differed and 8 raised in pm4py only; after: 473 equal, 47 raise alike |
| Overlap family vs pm4py (`overlapcsv.py`: 30 plain, 30 with blank cells and nanoseconds) | 180 | 138 equal; 14 uploads with an event that starts after it completes fail the family (declared) |
| Round BM's `/api/mine` CSV sweep (`minecsv.py`, 30 plain, 30 with a start column) | 240 | all equal |
| Full ctest, script tests, frontend typecheck and tests, fixture replay | 472 ctests, 406 script tests, 10,729 frontend tests, 2,673 responses of 16 manifests | all pass; 8 active-source fixtures rewritten (heuristic decoration now runs on custom literal selectors, CSV streams in frame order, XES custom clock wait sample) |

`minera_review_bn1_tests` binds the batches' default event id on CSV

## Review BO1: re-review of round BN, standard keys and the frame's own copies on CSV uploads, batches on the frame's typed cells, CSV conversions and the CLI's batches (2026-11-12)

Round BO re-reviewed BN (the session routes and workbenches on CSV frames,
the frame's date dtypes, the batches' `@@index`, NaT starts and inverted
events, the heuristics fallbacks) with fresh seeds and took its targets:
the upload workbenches and session routes on CSV uploads with custom
headers and the standard keys, the batches' log variant with a blank
resource, the conversions of a CSV frame, the CLI's batches on CSV inputs
and `str()` names of non-text keys in the batches. The device check on the
Mac was skipped (the round's thread had no device linked). Findings, all
fixed:

- **BO1-1 The standard keys on a CSV upload with its own headers.**
  `format_dataframe` adds `case:concept:name`, `concept:name` and
  `time:timestamp` as copies of the selected columns, so pm4py reads an
  upload whose columns are `case,act,ts` under the standard keys too.
  Minera's Declare and log skeleton workbenches on the DataFrame and
  LazyFrame shapes, the footprints workbench (`entire_dataframe`,
  `polars_lazyframes`, and its diagnostics case key),
  `/api/discover-constraints` (conformance activity key, diagnostics case
  key) and the alpha and inductive workflow discovery with supplied keys
  refused them (`missing column 'concept:name'`) or answered otherwise than
  for the same upload under the standard headers. A standard key now names
  the selected column on a CSV upload's views (`csv_frame_key`), when that
  column is one of the CSV's (an optional literal column the CSV lacks names
  nothing).
- **BO1-2 A CSV's own `concept:name`, `time:timestamp` or
  `case:concept:name` column.** When the selected columns have other names,
  `format_dataframe` drops the CSV's column of a copy's name and appends the
  copy, so pm4py's frame and its log hold the selected cells under that key.
  Minera's import kept the CSV's column as an event attribute, which
  shadowed the selection: token replay, Declare, the constraints, the DFG,
  the correlation miner, the temporal profile and the transition system read
  the other column's values (activities `X`, `Y`, `Z`). The batch import
  now leaves such a column out, and the frame's column order (the LLM
  abstractions' frame view) is the header without the replaced columns, the
  copies, then `@@index` and `@@case_index` (a CSV's own `@@index` is not
  listed twice).
- **BO1-3 The date unit of rows the frame drops (re-review of BN1-2).** BN
  read the sub-microsecond digits from the upload's table, which lacks the
  rows the import drops (a blank case, for one), so a frame whose only
  nanosecond cell sat in such a row was declared `[us, UTC]`: the pandas
  batches read seconds a thousand times too large there (1 of 60 nanosecond
  uploads), and the DFG concurrent events' error named the wrong unit. The
  import now records the unit of every date column over all data rows
  (`DataFrameColumn::nanoseconds`).
- **BO1-4 The batches on the frame's typed cells.** read_csv types a CSV
  column of numbers as ints, or floats when it has a gap or a decimal, and
  the batches group and name by those values: a numeric resource with a gap
  is `1.0`, ints sort as numbers, a column of numbers or bools selected as
  the activity is `1.5`, `2.0`, `True`. A blank resource is NaN: the log
  variant (a dict of the events' keys) groups pandas' one `np.nan` of a
  text column as `nan`, and sorting it beside a text resource of the same
  activity and batch count raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between
  instances of 'float' and 'str'`; a NaN of a float column is a float of its
  own row and never shares a group. The Polars variant raises `the
  activity column should be of type string.` for such an activity column.
  Minera read the CSV text: labels `1` and `2`, a blank resource grouped
  under `""`, no TypeError and no Polars refusal. The batches' frame (and
  the log variant's events) now hold the typed cells, and a key the frame
  lacks raises `KeyError` in the log variant.
- **BO1-5 Batches with an inverted event in `/api/mine` and the CLI.**
  BN1-4 made the batches take an event that starts after it completes as it
  is, but the analysis output still checked each batch's events against its
  range, so `/api/mine` and the CLI with batches and a start column failed
  the whole response (`batch discovery has invalid event range`). The check
  now accepts such batches (and on a CSV frame no longer compares a group's
  typed labels with the events' text).
- **BO1-6 The CLI's batches on a CSV input.** `minera_export --batches`
  with the pandas and Polars variants read a table made from the log,
  without the frame's `@@index` and date dtypes: pandas gave plain seconds
  where pm4py's microsecond frame gives them scaled down a thousandfold, and
  events alike in every other value collapsed (36 of 40 pandas and 4 of 40
  Polars results differed). The CLI now reads the CSV's frame as the server
  reads an upload (`csv_frame_table.hpp`, shared by both).

Declarations:

- `/api/log-convert` on a CSV upload keeps Minera's representation: the
  event log, stream and table hold the selected cells once, under their
  first-class roles and as CSV text; pm4py's `convert_to_event_log` and
  `convert_to_event_stream` of the frame also hold the standard copies,
  `@@index`, `@@case_index`, typed cells and NaN or NaT for blank cells (as
  the XES downloads, "CSV columns are not repeated" and "CSV attribute
  columns are XES strings"). The rows, their order, their cases,
  activities, timestamps and resources are pm4py's (`convcsv.py`).
- `pm4py.discover_batches` on a DataFrame first runs pm4py's column check
  (an activity column of text without empty values); Minera's pandas
  variant runs the batches algorithm as pm4py's algorithm does without it
  (also the only path with a start column, which `pm4py.discover_batches`
  cannot pass), so it computes on a number or bool activity column. The
  Polars variant checks in both, sometimes with another of the check's
  messages (`should not contain any empty value`, `a required table cell is
  missing`) or another operand order in a TypeError.
- Minera's role names for the batches' keys (`org:resource`, `resource`,
  `activity`, `timestamp`) name the selected column of a CSV upload, or no
  resource (`""`) when the upload selects none; pm4py's frame has no
  `org:resource` column unless the CSV has one and raises `KeyError`. The
  activity and case columns selected at upload stay text in the batches:
  the routes select them for the frame's text copies `concept:name` and
  `case:concept:name`, so pm4py keyed by the column's own name orders ties
  of a number column as numbers where Minera orders them as text (the
  labels are the same), and the Polars case check on an emptied frame
  (whose case column is a float column) is not raised.
- The harness's Polars frames follow `pl.from_pandas` (`nan_to_null`): a
  NaN float is null there, as in Minera's Polars batches.
- The CSV timestamp columns of plain numbers and "roles to diagnostics
  groups" (round AT) are still with Philipp.

## Review BP1: re-review of round BO, the DataFrame spectrum's instants, the CLI's DataFrame modes on CSV inputs and log families keyed by a CSV's own headers (2026-11-12)

Round BP checked BO's CI run, re-reviewed BO (the standard keys and the frame's own copies on
CSV uploads, the batches on the frame's typed cells, the CLI's batches)
with fresh seeds: the metamorphic standard keys on 16 session routes
(`keystd.py`, 60 uploads with and without the CSV's own junk standard
columns, three shapes), the Declare and log skeleton workbenches
(`declcsv.py`, 75 uploads), the batches (`batchcsv.py`, 240 uploads over
eight shapes) and the CLI's batches (`clibatch.py`, 120) answered as pm4py
or raised alike, but for the cases BO declared. It then took BO's targets:
the CLI's other DataFrame modes on CSV inputs and the families that read
the upload's log under a key. The device check on the Mac was skipped (the
round's thread had no device linked). Findings, all fixed:

- **BP1-1 The DataFrame spectrum's instants.** pm4py's DataFrame
  performance spectrum (connected and disconnected) reads the timestamp
  column as its int64 units divided by 1e9: a microsecond column (pandas
  3's default, an XES frame's too) gives the seconds scaled down a
  thousandfold, exactly divided (`1577836.809`), a nanosecond column (a
  CSV with digits below the microsecond, or a typed table declared
  `datetime64[ns, UTC]`) the seconds themselves (`1577836809.1234567`).
  Minera multiplied the parsed seconds by 0.001 whatever the unit: one ulp
  off in about one answer of ten (`1577836.8090000001`), and a nanosecond
  frame's instants a thousandfold too small, on the server's spectrum route
  and in the CLI. The LazyFrame variants read epoch microseconds over 1e6,
  so a nanosecond cell is truncated (`1577836809.123456`); Minera kept the
  nanoseconds. The DataFrame components now compute the instant from the
  cell's exact units and the column's declared unit (`frame_instant`), the
  LazyFrame ones from its truncated microseconds.
- **BP1-2 The CLI's DFG adapters and spectrum on a CSV input.**
  `minera_export --dfg-dataframe-output` and the DataFrame and LazyFrame
  spectrum variants read a table made from the log: the partial order with
  a start column paired the log's rows instead of the frame's `@@index`
  (12 to 23 of 30 answers differed), and the spectrum had no datetime unit.
  The CLI now reads the CSV's frame as the server reads an upload
  (`csv_input_source`): the pandas adapters with `@@index` and the NaN cells
  null, the Polars ones on the frame, the standard keys naming the selected
  columns (`csv_frame_key`).
- **BP1-3 Log families keyed by a CSV's own column headers.** pm4py reads
  `activity_key="act"` (or `"res"`, or a start and completion column) on a
  CSV upload's frame as that column. Minera's rework, chaotic activities,
  variant statistics, boundary activities, trace clustering, decision
  replay and interval overlap looked the key up among the events' attributes
  only, where the import keeps the selected columns under their roles, and
  refused it (`event is missing activity attribute 'act'`, `invalid
  completion timestamp`), in the CLI and on the server's routes. They now
  read the selected column through its source key
  (`reference_selected_field`); passed and service time already did (their
  frame path).
- **BP1-4 Round BO's Windows build.** BO's CI run (43293820797) passed on
  Linux and macOS but MSVC refused `minera_export.cpp`: the CLI's frame
  helper took the input as `std::string`, and a `std::filesystem::path`
  does not convert to it on Windows (`error C2664`). The helpers now take
  the path.

Declarations:

- pm4py's log variants on a CSV upload read its frame's log, whose
  timestamps are pandas `Timestamp`s: `Timestamp.timestamp()` rounds to
  microseconds, so a cell with nanosecond digits is `1577837040.123457`
  there; Minera's log variants keep the parsed nanoseconds
  (`1577837040.1234567`; 2 of 30 nanosecond uploads in the spectrum's log
  variants).
- The DataFrame routes keyed by a number column (the frame's typed cells
  beyond the batches) read its cells as text: pm4py's pandas minimum
  self-distances and spectrum raise `TypeError` on an int activity column,
  and the Polars minimum self-distances name a float column's activities
  `1.0`.
- The CSV timestamp columns of plain numbers and "roles to diagnostics
  groups" (round AT) are still with Philipp.

Verification (scripts in the project files under `review-harness/round-bp/`;
"before" is round BO's CLI and server on the same scripts and seeds):

| Check | Comparisons | Result |
|---|---|---|
| CLI spectrum (four DataFrame and LazyFrame variants) and MSD (pandas, Polars) on CSV inputs vs pm4py on the frame (`clidf.py`: 30 plain, 30 with fractional and nanosecond cells, 30 with blanks and the CSV's own keys) | 540 | before: 16 DataFrame answers an ulp off, 22 a thousandfold too small, 6 LazyFrame answers with untruncated nanoseconds; after: all equal, 3 raise alike; MSD equal before and after |
| Server spectrum route vs pm4py (`spectsrv.py`: 30 nanosecond CSV uploads, 30 fractional XES uploads, 30 CSV uploads with blanks as LazyFrame; six variants) | 540 | before: 42 DataFrame and 4 LazyFrame answers differed; after: all equal but 4 log answers with nanosecond cells (declared) |
| CLI DFG adapters (graph, partial order, concurrent events) on CSV inputs vs pm4py's `df_statistics` on the frame (`clidfg.py`: 30 with a start column, 30 with blanks and options, 30 with nanoseconds) | 360 | before: 56 of 90 partial orders differed; after: all equal, 1 raises alike |
| CLI log families keyed by the CSV's own headers vs the standard keys, and rework by resource vs pm4py (`clikeys.py`: 40 uploads, with and without blanks; nine checks) | 360 | before: 276 refused or differed; after: all the same or equal, 4 clusterings raise alike |
| CLI activity position summary (pandas, log) vs pm4py (`clipos.py`, 80 uploads) | 160 | all equal |
| BO's sweeps re-run on fresh seeds (`keystd.py`, `declcsv.py`, `batchcsv.py`, `clibatch.py`) | about 2,500 | all the same, equal or raise alike, but the cases BO and BL declared |
| Full suites: ctest, script tests, frontend tests, fixture replay | 474 ctests, 406 script tests, 10,729 frontend tests, 2,673 responses of 16 manifests | all pass; one active-source fixture recaptured (a typed table declared `datetime64[ns, UTC]`: its DataFrame spectrum is in seconds, as pandas gives it) |

`minera_review_bp1_tests` binds the DataFrame spectrum's instants on
microsecond, nanosecond and undeclared columns, the LazyFrame truncation,
and the rework, variant statistics, chaotic activities, start activities
and overlap keyed by a CSV's own headers.

## Review BQ1: re-review of round BP, the log families on nanosecond CSV cells, CSV headers in the tree and Petri lookups, and the CLI's temporal profile and correlation (2026-11-12)

Round BQ checked BP's CI run (43304285286: Linux, macOS, the frontend, the
script tests and the verifier passed; the Windows build passed with BP's
MSVC fix and its ctest, still running when the round closed, passed
afterwards: all six jobs of the run are green, as round BR checked),
re-reviewed BP (the DataFrame spectrum's `frame_instant`, the CLI's
`csv_input_source` callers, the `reference_selected_field` fallbacks) on
fresh seeds, and took BP's targets: the lookups BP left unchanged on a CSV's
own headers, the log families on nanosecond cells, and the CLI's remaining
CSV modes. The device check on the Mac was skipped (the round's thread had
no device linked). Findings, all fixed:

- **BQ1-1 The spectrum's log variants on nanosecond cells.** pm4py's log
  variants read the frame's log, whose instants are `Timestamp.timestamp()`
  (rounded to the microsecond: `1577836805.123457`), and sort a trace by the
  exact `datetime64` (two cells tens of nanoseconds apart sort apart, though
  they are one double). Minera kept the parsed nanoseconds
  (`1577836805.1234567`) and sorted by the double, so ties followed the
  file. The log components now sort by the exact instant (`order_key`) and
  give a nanosecond cell's instant rounded to the microsecond
  (`log_instant`); the DataFrame and LazyFrame components sort by the exact
  instant too. This withdraws BP's declaration on the spectrum's log
  variants.
- **BQ1-2 The temporal profile and its conformance on logs and streams.**
  pm4py's EventLog discovery and conformance take differences of
  `Timestamp.timestamp()` floats (`a>b=60.86419701576233`, where the exact
  difference is `60.864197532`). Minera's log and stream variants on a
  nanosecond CSV upload took differences of the exact seconds: 27 of 30
  uploads differed in discovery and conformance, with and without a start
  column. The log path now reads a nanosecond cell as the rounded float
  (`event_instant` with `python_epoch`); the DataFrame variants keep the
  exact units.
- **BQ1-3 The CLI's temporal profile.** `minera_export` ran the EventLog
  discovery on a CSV input, where the server's mine route reads the upload
  as pm4py's DataFrame: 24 of 30 plain inputs gave the log's answer (ulps
  off) and 29 of 30 inputs with nanosecond cells, blanks and a start column
  differed. The CLI now calls `discover_temporal_profile_as_uploaded`, as
  the server does.
- **BQ1-4 The correlation miner's durations.** pm4py's correlation miner, on
  a DataFrame and on a log, reads `Timestamp.timestamp()` floats; Minera
  read the exact seconds, so every variant's performance DFG on a
  nanosecond upload was an ulp or more off (20 of 25 uploads in each of 12
  variant and adapter pairs on the server, 110 of 120 answers in the CLI).
  The selected timestamps now round a nanosecond cell to the microsecond
  (`python_epoch_seconds`); sorting stays on those floats and the input
  order, as pandas' stable sort of the rounded column.
- **BQ1-5 Tree reduction keyed by a CSV's own headers.**
  `/api/reduce-process-tree` with `activity_key=act` (or `res`) raised
  `event is missing activity attribute` on every CSV upload: the reduction
  looked the key up among the events' attributes only, and the cached
  Inductive log projects the miner's key over the selected header. The
  reduction now reads a selected column through its source key
  (`reference_selected_field`), and the route prepares the Inductive log
  under an explicit key other than the miner's (`inductive_log_for_key`):
  `act` gives the `concept:name` answer, `res` pm4py's reduction on the
  resource column.
- **BQ1-6 The Petri usage comparison with an explicit key.**
  `/api/compare-petri` on the Inductive model with `activity_attribute=act`
  failed on all 40 swept uploads: the reference and the session log were
  prepared under the miner's key, which hid the header. Both logs are now
  prepared under the explicit key, so `act` gives the `concept:name` answer.

Checked without findings: the CLI's transition system on CSV inputs (three
views, both directions, windows 1 to 3, with and without blanks) against
pm4py's states and transitions; DFG precision, alpha and heuristics keyed by
a CSV's own headers and DFG precision on the resource column; cycle time,
case arrival and dispersion on nanosecond uploads; BP's CLI sweeps (DataFrame
and LazyFrame spectrum, MSD, the DFG adapters, the header-keyed log families)
on fresh seeds.

Declarations:

- pm4py's correlation LP (cvxopt) sometimes returns a frequency plan that is
  not optimal: on 2 of 25 nanosecond uploads (and 2 of 40 CLI inputs) its
  classic and classic_split plans cost more under pm4py's own cost matrix than the optimum (scipy's
  `linprog`, `3614.74` against `3609.24`), while the precede-succeed and
  duration matrices are identical to Minera's. Minera returns the optimal
  plan. Plans that differ while both are optimal are the transportation
  ties declared with the correlation miner.
- Case statistics on a nanosecond column: pm4py's `startTime` and `endTime`
  are the int64 units floor-divided by 10**9, whole seconds there (the
  microsecond case is round AW's declaration); Minera keeps the epoch
  seconds.
- Number-keyed DataFrame routes stay as BP declared them; the CSV timestamp
  columns of plain numbers and "roles to diagnostics groups" (round AT) are
  still with Philipp.

Verification (scripts in the project files under `review-harness/round-bq/`;
"before" is round BP's CLI and server on the same scripts and seeds):

| Check | Comparisons | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Spectrum (six variants) on the server vs pm4py (`spectsrv.py` of round BP: 40 CSV uploads with fractional and nanosecond cells, 30 XES uploads) | 420 | before (the CSV uploads): 6 log answers differed; after: all equal, 2 raise alike |
| Temporal profile and conformance on `/api/analyze-behavior` (log, stream, DataFrame, LazyFrame) vs pm4py (`tpns.py`: 30 nanosecond uploads, 30 with a start column) | 480 | before: 216 log and stream answers differed; after: all equal |
| CLI and server temporal profile vs pm4py's DataFrame discovery (`clitp.py`: 30 plain inputs, 30 with nanoseconds, blanks and a start column) | 120 | before: 25 CLI answers equal to the log's, 29 differed; after: all equal |
| Correlation on `/api/analyze-behavior` (three variants, four adapters) vs pm4py (`corrsweep.py`: 25 CSV uploads of whole seconds, 25 with fractional and microsecond cells, 25 with nanosecond cells, 25 XES uploads) | 1,200 | before: 240 nanosecond performance DFGs differed; after: 1,144 equal, 16 frequency plans where pm4py's is not optimal (declared) and 40 where both are optimal (declared ties) |
| CLI correlation (three variants) vs pm4py (`clicorr.py`, 40 nanosecond inputs) | 120 | before: 110 performance DFGs differed; after: 115 equal, 4 suboptimal pm4py plans, 1 optimal tie |
| Lookups keyed by a CSV's own headers (`hdrkeys.py`, 40 uploads: tree reduction, Petri comparison, DFG precision, alpha, heuristics with `act` vs `concept:name`; tree reduction and DFG precision on `res` vs pm4py) | 277 | before: 120 refused (tree reduction and Petri comparison); after: all the same or equal |
